Title: Kunstig ø skal være gigantisk batteri for vindmøllestrøm
Full text:
A Dutch advisory firm proposes to build an artificial island surrounded by wind turbines. They have to pump water from a lake in the middle of the island into the sea when the wind blows. During quiet periods, the water flows back to the lake and drives the island's turbines.

The Dutch counseling and testing company Kema has drawn a proposal for an artificial island that can serve as a much needed warehouse for wind turbine power.

The island must be 10 kilometers long and six kilometers wide, so there will be plenty of room to set up wind turbines. In the middle of the island lies a giant lake that is functioning as a battery.

When the wind blows, the wind turbines pump water out of the lake to the surrounding sea. In quiet weather where there is a need to generate electricity, the water flows back into turbines.

According to the Dutch advisers, the lake will be able to deliver 1,500 MW for at least 12 hours, which corresponds to a large power plant.

For the time being, however, there are very initial studies, but Kema finds that the pumps to the lake are at least commercially available today. A later retail study must, among other things, offer where it should be, and then it may be that the stable and environmentally friendly energy supply will also be appreciated.

Kema has devised the concept with the support of a number of energy companies.

Title: Kunstige energiøer skal gemme vindkraften
Full text:
Danish architectural firm launches the concept of artificial islands with basins in the middle, which are pumped empty when there is excess of electricity and is filled when more power is needed.

The Danish company Gottlieb Paludan Arkitekter now offers a different suggestion of how excess wind turbine power can be stored.

According to the company, it must be done on artificial islands around the Danish waters, where large water pools in the middle of the island are emptied when there is wind power in surplus and is filled with flowing seawater when there is a lack of electricity. The flowing water drives some turbines that produce electricity.

The project is presented at the large energy and climate conference Nordic Climate Solutions in the Bella Center today, Tuesday.

For example, the architectural firm - with the help of Risø DTU - has expected that an artificial island south of Avedøre with a size of 4.9 square kilometers will be able to accommodate a 22.3 million cubic meter water pool.

The bottom of the basin is 40 meters below sea level, and you operate with a fall height of at least 25 meters. Thus, the warehouse will be able to produce 2300 MWh power from empty to filled basin. This corresponds to MAKS capacity from the Avedøre plant for three hours.

"At the same time, the idea is that the island and the basin can be utilized for algae production, energy arrows and possibly a solar power plant," says communications manager Sten Søring from Gottlieb Paludan Architects.

Obviously in connection with bridge buildings
He adds that there are many options for placing such artificial warehouses in the Danish waters - not least in connection with bridge buildings, where these islands are still being built.

The project expects an energy loss of about 25 percent in this storage method, which according to Sten Søring is at the pessimistic end of the known estimates of "pumped hydro" called the storage technique.

The architects have not yet counted the economy of the project, but this must be done now - together with studies of construction methods and formalities about building artificial islands at sea.

At the same time, together with Risø and a Dutch company, Kema, which has previously launched the idea of ​​storing wind turbine power in artificial islands, will look at the possibilities of obtaining EU support to work on the concept.

Title: Tre lande går sammen om kunstig energi-ø midt i Nordsøen
Full text:
The Netherlands, Germany and Denmark are now investigating whether a giant artificial island at Doggerbanke in the middle of the North Sea can make the future expansion of wind energy better and cheaper.

The Netherlands, Germany and Denmark are now joining forces to explore the reason for establishing a six square kilometer artificial 'energy island' with runway and port at Doggerbanke in the North Sea.

On the island, offshore wind farms from different countries in the North Sea must be linked together.

Therefore, on March 23, Danske Energinet.dk signs an agreement with the electricity transmission companies in the Netherlands and Germany, which is called Tennne in both countries, to explore the possibility of making a hub for wind energy in the middle of England, Denmark, the Netherlands and Norway.

This is what Energinet.dk writes in a press release.

"It may sound crazy and science fiction -like, but an island on Doggerbanke can prove to make the wind energy of the future much cheaper and more efficient," says Torben Glar Nielsen, technical director of Energinet.dk.

An island per 30 GW Wind Power
Around the island, several thousand offshore wind turbines can be set up, and the flow from several countries' offshore wind farms can be collected and sent across to consumers in the North Sea countries.

It is imagined that an island will be a hub for maybe 30 GW of wind turbine capacity and that in the long term there will be a total of 70-100 GW wind turbines and perhaps more artificial islands on Doggerbanke, where the water depth is relatively low.

70 GW can supply 80 million Europeans with electricity.

One of the benefits of the island model is that the distance between offshore wind turbines and the network connection becomes shorter, making it possible to use AC Technology.

It can reduce the cost of the expensive DC converters (converter stations) and long cables, which would otherwise be necessary when the parks of the future need to be built further and further out to sea.

At the same time, the submarine cables that will transport the flow from the artificial island to the North Sea countries will be able to act as landing cables and as electric motorways for trade between the countries.

Landing cables are used today approx. half the time because it doesn't always blow. By turning them into commercial cables, they can be used closer to 100 percent.

Less transport time for gear and manpower
There are already a number of electricity cables today that connect the electricity systems in the countries around the North Sea, and they may be able to be linked to the energy island.

The idea of ​​the island is also that spare parts for both converter stations, wind turbines and electric components can be stored on the island.

It will provide much less transport time on the high seas for both equipment and manpower.

The plan for an artificial island at Doggerbanke is fostered by Tennne and is based on the EU's assessment that wind production in the North Sea region can be doubled by 2030.

At the same time, the energy ministers from the North Sea countries last year entered into an agreement to promote the cooperation on offshore wind.

Need large-scale solutions
Torben Glar Nielsen, technical director at Energinet.dk, points out that it is Energinet.dk who is responsible for getting the electricity from the offshore wind turbines ashore and up to consumers.

Therefore, one must constantly press, so that the price of landing and foreign connections also falls:

"Here, innovative large -scale solutions are needed, and here an 'energy hub' in the North Sea is definitely worth investigating very thoroughly," he says.

He adds that as more mills arrive, it will be necessary to look further and further at sea to make room for new offshore wind farms.

Torben Glar Nielsen further explains that the offshore wind farm, which Denmark is erecting on Kriegers Flak in the Baltic Sea, forms the school for a Doggerbanke project.

It connects Danish and German offshore wind farms - while also being used as electric motorways from Denmark to Germany or vice versa.

Furthermore, the Kriegers Flak project links two different electrical systems and frequency areas, the Nordic and central European, with a converter station in Germany.

Title: Havmøllerne får egen ø ved Lolland
Full text:
The company By & Landscape in Nakskov plans to establish an energy island for offshore wind turbines off the coast in the Langeland Belt at the port city of Tårs for a three -digit million.

In fact, you could establish a landmill or an offshore wind farm instead, but with an energy island you get all the benefits of offshore wind turbines and eliminate part of the resistance that is usually around wind turbines.

- There are a lot of prejudices around wind turbines - the whole point of an energy island is that you get all the benefits of offshore wind but not the costs, we put such large offshore wind turbines on land in the sea where they bother far fewer neighbors, explains Philip Rasmussen from City & Landscape.

20 offshore wind turbines on artificial island
The energy island created by curbing and digging out becomes of a non -dear size. It must house up to 20 of the large offshore wind turbines.

The energy island is established at the same time and in immediate connection with the new ferry port in Tårs, which makes the maintenance and repairs of the mills far cheaper than if the mills stood far out on the sea.

- It is somewhat easier for installers and service people to cycle out to the mills when a nut is to be changed rather than a ship being sent out, says Philip Rasmussen.

An energy island to climate trouble
When By & Landscape just chooses the waters off Lolland, it is of course because here you have yourself housed. But it is also because the energy set-up on Lolland, the culture if you will, is the right one.

- We (Lolland, ed.) Produce five times as much power as we use ourselves. Vestas produces at Nakskov Harbor. There is a culture around green stream present that it is easy to talk to our project in, says Philip Rasmussen.

The project costs about DKK 200 million and will create 2500 jobs.

Title: Kunstig energiø i Nordsøen er teknisk mulig: Skal stå klar om 12 år
Full text:
New preliminary study shows that it is technically and economically realistic to build an artificial energy island in the middle of the North Sea with a capacity of up to 15 GW in the early 2030s. Now Danish, German, and Dutch electricity transmission companies reach out to the politicians.

Two years ago, Danske Energinet went together the electricity transmission companies in the Netherlands and Germany to explore the possibilities of establishing a six square kilometer artificial 'energy island' with runway and port at Doggerbanke in the North Sea.

The idea of ​​an energy island in the North Sea is to gather the electricity from several countries' offshore wind farms and send it crosswise to consumers in the North Sea countries.

"It may sound crazy and science fiction-like, but an island on Doggerbanke may prove to make the wind energy of the future much cheaper and more efficient," said Torben Glar, technical director of Energinet, in 2017 about the visions.

Now the International North Sea Wind Power Hub Consortium, which is behind the idea of ​​an energy island, has conducted a number of feasibility studies and preliminary test results.

“The most important thing is that in Denmark and the rest of Europe we have to be converted to 100 percent renewable energy within a short number of years. It requires us to solve the trilemma of energy, ie to ensure security of supply, switch to renewable energy and both at a competitive price. One or more large-scale energy islands are important for solving the trilemma. We can use the energy islands to pick up electricity ashore more efficiently, but also to trade electricity between the countries when it is not blowing, ”says Torben Glar, who is also a steering committee member of the North Sea Wind Power Hub Consortium, today to the Engineer.

On Tuesday, the partners in the International Consortium North Sea Wind Power Hub (NSWPH) present the results of the project's assessment phase. Over the past few months, the consortium has analyzed the possibilities and conditions of establishing one or more energy islands in the North Sea.

The main conclusion is clear: One or more energy islands in the North Sea are both technically and financially feasible, and the ambition is to have the first energy island in operation in the early 2030s.

Significant changes on the way
Although the vision is roughly the same, the project has changed in several areas. The biggest change is that one has moved from one large energy island with a capacity of 30 GW to several smaller energy islands that must be able to collect and act as a node for 10-15 GW wind turbine capacity. The assumption is that in the long term there will be up to 180 GW until the year 2045 at Doggerbanke, where the water depth is relatively low.

»Several smaller islands are more optimal. The further away from the island of the offshore wind turbines, the less optimal the island will function as a distribution center. So we expect 10-15 GW per island and up to 15 islands. In terms of safety, it is also a distributed to have more islands. At the same time, the locations have not yet been determined. Doggerbanke is laid out as Natura 2000 area, and therefore it will not be optimal with a large island in that area, ”says Torben Glar.

70 GW can supply 80 million Europeans with electricity. One of the advantages of the island model is that the distance between offshore wind turbines and the network connection becomes shorter, making it possible to use AC Technology

Defense and the fishermen need to move
In order for the Energy Islands to become a reality, it requires new political agreements across borders, says the consortium behind. Partly because international studies and scenarios show that the current roll-out speed on offshore wind is insufficient to achieve the targets in the Paris Agreement and partly because the space is becoming more cramped in the North Sea.

»The most important prerequisite is that there is a political will to build the necessary offshore wind farms in the North Sea. The energy islands have no function without new offshore wind farms. In the North Sea, there are many different actors today, such as the defense, fishing, and the gas sector. We have all been used to having plenty of space in the North Sea, but when we need so much wind energy, it will be an advantage to be able to identify the most optimal areas for wind. It probably requires political agreements. At the same time, the Dutch, German, English governments must also be involved in a sensible rate of development, so that it will be stable roll -out with lighter project management and better prices, ”says Torben Glar.

In Denmark, Energinet does not have to kick doors in to get the support of the energy island of the new Social Democratic government. In the so -called understanding paper, which the government wrote with its parliamentary basis, one can briefly read:

“A new government will adopt a climate action plan. Among other things, the action plan must also include the following elements: Examination of the possibility of Denmark together with the North Sea countries preparing a common strategy to significantly expand and utilize the offshore wind potential. Explore the possibility of Denmark by 2030 the building world first energy island with a minimum of 10 GW connected. "

The engineer would have liked to have asked Climate Minister Dan Jørgensen (S) about the government's support for an energy island in the North Sea, but the minister canceled the interview with the Engineer at short notice due to a pressed calendar.

Storing energy in the center
In addition to acting as a link between the different national transmission networks, the energy island must also be able to store energy from the offshore wind turbines in the middle of the North Sea. However, what technologies are not determined.

“We must be able to store energy in a technically sound way by 2040-2050, when we only have to use renewable energy. It can be Power to gas (P2G), heat storage or ellager with batteries. We need to investigate what works best, ”says Torben Glar.

Specifically, the consortium looks at how to convert power to gas so that it can be used for fuel on, among other things, ships.

»We look a lot at how we can use the islands to convert electricity to gas, so we can use make a new form of sector coupling where we tie offshore wind turbine power to the transport sector. Then the wind turbines not only become a source of power, but also the source of fuel as hydrogen on ships, ”says Torben Glar.

It can also alleviate bottlenecks on the electricity transmission network to convert the electricity into gas once it has been sent ashore, and then transport the gas to areas with great demand far in land.

However, when the first energy island with a capacity of 10-15 GW can be ready in the early 2030s, it will probably only be electrically connected to land with associated conversion to gas on land. It is not technically possible to make the conversion from electricity to gas out on the artificial island with the available technologies today.

The price depends on where the islands are placed
“We don't have a financial framework ready. It can be a sand island, a concrete foundation that we know from wind turbines, a lower box or steel foundations. We need to look into this when we have appointed the right place. If it is 20 meters of water, it requires one solution, while 40 meters of water provides other conditions. Of course, the big expense will be to build the necessary offshore wind farms to deliver the energy to the island, ”says Torben Glar.

Title: Ørsted: Placér den første energi-ø ved Bornholm
Full text:
The energy company believes that it is more realistic and necessary to build a huge offshore wind farm on an already designated shallow area in the Baltic off Bornholm, from which the current can be distributed to both Denmark, Sweden and Poland.

In the energy agreement from last year, nine parties decided that three new, large offshore wind farms will be built by 2030, of which the first is placed off West Jutland, while it has not yet been decided where the next two parks will be located.

At the same time, the government's so-called understanding paper with its support parties shows that it will "explore the possibility of Denmark by 2030 building the first energy island with a minimum of 10 GW connected", which the state's company Energinet with more binoculars on the North Sea.

Now the energy company Ørsted is mixing in the debate with a proposal to instead place this energy island as part of a so-called offshore wind cluster in the Baltic Sea west of Bornholm, where the water depth is only 15-20 meters at the lowest place.

It is an area that, according to a screening of areas for offshore wind turbines, conducted by the Danish Energy Agency in early 2019, is suitable for housing up to 3.1 GW offshore wind turbine capacity. It is therefore already reserved for state offering of offshore wind.

Up to 3-5 gw offshore wind
"Before we build large Sand Islands in the North Sea, we suggest that we combine existing plans for transmission connections and offshore wind areas with an island of granite that we already have, namely Bornholm," says Martin Neubert, CEO and CEO of Ørsted Offshore .

The company's vision is-with Bornholm as a hub-to connect Denmark with two or three other countries, such as Poland, Sweden and possibly. Germany, and in the long term, together up to 3-5 GW of offshore wind capacity.

The first step in the vision is to offer an offshore wind park of 1 GW at Rønne Banke southwest of Bornholm as well as connect Denmark and Poland.

Security of supply to Zealand
The offshore wind park and the transmission connection to Poland can ensure a high security of supply in Zealand and at the same time supply the large quantities of electricity that can operate the green electrification of society. The transmission cables on the sea will be buried.

"We specifically propose that this tender contains both the offshore wind farm as well as the transmission cables from Zealand across Bornholm to Poland to ensure an optimal technical solution at the cheapest price," says Martin Neubert.

Ørsted points out that Energinet has already proposed a transmission link between Zealand and Poland in the EU's "Ten Year Network Development Plan" and that it is a realistic project to combine this connection with an offshore wind park of 1 GW that can ensure reliable and cheap electricity to Denmark and Poland in 2028.

Next phase is sustainable hydrogen
In addition, the vision paves the way for the next phase in Denmark's green transition, where the production of sustainable hydrogen can make air traffic, shipping and heavy road transport CO2 neutral, thus providing a decisive and necessary contribution to the government's ambition to lower Denmark's CO2 emissions by 70 percent by 2030.

"The vision can secure Denmark's place in the green transition of the future, where through the production of sustainable hydrogen from offshore winds we can change parts of society that lack green solutions today," Neubert points out.

However, the company emphasizes that there are no specific plans for the location of a hydrogen factory.

The European Commission has previously estimated that up to 450 GW of offshore wind capacity to supply electricity to electric cars and the heating sector, but also for the production of sustainable hydrogen on a large scale.

According to Ørsted, this target can only be met by seting the pace and rethinking the development of offshore wind, so that the focus is on offshore wind clusters with transmission to several countries:

“We need to dramatically raise the pace of the expansion of offshore wind and transmission if we are to reach the goal. With Bornholm, Denmark and Poland have a unique opportunity to gain necessary experience with offshore wind clusters that can be scaled to future energy islands and at the same time contribute significantly to the green transition and security of supply in both countries, ”says Martin Neubert.

Project requires more analyzes
Ørsted first presented his idea in Politiken, where it gets a nice reception by Brian Vad Mathiesen, professor of energy planning at Aalborg University and director of the Green Think Tank, Concito, Christian Ibsen.

Brian Vad Mathiesen calls it against the newspaper a "really good and constructive" project, which, however, requires thorough analyzes.

“It's far more realizable than these airy thoughts about a huge energy island far out in the sea, with 10 gigawatts or more. The challenge lies in finding suitable locations for large quantities of renewable energy, which are at the same time close to some large consumer centers. This is an example of the fact that you can, ”says the professor of Politiken.

Christian Ibsen has the same attitude according to Politiken. He also points out that a huge facility at Bornholm does not block that one day you can also build out in the North Sea.

Title: Finanslov: Professor roser forundersøgelser til energi-øer
Full text:
Upcoming 'Energy Islands' in the North Sea and at Bornholm can support the production of green liquid fuels. Professor Henrik Wenzel is happy about this, but he also warns that we can lose important synergy benefits if we choose the wrong technical solutions.

It is fundamentally positive that the government of the Finance Act for 2020 directly writes that a preliminary investigation for energy islands must now be initiated and support Power-to X technology, "says Henzel Professor Henrik Wenzel. But he also warns that with energy islands we risk losing important synergies in the production of liquid green fuels.

Furthermore, the agreement text states that 'Power-to-X can potentially support effective utilization of large quantities of offshore wind stream from a possible. Energiø, why funds are also allocated for research, development and demonstration schemes for Power-to-X. "

In total, DKK 30 million is allocated. DKK 2020, DKK 27 million. DKK 2021 and DKK 8 million. DKK 2022.

Ørsted will start with small energy island at Bronholm
The question of energy islands has been up and turning several times, most recently this summer here in the Engineer, where the consortium “North Sea Wind Power Hub” described that a network of energy islands in the North Sea of ​​every 10 GW was both technically and financially possible. For example, the islands could be located on Dogger Banke.

At the end of November, Ørsted further argued that an energy island of 1 GW could be located at Rønne Banke southwest of Bornholm and connect Denmark and Poland electric.

Henrik Wenzel emphasizes that if such energy islands are built, then it is important that only electricity is brought ashore and thus not hydrogen produced on the island itself:

“Then we lose the synergies that occur in the process of making hydrogen, synthesis gases and on to liquid green fuels. First and foremost, surplus heat that can be utilized in the district heating network, ”he says.

As an example, he mentions that if the electrolysis is named the SOEC method, it is a really good idea to bring the heat from the process where green synthetic gas is converted into a liquid fuel, back to the electrolysis process and then use the residual heat for district heating.

Therefore, it is also important that the production itself will be near a district heating network.

In dialogue with global energy company
He, together with his research group and NIRAS, recently published the report "Nordic GTL-A Pre-Feasibility Study on Sustainable Aviation Fuel From Biogas, Hydrogen and CO2", where calculations show that with the proper integration of green electricity, hydrogen, biogas and CO2, it will be possible to make liquid fuel for air traffic, which is only twice as expensive as fossil fuel in day.

Right now, efforts are being made to get started on a specific project in collaboration with a global energy company. The first step will be to transform methanized biogas directly into a liquid fuel.

Subsequently, the idea is that production is increased by adding process steps where green hydrogen and CO2 are included:

»The first part is known technology and we can go directly to a full -scale system. But when we move forward and need to use hydrogen and CO2 to increase production, demonstration projects are needed and here the agreement text from the Finance Act can be interesting, ”he says.

Title: Gas-skepsis stemt ned: Parlament godkender EU-liste over 151 infrastruktur-projekter
Full text:
The 151 projects include a lot of natural gas projects and therefore the green group voted in parliament against approving the list, but a large majority said yes.

The EU Parliament on Wednesday approved a list of 151 cross-border energy infrastructure projects that the EU Commission has selected as worthy of seeking EU support.

Among the projects on the so-called PCI list are the energy island of the North Sea, the Baltic Pipe gas lines between Denmark and Poland as well as a total of 55 natural gas infrastructure projects.

Precisely the many projects with natural gas have led the Green Group in the EU parliament to vote no to the list and encourage other MPs to do the same.

Outdated infrastructure
For example, the Danish SF Margrethe Auken wrote in the Altinget that gas pipes like these will freeze Europe in the fossil age and waste billions of euros on infrastructure which will soon be outdated:

"Don't forget that every euro we are wasting here should instead have gone to research, renewable energy or green change of agriculture," she wrote in her call.

But not many people listened to the invitation: Only 169 voted against the list, while 443 voted for, the Polish delegation writes in a press release.

Many new cable connections
In addition to the Energy Island in the North Sea-such as Energinet and a few other transmission-responsible companies are planning to build and which are specifically mentioned in the government's agreement with the support parties-the list also contains the major electric infrastructure projects connecting Norway and the UK ( North Sea Link and North Connect), wired between Denmark and the UK (Viking Link) and connections between the Netherlands and Germany and the UK respectively.

PCI projects are cross-border energy infrastructure projects of strategic importance to the Union.

Projects on the PCI list, which are updated every two years, benefit from more lenient administrative treatment and can thus also receive financing from the Connecting Europe funds.

Title: Ros til klimaudspil med to energiøer: Men et væsentligt kapacitetsproblem truer
Full text:
The government's climate plan will boost the development of green liquid fuels. Energy professor is concerned that liquid green fuels are more complex than politicians think. IDA's chairman gives the plan a "neat 7 number".

According to the government's climate plan, which has just been presented, two energy islands must be built in connection with the erection of 4 GW of new offshore wind turbine capacity. The goal of the islands is to create a hub for the collection and distribution of green energy, both in the form of electricity and liquid green fuels.

Thus, a technological investment in the development of Power-T-X (PTX) is planned, where green electricity is transformed into an alternative fuel, which can be used in, for example, the heavy part of the transport sector, aircraft, ships and in the industry:

“We can no longer make individual offshore wind farms. It must be energy islands where we can gather both the introduction of green energy to land and where hydrogen and liquid fuels can be produced, ”said Climate, Energy and Supply Minister Dan Jørgensen at the presentation of the plan.

The two energy islands must be placed respectively. in the North Sea and in the Baltic Sea off Bornholm. For each of them, 2,000 MW of wind power or more than twice as much as built today. The government's proposal is almost similar to what IDA has proposed in the latest report: IDA's climate response: Transport and energy solutions 2030, where a target of a total of 6,630 MW of offshore wind is set by 2030.

The development with energy islands and PTX technology must be seen in the context of a goal of capturing and stocking-possibly. utilization - CO2 from flue gas. Initially from the fossil sources that cannot be immediately replaced, but in the longer term also from biomass, so that there is actually negative CO2 emission.

Good plan with holes
Professor of Energy Planning at Aalborg University, Brian Vad Mathiesen, calls the idea of ​​energy islands really good, but also has some concerns about the announcement:

“It's really nice and something we've been talking about for several years. Now we get rid of funds so that over the next two to three years we can develop demonstration projects that show how PTX can work. It should preferably be done throughout the value chain, so we also get it tested in the trucks that actually have to drive on it, ”he says.

But he is also concerned that politicians are underestimating how complex such an energy system will be. Namely, there is still a lack of knowledge and models that show where the individual plants are best placed, technically and financially:

“It's about what it is for an infrastructure we want to build up for transporting the green energy. For example, it is best to place the production of hydrogen on the energy island itself, or must be carried ashore and then be transformed into liquid fuels, ”he says, emphasizing that we must not lock ourselves prematurely.

Regarding For the placement of the Energy Islands, he believes that Bornholm is an obvious place. With its location close to Sweden, Poland, Germany and Denmark, the island could become an effective means of displacing fossil fuels in those countries:

"I think it can be carried to be expanded by up to 5 GW," he says.

It is more questionable with the energy island in the North Sea. Here the distances are significantly longer, and today we do not have cables that are able to transfer more than the 2 GWs planned:

“I first think it will be on the other side of 2030 that we can get up in cable sizes that can transfer up to 10 GW, but when that happens we also have to expand that capacity so we can deliver green Power to the major energy -consuming centers in Northern Europe, ”says Brian Vad Mathiesen.

Overall, the professor calls the climate plan a good play, although he may well point to technical details that he is less fond of, and holes that have not been fully filled.

Climate Plan recognizes technology
The chairman of Ida, Thomas Damkjær Pedersen, is pleased that a first play has now come from the government on how to reach the CO2 reduction in 2030:

»The play recognizes that a technological focus is needed to achieve the goal. Many of the solutions we have also pointed out in our climate response from earlier this year. All in all, I want to give it a nice 7, ”he says.

The reason why we cannot get higher is, according to Thomas Damkjær Pedersen, that we have not yet got it translated into a national strategy and that we therefore do not know how.

But the fact that offshore wind farms are advanced and that the focus is now on the development and demonstration of PTX, so that it can go from demonstration systems to a large scale is absolutely necessary so that we can achieve the goals of CO2 reductions in 2030 and 2050, he says:

"Now I am looking forward to the plan being translated into an actual strategy for research and development in a collaboration between private and public actors," says Thomas Damkjær Pedersen.

Title: Regeringens storstilede klimaplan bidrager til en brøkdel af CO2-målet
Full text:
The government's proposal for the first part of the climate action plan only reduces CO2 emissions by 2 of the necessary 19 million. ton of CO2 until 2030.

Then the government finally came with its overall proposal to the first step in a climate action plan to lead us to the climate target for a CO2 reduction of 70 per cent. or 19 million tonnes of CO2 in 2030 - and which now has to be negotiated with the other parties behind the Climate Act.

The plan consists of six points and let it be said right away - it does not show how we reach the climate target, as it will simply give a reduction of 2 million. tonnes of CO2 out of the required 19 million. ton.

In turn, the government promised several initiatives later:

“We're not done. This is only the first chapter and after the summer holidays we will present new initiatives. But today we create a solid foundation for a climate -neutral Denmark - a foundation we can build on for many years ahead, ”said Finance Minister Nicolai Wammen at the press conference, where he also promised that one will create the basis for thousands of green Workplaces in the coming years can be created and can be preserved here in Denmark.

Long-term energy islands and power-to-x
When the measures do not give as much CO2 reduction, it is because several of them are very long-term and instead of here-and-now reductions in developing and scaling up the technologies we need in the long run. However, it is important to start technology development was also something that the Climate Council advised in its March report on the 70 percent target.

The long-term perspective is especially true of the proposal for the establishment of two energy islands and expansion with an extra 2 GW of offshore wind farms in the North Sea and in the Baltic Sea respectively, and this applies to the proposal to put turbo on the technology development of power-to-x and of CO2 catch and storage.

Specifically, the government suggests that we catch CO2 from, for example, the industry and then use it for green energy or pump it back into the ground. From 2024, the government will allocate DKK 400 million. DKK annually to a pool to capture and store CO2, which according to the proposal will reduce CO2 emissions by DKK 0.3 million. ton. CO2 per years in 2030. In addition, the government will create a unified strategy for CCUS to set the framework for future efforts.

In the PTX area, the government will start a partnership on a large-scale PTX plant that will produce green fuels for aircraft and cars and thus drive the cost of hydrogen down.

Pools for biogas and industry
Both the Energy Islands and the PTX/CCS The proposal thus costs nothing special until after 2024, but thus gives only 0.3 million. ton of CO2 reduction.

Green transition in the industry in the form of electrification and use of biogas, the government will promote via a subsidy pool of DKK 900 million. kroner from 2020 to 2024 for electrification plus a pool of 95 annually for biogas and other green gases; However, it will not come into play until 2024. It could reduce CO2 emissions by 0.3 million. ton by 2030.

At the same time, the government promises to work closely with the climate partnership of the financial sector to map the opportunities to mobilize private investments for the green transition in new ways.

When it comes to promoting energy efficiencyizations in buildings and industry for the benefit of the climate, the government will set aside funds to collect and exhibit data on buildings and their energy consumption. In addition, the energy labeling scheme is strengthened and recommendations about indoor climate are incorporated so that the building owners get an even better decision basis when they want to invest in energy improvements in e.g. the dwelling.

In addition, there must be demands for continued energy savings in the state's buildings until 2030, so that the state is ahead with the good example. All that together gives a reduction of just 47,000 tonnes by 2030.

The heating sector must be more green, which we have already heard of, that is, oil and gas stove must be replaced with district heating and heat pumps. The plan figures have been put on how much the electric heating charge should be lowered (to 0.8 øre per kWh) and the tax on fossil heat must be raised (from 56.7 øre per GJ to 62.3 øre per GJ), And that the grants for consumers who want to replace oil or gas stove will be between DKK 15,000 and DKK 25,000.

Surplus heat exempt from tax
It also appears that the tax on surplus heat is proposed to be removed and that the government considers that the mentioned reduction in the electric heating tax will help to make geothermal heat a profitable, green alternative.
The heating package reduces greenhouse gas emissions by DKK 0.7 million. ton of CO2 in 2030.

Finally, there is a green waste sector and more recycling, with 80 per cent. of the Danish plastic must be sorted out from the combustion by 2030, and we must have less combustion and import of waste and more sorting and recycling. At the same time, the government will make a circular economy a growth engine for Danish business.

The initiatives in the waste area result in a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions of DKK 0.7 million. tonnes of CO2 equivalents by 2030.

Where is transport, agriculture and CO2 tax
And then there is everything that is not included in the plan. There is not one word about initiatives in the transport sector or in agriculture-which are two major CO2 emitters-nor anything about a high CO2 tax, which both the Climate Council and the economic sages have proposed as the cheapest path to the climate target.

At the press conference in the Ministry of Finance, Climate, Energy and Supply Minister Dan Jørgensen responded to a question of whether it is not fair enough that those who swine the most pay the most- ie a CO2 tax:

“We are in the middle of a very big crisis. In many other countries in the world you have probably chosen to say: OK, efforts around climate, environment and other things, you have to push. We have chosen to say no, we will use this crisis as an opportunity. We want to create growth. This means that we must opt ​​out of instruments such as Large taxes on large companies or on the Danes' private consumption. We don't think that's a very good idea right now. "

Missing an overall plan
And finally, there is the big, overall question: When the plan here only gives two million. ton of CO2, how do we reach the rest of the way in 2030?

This is precisely the point - that is, this is not a comprehensive plan, but more about a handful of good beats - as different organizations as the Council for Green Change, Greenpeace and the trade association Dansk Energi.

The Green Change Council is disappointed with the overall level of ambition; Greenpeace calls it a half -hearted first shovel, which is found to be worrying, and finally Dansk Energi played out as important initiatives, but that it is not a climate plan:

“We miss a total climate plan. The entire energy sector lacks a framework and direction for how it should go ahead on the road to the target in 2030, when CO2 emissions must be reduced by 70 percent compared to 1990, ”says Lars Aagaard CEO Lars Aagaard.

We have ten years
At the press conference, DR asked exactly when we get the rest of the plan, and to this, Climate, Energy and Supply Minister Dan Jørgensen responded:

“We have about ten years to reach it. With the two million tonnes we have here with the 0.5 million tonnes we organized by the Finance Act agreement, we reach significantly more than the tenth we say we should reach. On that scale, it's quite ambitious, 'he said.

You can read the fact sheets from the players on the Ministry of Finance's website.

The government expects to convene the parties of the Folketing for the first negotiations of the play over the next week.

Title: Kæmpeanlæg i Storkøbenhavn skal producere 250.000 ton flydende bæredygtige brændstoffer
Full text:
In a new partnership, a number of large Danish companies are joining forces to develop a concrete production facility for the manufacture of sustainable fuels. Fully developed, it will save the atmosphere of 850,000 tonnes of CO2 annually.

By 2023, a new partnership will be ready with the first part of the 10 MW plant, which can produce sustainable fuels based on power from wind turbines. The plant will be placed in Greater Copenhagen and, among other things, be supplied with energy from the upcoming Energiø off Bornholm.

When the plant is fully expanded by 2030, 1,300 MW of electricity and the production of fuels will be at approximately 250,000 tonnes annually. Thus, they will be able to replace fossil fuels for road, sea and air transport and save the atomic at the nuclearosphere from 850,000 tonnes of CO2 annually.

This is what Ørsted writes in a press release where the partnership brings together large Danish companies, such as Copenhagen Airport, A.P.Møller-Maersk, DSV Panalpina, DFDS and SAS. Cowi and Boston Consulting Group serve as knowledge partners for the project, which is also supported by the City of Copenhagen.

Henrik Poulsen, CEO, Ørsted, says:

»Our vision of producing sustainable fuels in Greater Copenhagen will give us the necessary upscaling to industrial scale, which is needed to reduce the cost of production of sustained fuels so much that they can compete with fossil fuels. With the right political framework in place, this project could be a crucial step forward for the production of sustainable fuels in Denmark, which will strengthen Denmark's global leadership position in technologies and business models that can ensure a sustainable future. "

The plant must use electricity to form hydrogen based on water via electrolysis and thus be able to supply buses from Movia and heavy trucks from DSV Panalpina with hydrogen, A.P.Møller-Maersk will be able to get Mehanol for their ships and aircraft at Copenhagen Airport will be able to be provided with sustainable Jetfuel.

The first stage must, as mentioned, consist of a 10 MW system to produce hydrogen for buses and trucks. The second stage will be ready in 2027 and consist of a 250 MW system, which is expected to be fitted with electricity from an offshore wind farm off Bornholm. Here, hydrogen must be produced, which is combined with CO2, which is collected from point sources in Copenhagen. The goal is to produce methanol for maritime transport and jetfuel, so-called e-kerosin, for the air transport sector.

Last stage requires more wind turbines
The last stage will be ready in 2030 and utilize the full potential of offshore wind at Bornholm. The electrolysis capacity must be scaled up to 1.3 GW and enough sustainable CO2 must be collected so that 250,000 tonnes of fuel can be produced. It could potentially replace 30 percent of fossil fuels used at Copenhagen Airport by 2030.
Thomas Woldbye, CEO, Copenhagen Airports, says:

»The challenge of creating a future -proof and sustainable fuel is common to everyone in the transport sector, and the fact that we are now joining forces in a partnership is crucial for us to produce sustainable fuel in the necessary quantities. At the same time, it supports the ambitions to change Danish aviation to be completely without CO2 emissions in 2050 and make Denmark a pioneer in the development of the future climate-friendly fuels. "

However, the project can run into problems as the full expansion requires that the wind farm at Bornholm be expanded to 3 GW in 2030. In the climate plans presented by the government last week, only a park of 2 GW off Bornholm is planned.

Title: Professor: Tidsplan for havvindmøller kan skride med regeringens nye energiøer
Full text:
The price of establishing two energy islands with associated wind farms lacks to be elucidated. Member of the Climate Council fears that the time frame for the expansion with wind power is progressing.

A number of questions are unanswered with the government's proposal in the proposal for a climate plan to establish two so -called energy islands in Danish waters. The islands must each be coupled with an offshore wind farm of 2 GW and help reach the target of 70 percent CO2 reduction by 2030.

Poul Erik Morthorst, a professor at DTU and a member of the Climate Council, fears that the extension with offshore wind turbines is going on, so that we will not reach the finish in 2030, when the Climate Council has recommended that it be expanded by at least 5 GW.

This is partly due to the fact that the government in the plan for the Energe Islands has included three offshore wind farms adopted with the energy settlement in 2018, but where the first, Thor at 800-1000 MW, has been delayed at least one year, and for the two others are not in progress:

“I'm worried that time is running and we're getting behind. I would rather have seen that we established the three times 800 MW offshore wind farms, which were agreed in 2018 and then started the energy islands, ”he says.

New energy island is millions of years old
Specifically, the government's proposal is that one of the Energy Islands should be in the North Sea and be built as a physical island about 100 km off the west coast of Jutland.

The other is not a new island, but a rewrite that a wind farm will be built on Rønne Banke south of Rønne with associated technical facilities on Bornholm.

The total capacity of 4 GW offshore wind is more than twice as much as is operating on the oceans around Denmark today.

In practice, both islands must be fully expanded as an "energy hub", where energy can be exchanged with neighboring countries, in the same way as the Kriegers Flak offshore wind farm, which is expected to go into operation in August - just on a much larger scale.

Due to the distances to land, the connections must be established with direct current cables and here there is still some technical development with coupling fields.

“If energy is to be exchanged between the countries, then it is not a very small thing to build rules for settlement. On top of that comes the whole question of any grants to such plants, ”says Poul Erik Morthorst.

EL to Zealand must be converted into fuel
In connection with the wind farm on Bornholm, Ørsted - in partnership with a number of players from the transport sector - has announced that production capacity must be built up for the manufacture of sustainable fuels at a plant in Greater Copenhagen. According to the government, these fuels must be used 'in sectors that cannot use green electricity directly, eg aviation, heavy transport, some processes in business, etc. via Power-to-X technology. "

The project means that a cable must be pulled from the Bornholm wind farm directly to Zealand. Fully expanded by 2030, it is expected that the plant has a capacity of 1.3 GW.

Such a plant will help complicate a number of political and regulatory challenges, and can make it difficult to reach the goal on time, says Poul Erik Morthorst:

»I can see the perspectives in an energy island in combination with eg. Electrolysis, but it would be a shame if it means the schedules are progressing, ”he says.

In addition to energy islands with offshore wind, the climate action plan consists of five other tracks. The government will also invest in green technologies, increase energy efficiencyization, ensure green heat to the Danes, change the industry and create a more green waste sector, it says.

Title: Analyse: Stram tidsramme kan sætte energiøer under pres
Full text:
Two giant wind farms and associated fuel production must be ready in ten years. Is it a short time, or is it just known technology that needs to be put together?

Denmark must expand with wind power at sea - a lot of wind power. The government suggested May 20 in its climate plan two energy islands with a total of 4 GW wind power attached, and this week Ørsted, together with a number of partners, could tell about a giant fuel -producing plant, they will build somewhere in Greater Copenhagen and supply electricity from one of these Energy Islands.

The whole thing may seem promising: the idea of ​​building wind farms at sea to both supply Denmark and the surrounding countries with electricity and produce sustainable fuels, so-called Power-to-X (PTX). The good news here is that most of the technology exists and already works industrially. A number of PTX demonstration systems are underway-but there is still a lack of experience with upscaling.

So when industry and politicians agree that this is the way forward to reach a 70 percent reduction in CO2 emissions by 2030, a large number of questions are still accumulating that can challenge technique, infrastructure and planning, and which Binded up by a ten -year timeframe that may suddenly seem tight.

But let's try to look at the specific proposal: In the North Sea, an island with space for housing, spare parts stock and converter station for a wind farm of 2 GW must be built, which over time can be expanded to 10-15 GW. It will be placed about 100 km off the west coast of Jutland and connected to several countries, probably Norway, Germany, the Netherlands, Denmark and possibly the UK.

The other large wind farm must be located off Bornholm and has been set by the government to 2 GW in size, while Ørsted in the project, which describes a new associated PTX factory located in Greater Copenhagen, expects the park to be expanded to 3 GW.

One of the benefits of building near Bornholm is - as head of energy economy at Ørsted Ulrik Stridbæk it explains to the Engineer - that there is already an island. Thus, it is possible to get started quickly in the Baltic Sea.

A converter station will distribute the energy from the wind farm to initially Denmark and Poland according to the same principle as the wind farm on Kriegers Flak south of Copenhagen, which is expected to go into operation in August this year, distributes energy to both Denmark, Germany and Sweden.

Gigantic electrolysis plant
The next step to be able to utilize the large quantities of wind power that will be produced is the establishment of a production plant in Greater Copenhagen, which can transform electricity into a chemical fuel; Initially hydrogen, but also methanol and jetfuel. Basic techniques for such a plant are already available today, and by 2030 it will be expanded in three stages to eventually be a gigantic factory with an electrolysis plant of 1.3 GW and production of 250,000 tonnes of fuel annually, some of which must be supplied with Carbon pulled out of the flue gas from Copenhagen power plants such as Amagerverket and ARC.

So far, so good. The plans are in place and most of the technique is known. Now the realization is lacking, and there are many unknowns, which Torben Glar Nielsen, technical director at Energinet, can also confirm. In particular, Energinet has focused on the plant in the North Sea through participation in the Collaboration North Sea Wind Power Hub, where the German and Dutch system operators have also participated. The project works with a scenario with several islands in the North Sea, including a Danish island approx. 100 km from the west coast. The analyzes show that 10-15 GW wind power around an island is appropriate. It makes sense to start with 2-3 GW, either as pure electricity production or as in the proposal at Bornholm to include a PTX plant and thus start the production of one of the fuels of the future.

In line with the expansion of wind turbines in the area, electricity can be transported between neighboring countries via DC cables and thus also utilize the cable capacity when it is not blowing. In the even longer term (until 2050) the island can be linked to other energy islands in the North Sea. One of the technical challenges applies to coupling fields to DC, where the development is probably in progress, but not in target.

In a comment last week to the government's climate plan, professor of energy planning at Aalborg University called Brian Vad Mathiesen the idea of ​​energy islands for really good. It was something that the researchers had been talking about for a number of years. But he also had concerns and emphasized that funds should now be set aside so that over the next two to three years we can develop demonstration projects that show how the entire infrastructure and PTX can actually work. It should preferably be investigated throughout the value chain, ie from wind turbines to a specific truck, which actually has to run on the fuel.

Much can postpone the expansion
Economically and in terms of planning, there is a risk that the entire idea basis will also run into challenges. According to the Climate Partnership for Energy, the state will have to allocate funding in the form of grants and targeted tax reliefs of DKK 5-7 billion. DKK annually by 2030, some of which are likely to go to the bet in energy islands and PTX.

In Berlingske on Tuesday this week, Climate, Energy and Supply Minister Dan Jørgensen (S) said that 2 GW wind power at Bornholm is already quite ambitious and that future analyzes should look at what pace to expand, depending on what we we even need to use and what they use in other countries. Thus, there must also be included in both political negotiations and cooperation with authorities in neighboring countries.

The rate of expansion can also be challenged, because if all the wind turbines at sea in the coming years are to be put under the Energiø concept, which the government is now proposing, then there is a risk that we will fall behind with the expansion, which one could read in Politiken on Tuesday . Political head of Wind Denmark Martin Bøndergaard considered that the plan would then give delays in a few years.

Both Ulrik Stridbæk and Torben Glar Nielsen agree that the principle behind energy islands is crucial for the future expansion with wind power at sea. In other words, we have reached a time when there is a need to go up purely technologically; Wind turbines on the sea are today competitive with more fossil alternatives, but if the price needs even further down and really have a climate effect on the continent, then it is no longer enough to expand the wind farms and connect them one at a time.

But they also both acknowledge that there are challenges, both in terms of technology and schedule. Or, as Ulrik Stridbæk puts it, now is the time to think in a paradigm shift, for the time being is scarce.

Title: Analyse: Derfor skal vi hellere bygge for mange end for få havmøller
Full text:
It can be difficult to keep up with the future need for green power because the road to the government's new energy islands is covered with obstacles. And then it becomes difficult to push out the old coal -fired works.

Every time a huge wind is blowing from the west, and the price of power falls to zero or less, you can read about over -expanding with wind turbines and a waste of social resources. Because when Danes cannot consume wind power, it must be exported. And the possible buyers may have even excess electricity or problems with the capacity of the electricity grid - and then wind turbines must be closed for a fee.

However, according to professionals, the problem until 2030 is not at all expanding with renewable energy such as wind turbines and solar cells - on the contrary, right now there is a great risk that we will lack green power when we round the New Year in well over 9 years and 6 months.

Such is the situation in the Danish electricity sector after the government came with the first part of a unified climate action plan last week.

Let's just take the numbers we need to hit: Energinet has in the report 'System Perspective at the 70%goal and large-scale offshore wind', from March this year looked at different scenarios for electricity consumption and expansion with VE-EL. Today, electricity consumption is about 36 TWh, and it will rise in the so -called basic scenario to 50 TWh by 2030. But if the electrification of almost all areas of the country really starts - more data centers, heating (heat pumps), industry (process heat) and transport (especially electric cars) - we can reach a consumption of 57 TWh by 2030. And if there is further effort to convert the energy into liquid fuels via PTX (Power-to-X), then there is the opportunity to reach a consumption of 70 TWH in 2030, ie almost a doubling compared to today.

Energy Islands is a paradigm shift
Therefore, the idea of ​​energy islands presented by the government in its climate action plan last week is a promising thought. The islands are called a paradigm shift compared to how we have so far built offshore wind turbines, as a park will no longer be connected to the electricity grid via a separate cable. Instead, the energy from the park will be collected on an island from which it is possible to distribute the one where it is needed.

Specifically, there is a prospect of 2 GW in the Baltic Sea and 2 GW in the North Sea. In the Baltic Sea, it will be Bornholm itself that will act as Energiø, with connection to Zealand and perhaps also Sweden, Germany and Poland according to what is system technically most appropriate. In the North Sea, the offshore wind farm will initially be 2 GW, but it will potentially be expanded to 10 GW.

The artificial island, which is to be built about 100 km off the West Coast, will, in addition to Jutland, potentially be connected to Norway, Germany, the Netherlands and possibly also the UK. In the plan, the government has included two of the three offshore wind farms, which were agreed in the energy settlement of 2018 in the Energy Islands. The third, called Thor at about 800 MW, is still expected to be built in the traditional way and be ready to operate around 2024.

The extra 4 GW offshore wind turbines and the expected production of about 18 TWH can quickly turn out to be both late and be too little if the need for WE-EL grows as in Energinet's prerequisites, the criticism from several sides reads. The consequence will be that the existing Danish coal -fired power plants will not be 'pressed out' by electricity production, and that Denmark is much more dependent on imports of electricity.

Coal power must be pressed out
A number of system experts that the Engineer has spoken to agree that if the offshore wind turbines are not built quickly enough, so that coal power is squeezed out of the system, then it will lead to the CO2 emission calculated as kg CO2/kWh in the system, not falls as rapidly as necessary if we are to reach the 70 percent by 2030.

And building fast enough need not be difficult or particularly expensive. The Climate Council's latest report states that wind turbines on land (and solar cells) can be established completely without or with very low support, and that offshore wind turbines will only need less support to push coal -fired electricity production out of the system.

For example, it is expected that Thor-Vindmølleparken will only need a supplement to the market price of approx. 7-9 øre per. kWh to compete with fossil electricity production.

Both the Climate Council and Energinet write in their reports that if the high goals of electricity consumption are to be achieved, then there will be a need to build far more offshore wind than the 4 GWs from the Energy Islands plus the agreed park Thor. The amount of extra GW ranges from 3-10 depending on how much of the energy consumption we get switched to electricity, for example for the production of liquid fuels via PTX.

The idea of ​​establishing energy islands can therefore prove to be a direct barrier to achieving the goals in 2030. Not because it is purely technological and energy economically a stupid idea. But because the process towards they are actually ready to supply electricity into the Danish system can pull long. This has already been shown in the supply of both rural and coastal mills, where the case processing is dragging long and construction projects are exposed.

On top of that comes a technological challenge. Namely, it may seem intriguing to think about an energy island and calculate how it can be part of a network of exchange connections and combinations with other WE technologies, such as PTX. But while much of the technology is known, answers still lack how electricity should be exchanged, both purely technically via coupling fields to direct current and purely financially between the countries involved and alternative uses, again with PTX as the best example.

Risk of under -expanding
Is there a risk that we will over -expand and thus create even more situations where wind turbines must be stopped or electricity must be exported for a fee? It actually happened a number of times in 2017, when wind turbines were stopped throughout the year for 84 hours in Western Denmark and 58 hours in Eastern Denmark. Overall, this meant that a production of 47 GWh, or the equivalent of consumption in 11,000 Danish homes, was wasted. It corresponded to 0.3 percent of the total wind power production that year. In 2019, a record was set as a record when wind turbines and solar cells together accounted for 133 percent of electricity consumption on Sunday 15 September. In fact, production from the wind turbines was 160 percent of consumption in the hours between 2 and 3 that night.

The answer to whether we can build too much is a clear no. With the government's climate plan, we are far from getting into a situation that we cannot handle technically using flexible electricity consumption and strong foreign connections, says professionals. The risk of under-expanding is far greater, because if that happens, access to the WE-Eel will become a bottleneck for electrification of Denmark-this is especially true if there is a seriousness behind the thoughts of PTX.

So it may well be that we eventually reach the goal in 2030, but the road there will be covered with a CO2 emission that could have been avoided. In other words, we will be tipped to the wrong side in the difficult balance between production and consumption of VE.

Title: Cowi-rapport: Regeringens energiøer giver dyrere havmøllestrøm
Full text:
The government's energy islands cost more billions more for the same number of GW than traditional offshore wind farms, a new report from COWI shows.

It will be several billion kroner more expensive to establish two so -called energy islands, where the electricity from the surrounding offshore wind farm is gathered, as the government proposes in its climate proposal than if traditional offshore wind farms are established closer to land.

It shows a new report from the consultancy firm COWI, which on behalf of the Danish Energy Agency has completed a fine screening of Danish sea areas to investigate the possibility of establishing individual offshore wind farms with direct connection to land as well as several continuous offshore wind farms connected to energy islands.

In the report, COWI estimates that a single offshore wind farm in the North Sea with an installed effect of 1 GW costs just under DKK 15.8 billion in total investment costs. Three individual offshore wind farms end up costing DKK 47.8 billion for 3 GW.

The total investment costs for an energy island with an effect of 3 GW are estimated by COWI to cost 58.2-58.6 billion kroner.

Compared to three traditional offshore wind farms with direct connection to land, COWI estimates that one of the government's energy islands will cost around DKK 11 billion more in total investment costs - corresponding to an additional cost of 23 percent.

COWI has also estimated lifetime costs per kWh based on final energy production as well as the total investment and operation and maintenance costs with a lifetime of 30 years and a discount rate of 8 percent.

It is estimated that the average costs over the entire life (LCOE) for the individual offshore wind farms in the North Sea amount to DKK 0.40 per year. kWh, while the same figure for an energy island is 0.46-0.49 kr. kWh.

The COWI report mentions that the areas have been updated, which is partly based on 'new information about interests in parts of the areas and partly based on changes in the prerequisites for the financial calculations'.

»Political assignments have also been provided to seek out opportunities to establish one or more so -called energy islands/hubs in marine areas outside those covered by 2018 Finescreening. The establishment of such energy islands/hubs opens the possibility of building significantly more offshore wind farms in new areas, ”writes COWI.

Still a desire for traditional offshore wind turbines
According to Martin Risum Bøndergaard, who is the political head of the Sector Community for Wind, Wind Denmark, it is not surprising that COWI comes to the conclusion that it is cheaper to build individual parks closer to land.

“Of course, this should also be taken into account politically, so that you continue to focus on getting the cheapest possible offshore wind by building individual parks, while also investing in the big visions of energy islands and thus creating an opportunity to utilize sea -winning resources further from land and could export the green energy to the rest of Europe, ”he says.

Martin Risum Bøndergaard believes that it will be unwise if the Folketing chooses to "put all the offshore wind turbine eggs in a basket" by focusing exclusively on the energy islands and waving goodbye to the three offshore wind farms from the energy agreement 2018.

»Then you make the offshore wind more expensive than necessary, and you say goodbye to some really attractive and cheap offshore wind farms, which will be very good compared to the desire also from the government that Denmark should be strong in the new technology of energy storage and - Conversion via the so-called Power-to-X, where you use energy from wind to convert to hydrogen and liquid fuels, ”he says.

Director of the Council for Green Change Claus Ekman also hopes that the government will maintain the plans to establish the most cost -effective offshore wind turbines. He wonders that last year, the Finance Act was allocated millions to do investigations of the Energy Islands, and that the government has now announced that they must be established by 2030 without presenting the results of the investigations.

“The government has been hopeful of two energy islands by 2030 instead of actually getting offshore winds up, and there are still specific proposals for financing and fixed dates for the tenders. We are in a hurry, because it typically takes six, seven or eight years, from the political decision on an offshore wind turbine project until it is finished, ”he says.

Claus Ekman believes that this and now are about getting the sufficient GW offered by 2030 and that these GW should be offered as traditional offshore wind farms.

“At the same time, it makes sense to look further into the horizon, so that in the long term you can clarify the economy and - when the time is right - the establishment of energy islands begins. I think it is very much for the government for signals, and it is fine that you focus on making energy islands, but it is premature to announce that you want them by 2030. These are some nice signals, but the government has to become more concrete, ”he says.

A brand new era
As part of the first part of the Climate Action Plan, the government announced that it wants to establish two energy islands with offshore winds to deliver 4 GW of offshore wind or more than twice as much as erected today.

A little more specifically, it is proposed to establish the two energy islands by 2030: one in the North Sea of ​​2 GW with room for at least 10 GW in the long term and one in the Baltic Sea of ​​2 GW.

The energy islands must not only produce electricity, but also in the long term be able to connect technologies that can store or transform this green current into, for example, fuels (so-called power-to-x ”).

Climate Minister Dan Jørgensen (S) said in a press release in connection with the presentation of the Climate Action Plan that with "the establishment of the world's first two energy islands we begin a whole new era in the Danish wind adventure".

“We are massively increasing the amount of offshore wind, and at the same time we will make it possible to use the green power in the tank of trucks, cargo ships and aircraft. We present a package that provides both CO2 reductions in the short term and puts out development traces to the climate-neutral Denmark of the future, ”he explained.

Title: Rådgiver om power-to-x: Samspil mellem vind og elektrolyseanlæg bliver svært
Full text:
As a technical advisor to the partnership behind the ambitious Power-to-X project in Greater Copenhagen, COWI primarily sees the project as a new link of already existing technologies

The interaction between a variable electricity supply from the offshore wind farms, a stable fuel production and deliveries of district heating is the major challenge when it comes to designing a large power-to-X plant.

This is explained by technical manager Jeppe Grue from COWI, who has been selected as a technical advisor on the large power-to-x vision, which was recently launched by, among others, Ørsted, Maersk and Copenhagen Airports.

"The big challenge lies in getting the power-to-X system to run flexibly, so it can play with the electric and heating system and absorb the large variations in electricity production that the renewable energy sources naturally offer," he points out and points out adds that some of the intermediate stores of hydrogen will probably be needed to make it all come together.

Over the next ten years, the large power-to-X project will establish a production of first green hydrogen and later green fuels such as methanol and jet fuel (kerosis) for aircraft and maritime transport on the basis of electrolysis.

The engineer has tried to put a few more figures on the big project, but much is simply not set or clarified yet.

Running in three stages
However, technical manager Jeppe Grue would like to explain that much is about how the individual technologies play together:

»The individual elements of the project are such existing and well -known technologies. Our task will be to combine them in the best possible way in a new way and at the same time scale up the solutions to industrial scales, ”he says, adding that the few electrolysis projects that already exist around the world have typically been much smaller.

The project will run in three stages. The first stage to be implemented in 2023 consists of a 10 MW electrolysis system to produce green hydrogen for direct use in buses and trucks. The plant will be placed in Greater Copenhagen, where Ørsted already has a smaller hydrogen project along the way with just 2 MW electrolysis capacity at the Avedøreværket.

The second stage to be realized in 2027 includes an electrolysis system of 250 MW. The hydrogen produced must be combined with the collection of sustainable CO2 from point sources in Greater Copenhagen, so that methanol can be produced for maritime transport and persistent jet fuel (E-kerosin) to the aviation sector.

Finally, there is the third stage where the electrolysis capacity is increased to 1.3 GW in 2030.

The plant will be able to produce 250,000 tonnes of sustainable fuel annually for use in buses, trucks, ships and aircraft. This corresponds to 30 per cent. of the fuel refueled at Copenhagen Airport.

Power from 3 GW offshore wind
Power for the electrolysis process will come from offshore wind farms - in 2027 from a new offshore wind farm at Bornholm at 2 GW, which the government has proposed.

In order to supply 1.3 GW electrolysis capacity, according to the project partners, the project partners are required 3 GW offshore wind turbine capacity, and the project partners therefore propose the park expanded.

If you ask Ørsted why the capacity should be so large, it is explained by the fact that the wind turbines are not running all the time. Ørsted expects offshore wind farms to produce at full pressure in 47 per cent. of the time.

Another thing that needs to be clarified is what type of electrolysis should be used for hydrogen production: alkaline electrolysis, PEM electrolysis or SOEC, which is a reverse fuel cell.

"We want to get started quickly, so it will be natural for us to concentrate on available technologies, and there lies the alkaline electrolysis or PEM cell," explains Jeppe Grue.

Energy loss of 30-40 per cent.
As far as the energy loss in the electrolysis process is concerned, it is a rule of thumb of between 30 and 40 per cent, but here Jeppe Grue points out that one must look at the efficiency of the entire plant together and that the excess heat is intended to be utilized for District heating.

Finding the right physical location of the plant is also part of Cowi's task, but yet nothing has been decided.

If you ask Ørsted again, the press officer confirms that the electrolysis technology has not been decided, and that it is also not decided where the plants should be, but that they will probably be placed at Avedøre or at Amager.

Green or black CO2 source
To be able to fabricate green methanol and green jet fuel, a green CO2 source is required and whether the CO2 source is green depends on whether the CO2 is taken out of the smoke when burning fossil fuels, the smoke from biomass or from biogas.

Ørsted states that it has not yet been stuck to point sources, but that the most likely options are CO2 from biomass power plants, waste -fired works or a combination.

"We are aware that waste contains a proportion of biologically based waste and a fossil -based share, and we will relate to this if we end up choosing CO2 from waste -fired works," Ørsted said in an email.

The project itself has stated that the 250,000 tonnes of green fuel could reduce CO2 emissions by 850,000 tonnes of CO2 in 2030 when it replaces the corresponding amount of fossil fuels.

In comparison, the report from aviation climate partnership states that Danish aviation today will emit DKK 3.2 million. tonnes of CO2 (foreign and domestic), which is why the project's production will thus be able to reduce emissions from aviation by just over a quarter if aviation is allowed to buy the entire plant's production of green fuels.

Nice, but expensive
Building an electrolysis system with a capacity of 1.3 GW electrolysis plant is neither a small or cheap case.

For example, if you look in, for example, the Energy Foundation's 'Roadmap for Electrification', the price of such a 1.3 GW electrolysis system with associated offshore wind can easily run up to DKK 24 billion. kroner in acquisition, which gives a hydrogen price of about 150 kr. GJ.

If you need to produce methanol or jetfuel, the cost increases by a factor of three.

Energinet writes in its' system perspective analysis at 70 per cent. offshore wind 'from March this year, that PTX measures are expected to cost DKK 1,500-3,000 per year. ton of saved CO2. In comparison, direct electrification costs-ie use of electricity in heating, transport or industry DKK 300-1,500 per year. ton.

According to the Climate Council, the Climate Partnership for Energy and Supply has a significant focus on Power-to-X (including CCU) due to its future potential, and here they have grossly estimated the cost of PTX to 5-7 billion. DKK and the reduction potential to DKK 1.9 million. tonnes corresponding to a shadow price of DKK 2,600-3,700 per tonne. ton of CO2.

Title: Bred klimaaftale indgået: Her er hovedelementerne
Full text:
The government and a broad majority in the Folketing have entered into a climate agreement that, together with the climate agreement for waste, provides CO2 reductions of DKK 3.4 million. ton by 2030.

After almost eight hours of negotiations, which began with Finance Minister Nicolai Wammen (S) on Sunday at 17, the government and almost all the parties of the Folketing except New Citizens have agreed on Monday night on Monday on a climate agreement on green transition of the energy sector and industry.

In total, the agreement, together with the Climate Agreement for Waste Agreement, results in CO2 reductions of DKK 3.4 million. Ton in 2030, according to the Facts of the Climate, Energy and Supply Ministry of the Agreement.

"With the agreement today, Denmark is again at the forefront of the green transition, and at the same time we pave the way for a green recovery of the economy with some of the biggest long -term infrastructure investments ever," says Finance Minister Nicolai Wammen (S) in a press release.

"I am very proud that we have succeeded in making a wide green deal that both gets us closer to reaching our climate targets and in the long term will create thousands of Danish green jobs," he says.

The world's first energy islands are established
The agreement means that Denmark, as the first country in the world, will start the establishment of two energy islands by 2030 of a total of 5 GW - one must be Bornholm with a capacity of 2 GW, while an artificial island is to be built in the North Sea with a capacity of 3 GW.

In addition, the establishment of Park 2 from Energy Agreement 18 of approx. 1 GW at Hesselø. Ie A total of 6 GW offshore wind or more than three times as much as Denmark's current amount of offshore wind.

In addition to producing electricity, the energy islands must also be connected in the long term technologies that can store or transform the green power into green fuels, so-called power-to-x.

»With the establishment of the world's first two energy islands and the world's biggest investment in green fuels, Denmark is seriously taking global climate leadership again.
