The government fails the Climate Act and its international responsibility with a hockey system model and unrealistic expectations of the potential of immature technologies to reduce CO2 emissions, NGOs believe.

The government's climate policy does not live up to the Climate Act nor Denmark's international obligations to be a pioneer and reduce CO2 emissions by 70 percent by 2030. This is partly due to the government's rate on 'immature technologies' such as catching and storing CO2 (CCS).

This is what the announcement of 14 NGOs, including Greenpeace, the Council for Green Change and the Danish Society for Nature Conservation, sounds in a note entitled 'Do climate policy live up to the Climate Act? An evaluation of whether the government's hockey stake strategy lives up to the Climate Act '.

The government's so-called hockey mate model expresses a flat graph of CO2 reductions for the first several years when very small reductions are picked up before eventually bending sharply upward with large reductions in the years just before 2030. . There are two reasons for that, ”the note states.

First, the organizations believe that the Hockey Social Model is not compatible with Denmark's obligation according to the Paris Agreement to reduce the country's CO2 emissions by 70 percent by 2030. This is justified by the fact that the target is based on »an assumption that linear is reduced Up to 2030 and on to Netto-Nul by 2040 '.

“It is crucial because it is the total amount of greenhouse gases discharged that counts when we have to slow down the climate crisis. And we emit significantly more CO2 from now to 2030 with the hockey stake approach than if we reduce linearly. With a hockey approach, Denmark does not comply with the greenhouse gas budget and thus fails the Paris Agreement, ”the NGOs write.

Therefore, it is proposed that the government's current bid for a minimum sub -target by 2025, a 46 percent reduction, is changed to a minimum of the linear target of 54.8 percent to avoid a cumulated additional emission by 2030 of 40.7 million tonnes of CO2.

Hockey Garden is based on immature technologies
The organizations also point out that the argument for the Hockey Garden is based on "technological development will make it possible and cheaper to achieve large reductions just before 2030". But it is neither "credible, wise or cheap to await technological development to reach the 70 percent," they say:

“If it is up to the government, immature technologies must account for the vast majority of total reductions - not least through the catch and storage of CO2 (CCS). The government's suggestions on what the technological fixes can contribute is so temporally unrealistic and costly that the prerequisite for a hockey reduction is not present. "

The organizations highlight CCS technology, which according to the government's climate program has a technical reduction potential of DKK 4-9 million. tonnes in 2030, equivalent to 29-66 percent of the lack of reductions to achieve the Paris Agreement's target.

"That estimate has both researchers and a very large part of the relevant market players questioned the realism of realism. That such great potential is questionable, there are several reasons," the note states, partly because:

»The very high estimate of the potential for CCS assumes that virtually all major point emission sources (cogeneration, waste incineration, process industry, biogas) will have installed CO2 capture, and that many of these sources also in 2030 and the subsequent many years will have a lot big CO2 emissions. "

According to the memo, it will require "significant lifetime extensions of the plants, and with the declared political ambitions to reduce the amounts of waste and electrify the electricity sector, the heating sector and parts of the process industry, these prerequisites are therefore very problematic".

In addition, Denmark has an unspeakable high consumption of solid biomass in the cogeneration, which should be greatly reduced over the next decade, it is added. In addition, the note mentions that the real price for establishing CCS is still unknown, "but is likely to be among the most expensive technologies for CO2 reduction".

The Minister of Climate rejects criticism and points to energy islands
The 14 NGOs recommend that the government reschedule its course to live up to the words of the Climate Act, drop its hockey-tag approach and, as a "absolute minimum", pursues a linear reduction path, equivalent to a sub-target of 54.8 percent in 2025.

"If you are based on the year for the conclusion of the Paris Agreement, the reduction target should be 60 percent," they write, and also mention that the government's bid for the "immature" technologies' potential is not realistic.

"Much more should be focused on real here-and-now reductions and put far more realistic expectations of technology development and its potential," the organizations write, adding that the agreements entered into and settlement on, among other things, transport, green tax reform, energy and industry May be renegotiated in 2021.

»Even with the prospect of further reductions in construction and agriculture, we must see a more credible bid to get all sectors more ambitious in the transition. The goal of the renegotiations must be to make it probable that the 70 percent target will be achieved by 2030, and that we live up to the Paris Agreement and our historical and moral responsibility to lead the way. "

The memo points out that "a guiding principle in the Climate Act, that Denmark must be a pioneering country in international climate action" and that the Hockey Coast model is not compatible with that ambition.

Here, it is pointed out that the UN's 'Emission Gap Report 2020' assigns a reverse hockey stake to reach the goal of limiting the global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees by the end of this century.

"If the rest of the world follows the government's strategy and postpone the real reductions while focusing massively on uncertain plans for negative emissions, then already by 2030, the total emissions will far exceed the CO2 budget for 1.5 degrees," the 14 NGOs write is.

In a written commentary on Information, Climate Minister Dan Jørgensen (S) rejects the NGOs' criticism and calls it an "objectively wrong statement" that Denmark should not be well on its way to a CO2 reduction of 70 percent by 2030.

Dan Jørgensen points out that the government has made "a large number of historical agreements" such as the Climate Act, the Energy Islands and the cancellation of new oil hunting in the North Sea in the past year.

Denmark risks having too few offshore wind turbines in 2030 to cover the electricity consumption for electrolysis and power-to-x (PTX), which is necessary to meet the 70 percent reduction in CO2 emissions.

This is the consequence that the schedule for the establishment of the two upcoming energy islands and a total of 5 GW of new offshore wind seems to be teeming after the latest political agreement in the area.

Electricity consumption for PTX - Production of hydrogen and green fuels for the transport sector in particular - depends on many factors and is uncertain to predict, but is based on two overlapping estimates from the consultancy company EA Energy Analysis and the Industry Organization Dansk Energi, respectively, an electricity consumption is expected to be between 15 and 20 TWH in 2030.

At the same time, a survey of specific Danish PTX projects carried out by the Engineer shows that there are currently plans to expand the electrolysis capacity of up to 4.5 GW-which already exceeds the preconditions that many projections are based on.

“If it goes as it seems with PTX at the moment, then we have to revise our portfolio of renewable energy, so that we are sure that offshore wind will come to meet the electrolysis requirement. The game changer here is if the PTX development goes faster than anyone had expected, and here is our most important buffer the sea wind, ”says professor of energy planning at Aalborg University Brian Vad Mathiesen.

And there can easily be a piece to the target, because according to the figures behind the Danish Energy Agency's upcoming climate write -off writing, only about 14 TWh new offshore wind production will be added annually until 2030 if none of the energy islands become ready before then.

An 'unacceptable' uncertainty
When the political decision to erect the two energy islands in the Baltic Sea and the North Sea was made this summer, respectively, it was with the promise that they should be completed by 2030 with a total of 5 GW of new offshore winds connected.

But in a partial agreement from the beginning of February, it seems that the island in the North Sea with 3 GW connected "is deemed difficult to realize" before 2033, and that the offshore wind by the island in the Baltic (Bornholm) may be expanded step -by to step to after 2030.

Since offshore wind is exposed as the most important renewable energy source to supply power to PTX, the actors in the green transition cannot be served with uncertainty, says energy sale and partner in EA Energy Analysis Hans-Henrik Lindboe:

"If we want to feed part of our transport and industrial sectors with PTX fuel by 2030, we- with everything we know now- cannot accept uncertainty and delay in the offshore wind," he says.

Hans-Henrik Lindboe is completely unaware of the new timeframe for the energy island of the North Sea, which he believes can easily be realized before 2030.

You agree with this approach at Dansk Energi.

“I think the deal is unnecessarily conservative. I do not see reason why there should be this postponement. The time frame should probably depend on what the bidders of the project think is realistic, rather than what the politicians have said in an agreement, ”says Torsten Hasforth, senior economist at Dansk Energi.

In addition to the problem of obtaining enough green power to PTX, a number of experts and professionals point out that Denmark lacks a coherent strategy for the PTX projects being invested in.

"The projects are largely driven by the business case that you have just been able to see for the individual project, rather than how the plant can be included in the overall energy system," points out Professor Jacob Østergaard of DTU Elektro.

Title: Ministerium afviser tilkobling af havvind fra Nordsøen før energiø er helt færdig: »Helt skørt«
Full text:
The government believes there is plenty of green power for the development of power-to-X by 2030 and therefore refuses to expand and connect the offshore wind to Energiø North Sea step-by-step. Professionals point out, on the contrary, that it can mean supply of black power.

If Denmark is to go to the target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 70 percent by 2030, several reports point out that we need an extension of electrolysis capacity to displace fossil fuels via power-to-x. As the engineer mapped last week, concrete projects have now been announced with a total of 4.5 GW electrolysis capacity in 2030.

But we do not immediately have the prospect of a WE capacity that can match the expansion of electrolysis plants.

As the Engineer described last week, several professionals and experts therefore strongly urge the Energiø Nordsøen to be expanded step -by -step, just as it has been agreed to do with Energiø Bornholm, whose grid connection agreements from the island to partner countries pull out to the other side of 2030.

But it cannot be done in the North Sea, says the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Supply in a written response to the Engineer's Energy Media, Gridtech, and thus there is no prospect of getting the offshore wind from the island in the North Sea ashore before 2030. The latest political agreement on the Energy Islands is estimated to be the island in the North Sea, namely to get ready before 2033.

Ministry: Zero connection before the island is ready
»The energy island in the North Sea is dependent on establishing a physical island construction in the North Sea, where the produced offshore wind can be collected and redistributed. With the agreement of February 4, 2021, there is ownership and construction of energy islands, etc. Making a decision that the construction of the North Sea must be an artificial reclamed island. Only when this island construction is ready will it be possible to connect the electricity grid and offshore wind capacity, ”the ministry writes to Gridtech.

In addition, the ministry emphasizes that the political settlement behind the islands depends on the prerequisite that the final projects will be self -supporting business:

“It is a prerequisite for the realization of the Energy Islands that they are profitable. It basically requires the power to be deposited. At present, it is expected that profitability and marketing of such large amounts of green current will require foreign connections. "

But experts maintain that the power from the Energy Islands is quite indispensable by 2030 if the 70 percent target is to be reached. On Friday, the Climate Council also voted in the choir with its status report on the government's previous climate efforts. On page 40 of the report, the council writes as follows:

»In addition, the Climate Council considers that it is critical for other reductions, eg through power-to-x and general electrification, that the offshore wind turbine capacity that with climate agreement for energy and industry, etc. 2020 now is associated with the Energy Islands, will be established. "

In the so-called climate program from last year, PTX appeared as one of the key measures in relation to the 70 percent target, and the government estimated that the technology could contribute reductions of between 0.5 and 3.5 million tonnes of CO2 equivalents.

In its commentary of the climate program, the Climate Council has since pointed out that it is necessary to realize the high estimates of all the government's identified reduction potentials if the target is to be achieved by 2030.

A pity answer
Torsten Hasforth, senior economist at Dansk Energi, calls the Ministry's answer to 'sorry' and is particularly concerned if the schedule for the offshore wind from Energiø Bornholm also ends up looking uncertain.

However, he recognizes the ministry's logic in waiting for the islands to have connections to other countries, as the associated offshore wind will probably be too big a mouthful to subside for Danish electricity consumers alone.

Conversely, the rigid approach can become a bet for the potential bidders of the offshore wind parks. He points out that today it is normal to add the capacity of offshore wind parks continuously, so that the first mills to be set up should not stand still and wait for the last mills to be erected.

"At least it will be an exciting task for those who have to bid on the offshore wind to Energiø North Sea, that the economy of the mills becomes completely dependent on when the island is finished and this 'prop' is raised so that the current can come ashore , 'Says Torsten Hasforth, emphasizing that it is further sharpened by the fact that the offshore wind parks for energy islands are far greater than previous projects.

Pears and bananas
GridTech has also asked the ministry how to make sure to ensure that the offshore wind development could keep up with the expansion of the electrolysis capacity by 2030.

To that, the Ministry replied:

»In the Danish Energy Agency's basic projection 2020, a GOV share of 111 per cent is expected. of Denmark's electricity consumption in 2030 without the establishment of the two energy islands. Thus, it is already with the agreed offshore wind capacity and assuming road expansion on land an "surplus of green stream", which can, for example, support a PTX development by 2030. "

Chief consultant at Wind Denmark, Thomas Young Hwan Westring Jensen believes that the reference to the basic projection in this context is very misleading.

"It is quite crazy to use the basic projection here, as it is a frozen policy scenario and therefore does not include the increased electricity consumption that 70 percent target will result in. It's a pure pear-and-banana comparison, ”he says.

Use prerequisites for the 70 percent target
He believes it would be more accurate to use the Danish Energy Agency's analysis prerequisites 2020, which, unlike the basic projection, aims to direct the road to the 70 percent target by 2030, including the necessary direct and indirect electrification.

In this projection, the board has provided 1 GW electrolysis capacity in 2030 with 5,000 annual operating hours, ie 5 TWH. According to Thomas Young Hwan Westring Jensen, this corresponds to the excess of electricity of 11 percentage points that the basic projection from last year reached.

“According to my calculations, one gigawatt will just be enough to fulfill the low estimate of technology's reduction potential of 0.5 million tonnes in the government's climate program. The only problem is that a postponement of the energy islands will mean that up to 23 TWh may be missing in 2030. If you are correct and deduct biomass as renewable energy, it will mean that green power is generally missing in 2030. And if you look at The high reduction potential of 3.5 million tonnes looks even worse as it will require another 30 TWH, ”says Thomas Young Hwan Westring Jensen.

Risking black power to PTX
At Dansk Energi, too, there is only the main shake over the use of basic projection as a management tool when it comes to the development of PTX.

The trade organization was at the forefront of the work of calculating the climate partnership for the energy and industrial sectors' bid for the best path to the conversion of society by 2030. If the electrification measures from that report are counted, Denmark will be transformed into a deficit, explains, explains Torsten Hasforth.

If the Energy Islands are kept completely out of the calculation, his calculations on the basis of the latest figures from the Danish Energy Agency (prerequisites for the upcoming KF21) show that only 85-90 percent of electricity consumption in 2030 will be offset by production capacity from VE.

“If we get the necessary electrification by 2030, but first the wind turbines will get the wind turbines, then the power risks turning black for a period of time and it would be a pity. It is not alarming, but it is not in any way an optimal solution described here in the answer, ”says Torsten Hasforth, referring to the ministry's approach to connection of Energiø North Sea.

He points out that a faster expansion of Ve can only benefit an upcoming PTX industry in Denmark, as their capital-heavy plants will depend on driving as many of the hours of the year as possible.

»The PTX adventure goes hand in hand with the fact that we also become an exporter of green power, because it will mean that we will be able to deliver in cheap electricity in a lot of day hours. If the balance between domestic electricity consumption and production becomes more delicate, our electricity price will also fluctuate more, and that will push the business case for the PTX systems, which will depend on running as many hours as possible, ”he says.

Title: Energiøernes øverste ansvarlige: »Alt ved de her ø-projekter er ret specielt«
Full text:
While several players are already waiting impatiently for the upcoming energy islands, work begins at sea soon. Our colleague at Gridtech has asked the head of the huge project how to make sure it gets as soon as possible.

Not only do the upcoming energy islands in the Baltic Sea and the North Sea respectively are the largest construction project in Danish history. And that the technical complexity pushes to the limits of engineering knowledge's utmost ability. And that the entire billion-dollar success is largely due to political dispositions in the countries around us. 

The giant project should preferably also be finished in a furious speed.

Originally, both islands were intended to be fully developed and connected to the respective partner countries by 2030. With a political sub -agreement on the islands from February, however, the deadline was postponed to 2033 for the island in the North Sea, while the schedule for the establishment of Energiø Bornholm also were made more fluid.

More than any other public instance, it is the Energinet that right now has the hands of the Energy Islands. Last year, the state -owned company was required to embark on the extensive preliminary investigations for all parts of the projects. They must be finished by 2024 and are expected to run in a price of more than one billion kroner. 

The studies include everything from seabed surveys for wind farms to screening the any lines of the HVDC connections to the preparation of the requirements specifications of an artificial island construction as well as the plants to stand on it.

Everything is different
According to Energinet's top responsible for Energiø projects, Hanne Storm Edlefsen, it is a matter of a very short time before working with energy islands becomes far more visible than before. Thus, the first tender for assignments for the feasibility studies has already been completed and is expected to start during the spring.

“Within so terrible long, when the weather has turned into it, the first ships will sail out into the areas and begin investigations. Precisely to boost this process, we have distributed the tasks of many different suppliers that work in parallel on all aspects of the projects at once, ”says Hanne Storm Eldlefsen.

And so it is the essence of the approach that will ensure quick expedition in Energinet's part of the project: parallel processes. It is a way of working that Energinet has already practiced a lot in connection with establishing its now -large portfolio of interconnectors, she explains. The Viking Link connection to the UK is the latest and so far longest if the first laying phase also begins this spring.

But so far, Energinet has been able to concentrate on one cable at a time. During the feasibility studies to the Energy Islands, the system manager must so far relate to four potential new foreign cables at the same time. 

And that relationship emphasizes very well what kind of task that Energinet has been imposed. 

“Everything about these island projects is quite special, partly because it is the first time someone in the world is building such islands, and partly because it is so large quantities of offshore winds we are working with. Just the 'small' project at Bornholm is in itself the largest Danish offshore wind project, 'says Hanne Storm Edlefsen.

The actual outlet for the project has also turned upside down compared to normal practice, she explains, as connecting two countries' electrical systems with each other is usually something the TSOs themselves think of. This time it is political ordering work.

"It is also unusual for us to be in preliminary investigations at a time when there is not yet a belligerent agreement with another country to establish a foreign connection," she says.

The missing agreements, for example, mean that Energinet cannot investigate specific lines yet, but simply screen larger sea areas to get an idea of ​​where it is technically, environmentally and interested in terms of interest to draw the upcoming submarine cables.

Cables are the prerequisite
So far, the island in the North Sea has met most interest from abroad. The Netherlands, Belgium and Germany have thus entered into agreements at both state and TSO levels and are currently participating in the work to count on the best business case on each connection.

For the project at Bornholm, so far only Germany has formally entered into the collaboration, while Poland has been promoted as an obvious candidate. According to Hanne Storm Edlefsen, it is also hoped on the connection from the nearest Nordic countries. Here, Sweden could be a possible partner on the island in the Baltic Sea. For Norway, the island in the North Sea looks more obvious.

Right now, it is especially the foreign cables and negotiations with the interested countries that are filling with Hanne Storm Edlefsen. For it is precisely at this point that the two projects risk beaches. If you fail to make agreements on the cables at all, the projects actually look dead, as the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Supply Ministry has previously provided to Gridtech in an email:

“It is a prerequisite for the realization of the Energy Islands that they are profitable. It basically requires the power to be deposited. At present, it is expected that profitability and marketing of such large amounts of green current will require foreign connections. "

Construction choices delay the project
It is precisely the uncertainty in getting the foreign connections negotiated in place that is the reason why the February part politicians did not dare to guarantee an artificial island in the North Sea before 2033. And just working with the cables made the politicians even more difficult to decide that the island should be an artificial, reclaimed island rather than the more offshore-haired design form with steel platforms.

“The fact that you have chosen an artificially reclaimed island gives rise to some slightly long -term processes in relation to the organization of cable work. For example, we cannot engage in dialogue with the partner country about the specific requirements specifications for their part of the project before we know the connection conditions on the island quite precisely, ”says Hanne Storm Edlefsen.

This month, the Danish Energy Agency will hold the initial meetings with interested actors and consortia who would like to help build and partly own an artificial energy island in the North Sea. It must be done in partnership with a public body, which according to Hanne Storm Edlefsen could well be the Energinet himself, but there is no clarification yet.

So far, it is 'only' the foreign connections that the electricity network operator must be responsible for in the construction phase when the preliminary examinations are completed. And here the parallel processes will come into play again.

“We are preparing as best as possible on the day we then know what the island will look like. At that time, we will make sure to send tendering on everything from station buildings to cables at the same time and make sure that all components and materials are produced at the same time, so that our part of the construction phase can go as soon as possible, ”she says.

Title: Energi-øer og Power-to-X udfordrer net-udbygning
Full text:
Direct cable connection to PTX plants and abroad can make a quietly hated high voltage masts, according to a citizen group. Experts and Energinet, on the other hand, announce several wires.

Energy Mastslimbearms Wreath Morning Air

How should the energy island in the North Sea be connected to Denmark purely in terms of Denmark, and how is it going to affect the Danish high voltage network?

The questions are not yet clarified if you ask Energinet, which is responsible for the electricity transmission network in Denmark - but a local citizen group would like to give its bids.

The citizen group, which is against an upcoming expansion with 400-KV high-voltage lines in West Jutland, has read a number of reports from COWI to the Danish Energy Agency about the net connection between the offshore wind farms and the energy island in the North Sea.

And on the basis of data and prices from these reports, the citizen group believes that now very large quantities of offshore wind turbine power can be delivered directly abroad or to PTX systems with heavy DC cables, there will be no more need for such a high-voltage network inland.

Therefore, the high -voltage line in West Jutland should be abandoned immediately and instead converted to a couple of buried DC cables across the country that can transport offshore wind turbine power over to East Jutland, where the large electricity consumption is located.

A conversion that, according to the citizen group, will be 1-2.6 billion. cheaper than building the high voltage line with its 500 masts.

We have asked a couple of independent electric experts and Energinet whether the citizen group has a point, so the West Jutland high voltage line should be canceled.

There is a point
In short, the two experts deny that the hated high voltage line can now be dropped. But they also point out that the citizen group has a point in that much more offshore winds via the energy islands as well as supply of large, concentrated electricity consumers such as Power-to-X plants will influence and create new conditions for the expansion of the electricity transmission network.

Paul-Frederik Bach-f. Director of Elsam/Eltra and recognized analyst of the electricity market-points out that small countries like Denmark benefit from being strongly linked to an international network and that traffic here is north-south-way.

»The political agreement on energy islands means an increased focus on wind energy from the North Sea, but the addition of energy islands will not reduce the energy that will be ashore in Denmark and passed on through Danish networks. This means that north-south-going traffic is dominant, which characterizes the web's current and future structure, ”writes Paul-Frederik Bach in his answer to us.

He also points out that the West Jutland high -voltage connection is part of an international agreement on a reinforced transmission system from which Energinet does not have the opportunity to run.

Part of Viking Link
Civil engineer and partner in EA Energy Analysis Hans Henrik Lindboe, who has a past at Elkraft System, justifies its no with the fact that the 400-kv high voltage line is part of the project Viking Link cable between Denmark and England, and that the wire must act as a reserve if the cable to England of 1,400 MW falls out.

According to the 'constitution of the electricity grid', one must be able to match an outcome of the largest unit in the system - otherwise you risk that both Jutland and Funen go in black:

"You can't put Viking Link into operation without the West Coast connection, so the timing itself is the biggest obstacle if you, as the citizen group, want to avoid the unpopular overhead lines," he says.

Hans Henrik Lindboe adds that in a future with more and more renewable energy, we must generally have to pay us on the need for much more exchange with abroad and thus also the need for domestic infrastructure, which is unfortunately solved most securely with hated high voltage masts:

"Power-to-X system and an actual hydrogen infrastructure are one of the things that can limit the need for high-voltage lines in the future," he says.

Must collect from multiple plants
At Energinet, you also do not buy the citizen group's proposal on the grounds that the upcoming north-south-going 400-kv Air line along the west coast of Jutland from the border to Idomlund at Holstebro cannot be avoided.

Partly because, as mentioned earlier, it must serve as a backup for the Viking Link connection if it becomes faulty, and partly because it has to collect electricity from wind turbine and photovoltaic systems throughout West Jutland. Including electricity from the upcoming offshore wind farm Thor:

"These needs are not changed by establishing an energy island in the North Sea," states area manager Bjarne Brendstrup from Energinet.

A direct current line across Jutland cannot fulfill this task - as the citizen group has suggested - as Energinet needs to be able to collect the renewable energy established in West Jutland, and from there the power has been transported to consumption.

Brendstrup also explains that if you were to use direct current connections as suggested by the citizen group, the projects will be so complicated that they are not realistic to implement because many new components had to be built.

However, Bjarne Brendstrup would like to promise that in the future planning around the connection of the energy islands to the Danish electricity grid, much will be done to minimize the need for more high-voltage lines.

It is expected that the net connection of the energy island will happen at one or more central nodes in the 400-kv network in Jutland, and that connections in East Jutland are also considered. But right now is working to find the technically and financially best solution that at the same time minimizes the need for online developments to the extent possible:

»Electricity transmission relations are both expensive and to the nuisance of citizens, so it is clear that we would rather find other solutions, and therefore we are currently investigating a number of solutions to find the technically-economic best solution that at the same time minimizes the need for online developments, ”he says, adding that it is, among other things, about connecting the cables in the places where consumption is high.

Unpredictable change
Neither for Energinet there is doubt that the green transition will entail a high degree of electrification of Danish energy consumption and thus an increasing electricity consumption-both in the form of new consumers such as PTX plants and as a general increase in electricity consumption, Which will all affect the 400-KV network in Denmark.

At the same time, the development is now happening with unprecedented speed and is characterized by high unpredictability, as Energinet itself writes in one of its reports, and this means that one looks into a very uncertain future with many ways to achieve the politically determined climate objectives.

Last fall, for example, Energinet issued a report on long -term development needs for the electricity grid, which operated with different scenarios, which according to Bjarne Brendstrup are already outdated:

“The scenarios we worked with back then, we have to re-look now that the energy islands and plans for Power-to-X systems have come into the picture. It shows how fast the development is currently going, 'he says.

Title: Grønt søslag forude: Energiøer og naturvenner ønsker sig samme dele af Nordsøen
Full text:
While the Danish Nature Conservation Association and the Danish Fisheries Association have agreed on where there may be pristine areas on the Danish Sea, they are in direct conflict with the plans for wind turbines at the North Sea Energiø.

Fishermen and nature friends agree which 10 per cent. of the North Sea, Skagerrak and the Baltic Sea, which should be appointed to pristine sea, so that Denmark can get closer to living up to the EU's target of untouched sea. So far, so good.

However, the plan is in direct conflict with the plans for wind turbines and energy island in the North Sea, where the space is becoming increasingly cramped, because renewable energy and nature protection are filling more and more in areas where ship routes as well as oil and gas fields also continue to take up space.

Six of the 24 areas that the Danish Nature Conservation Association (DN) has recommended for untouched sea in collaboration with the Danish Fisheries Association, overlap with the North Sea's supply areas for energy. It shows maps that the Wind Denmark trade association and DN have made at the engineer's request.

The supply areas are areas that the Danish Energy Agency has designated for future locations for wind turbines - some of them in connection with the energy island that will become the world's first of its kind.

"Frontal attack against offshore wind"
"It's a frontal attack against offshore wind turbines," energy professor at Aalborg University Brian Vad Mathiesen puts out when the engineer asks about the plan from the two associations.

“At least it is clear that it is a party post that goes by all other stakeholders. To get a unified picture, you need some more parties, ”he continues.

Brian Vad Mathiesen points out that it is inevitable that offshore winds will fill "an essential part of the North Sea" when the energy form is to be expanded to meet the country's climate target.

"Conversely, the mills are constantly getting bigger, so it is possible that the energy can be produced in a smaller area than expected," he points out.

According to the wind turbine industry's interest organization Wind Denmark, it is especially the proximity to the North Sea's planned energy island that can pose a problem. The energy island is scheduled to be in the northern part of the area called by the Danish Energy Agency the North Sea III, where it will be surrounded by offshore wind farms to supply electricity to the island.

Initially, the parks must deliver 3 GW, but the area will eventually be expanded to 10 GW. And just here, all three of the designated areas can get in the way, so the parks are forced further away from the island, points out Thomas Hwan Jensen, chief consultant at Wind Denmark.

"For the energy island, it can mean that the wind turbines, which can be located in the North Sea II, must be moved further away, so that the project becomes more expensive and that planning becomes more cumbersome," he estimates.

If you ask DN, overlap between the tendering areas and the areas in the association's presentation is inevitable, because as much as 27 per cent. of the North Sea are included in tender areas. In addition, areas in use for other purposes.

“When you lay out areas for offshore wind, you take some very large areas that are only partially exploited. This is our best bet on where to place the areas with untouched sea, but we would like to have a dialogue with, for example, Wind Denmark about our areas in relation to their wishes for offshore wind, ”says Nature & Environment Political Advisor in the Association Therese Nissen .

The areas for offshore wind have been designated by the Danish Energy Agency as part of a screening where the board found a total of 40 GW of offshore wind. In comparison, approx. 1.7 GW offshore wind turbines in Denmark, while projects underway can come up with a total maximum capacity of an additional approx. 8.7 gw.

It is especially sea depths, conservation, the distance to land and traveled ship routes that limit wind turbine planning today.

Can wind turbines protect nature?
The proposal from DN and the Danish Fisheries Association aims to appoint 10 per cent. of the North Sea, Skagerrak, and the Baltic Sea around Bornholm, which must be completely untouched. If Denmark succeeds in appointing them, Denmark is approaching the EU's target of just 10 per cent. pristine sea throughout the Union.

In addition, the EU's target of 30 per cent. of the seas of the Union must be protected to some degree, as well as the Natura 2000 areas already designated.

Unpublished sea must be protected from buildings such as wind turbines, resource extraction of sand, oil and gas, fishing and so -called clapping, where sand and sludge are dumped in the sea. In addition, the Nature Conservation Association would like the areas to reduce ship traffic and that pipelines and cables did not cross the areas, all measuring at least 100 km2 per year. pcs.

Foundations are artificial reef
At Wind Denmark, Thomas Hwan Jensen believes that nature protection can in many cases go hand in hand with wind turbines, as several studies indicate that the foundations for wind turbines act as artificial reefs promoting biodiversity.

“In our view, there is nothing to indicate that wind turbines should have a deterrent effect on fish and marine mammals such as seals and guinea pigs. In fact, there is much to point out that they have a positive influence. It is therefore important to consider what pristine sea actually aims to protect. If, on the other hand, the consideration is for a vulnerable seabed, we cannot escape that the foundations can cause a loss, ”he points out.

The same point has Brian Vad Mathiesen:

“When offshore winds have to fill so much, it is quite crucial that we can benefit more interests in the same area and, for example, take natural considerations in the same place as we produce electricity. And studies from Horns Rev 1 and 2 indicate that it can be done, ”he emphasizes.

In the Danish Society for Nature Conservation, Therese Nissen knows the arguments of artificial reefs, but the association has emphasized identifying different habitats in the selected areas, which artificial reefs could change.

“In these areas it is about preserving nature. It is possible that wind turbines can be good as a reef, but thus they also transform a sandy bottom into reefs and attracts other species, ”she points out and compares with the situation on land where it is not legal to replace one habitat with another in a nature protection area.

For the association, it is important that the areas are designated for their biology and thus ensure coherence between the areas and that they are representative in relation to bottom types and depths, Therese Nissen points out.

“So if there are areas in our agreement that possibly. Overlaps with potential offshore wind areas, then DN and the Danish Fisheries Association like a dialogue with the wind sector about how climate and nature protection and conservation can easily go hand in hand, ”she says, and continues:

Not at all unrealistic
“We had an area that was directly where the energy island was to be. We have already moved this together with the Danish Fisheries Association before the plan came out, ”she says, elaborating that the association would like to take it up with Wind Denmark.

Overall, however, Wind Denmark is positive towards the target of 10 per cent. pristine sea.

“It doesn't sound unrealistic at all, and it allows us to be a pioneer in a new area. When reviewing Aarhus University's mapping of possible protected marine areas, which were carried out in connection with the upcoming sea plan, it should be possible to find alternative locations for the areas where there is an overlap. In this way, we ensure that the environment and climate go hand in hand, rather than turning into each other's contradictions, ”says Thomas Hwan Jensen.

Title: Den grønne omstilling kræver investeringer på 80 milliarder kroner i det danske elnet
Full text:
The Danish electricity network requires investments for up to DKK 80 billion by 2040, a new analysis from Ramboll shows.

The analysis, made for Wind Denmark, shows that huge sums must be invested in the electricity infection structure alone. The electrification of Danish society is a major part of the 2030 reduction target, and the Danish Energy Agency expects electricity consumption to rise by up to 83 percent by 2030 as a result of the green transition. 

In order to enable such an increase, investments in renewable energy production and the electric infrastructure must be made in particular to transport the renewable energy.

However, there are uncertainties about the actual amount as the cost of various elements and strategies remains unknown. For example, the upcoming energy islands are included in the analysis and intended to run up to about DKK 10 billion per year. Energiø. However, different approaches to construction and size can significantly affect the real price. 

The analysis is based on publicly available reports and analyzes of the need for the development of the electricity grid.

Title: Energianalytiker: Uden strøm fra energiøer i 2030 kommer 70-procent-målet i fare
Full text:
Energy sale Hans Henrik Lindboe criticizes the schedule for Energiø North Sea, which is only expected to be fully connected in 2033. The project should be made more independent of agreements on foreign connections, he believes.

The economy of the two giant energy island projects in the Baltic Sea and the North Sea are completely dependent on the establishment of a foreign connection for each of the islands for at least one other partner country. Due to uncertainty about when such cables can be established, the largest of the islands, Energiø North Sea, has now been postponed to 2033, and it has got a large number of energy players up in the red field.

One of them is energy salary Hans Henrik Lindboe, partner in EA Energy Analysis. According to him, the 70 percent target of the Climate Act is simply at risk of not being met unless both energy islands with a total of 5 GW offshore wind are fully connected to Denmark by 2030. Originally, both islands were to be completed and connected to the Danish electricity system as early as 2030. Provides deficit of 10 TWH in 2030

If we do not follow the electrification with the expansion of renewable energy, including especially on the large offshore parks, then we will not get the full gain from the rescheduling that we would otherwise like to see, ”says professors emeritus from DTU Vindenergi and a member of the Climate Council , Poul Erik Morthorst.

However, he suggests a slightly different solution to the scarcity of ve-stream until 2030:

Title: Forskere: Sådan undgår pattedyr høreskader fra Energi-ø-undersøgelser
Full text:
Although acoustic measurement of the seabed before building energy islands can cause permanent hearing damage to marine mammals, it can easily be avoided, researchers conclude prior to the studies.

Before energy islands can be built in the North Sea and the Baltic Sea, the seabed must be mapped precisely, and one of the methods uses acoustic shock waves so powerful that they risk damaging the hearing on marine mammals permanently.

Researchers from DCE at Aarhus University have therefore examined precisely how the acoustic shock waves from a so -called kicker affect the populations of guinea pigs, white nose, minke whale, spotted seal and gray seal in the North Sea.

This is stated in a press release from DCE, which together with NIRAS has prepared a report for each of the energy islands' areas prior to the strategic environmental impact assessments and the offer of concessions on the offshore wind farms.

Spark and air bubble
The kicker is used to make high -resolution measurements of the seabed using sound waves in the frequency range between 1 and 4 kHz. The waves are made by electrodes in the kicker, creating a spark that causes an air bubble that collapses and creates the sound wave.

This wave can thus be so powerful that marine mammals can take permanent damage from it, points out. Seals can be damaged within 50 meters of the kicker, guinea pigs 620 meters away and minke whales as much as 1400 meters from the study, the researchers point out.

In addition, all the species included in the study will respond to the sound at a distance of 11 km from the study ship. However, the solution to the marine mammals' hearing problems is right, the researchers point out.

"The risk of permanent hearing loss for marine mammals can probably be reduced to negligible when using a soft start procedure as a mitigation measure," states the report on the North Sea's Energiø.

Soft start means that the appliance initially works at lower strength or at longer intervals, thus scaring animals in the area before turning it up on a strength that can cause permanent hearing loss.

Natura2000 areas may be hit
A 11 km radius from the study ship means that two Natura2000 areas in the Baltic Sea will be hit by the acoustic waves to a degree to affect the marine mammals. These are the areas of Adler and Rønne Banke, according to DCE's report on the Baltic Sea area.

The report suggests reducing the impact by moving the study area further away from the two areas. This is because the so-called JNCC guidelines for Natura2000 areas indicate that a maximum of 20 per cent. of the area must be affected by this type of disturbance.

The researchers from DCE conclude that the areas are combined in 34 per cent. of the area and therefore is more affected than the JNCC guideline prescribes. In addition, there are actually three areas, the worst affected is the Danish part of Rønne Banke, where as much as 59 per cent. is affected.

Other parts of the studies must be used to use devices that either make sounds outside the animals' hearing area or use magnetometer and are therefore silent, points out DCE, which has therefore not assessed these parts of the studies.

Corrected on 7/4 2021 12:15am: It appeared earlier from the last sentence of the article that one could choose to use other types of studies instead of the kicker. This is not the case, as the other two studies mentioned must be used in addition to the kicker in the feasibility studies and cannot replace this part of the study.

Title: Investorer bakker op om dyr energiø

Title: De skal undersøge havbunden under energiøen i Nordsøen
Full text:
The seabed under the upcoming energy island in the North Sea must be examined and mapped thoroughly before working to build the island itself and the large offshore wind farms around the island can start. Energinet has just assigned the task to two experienced marine survey companies, which are expected to sue with their ships in the North Sea in May.

The two companies are Fugro and MMT.

Their ships are charged with, among other things, seismic equipment, which will meticulously map the seabed under the more than 1000 square kilometers in the North Sea, where the artificially recessed energy island and the total 3 GW large offshore wind farms must be built, Energinet writes on its website.


- The geophysical studies must cover a very large area and it is important that the schedule is kept. That is why we are pleased that two very experienced and professional companies such as Fugro and MMT will carry out the studies at sea in the North Sea in the coming time, says Poul-Jacob Vilhelmsen, project manager for Energinet's work with the upcoming energy islands in Danish waters.

Together with other feasibility studies, the geophysical mapping of the seabed must make it possible to perform the construction work in connection with the energy island, the surrounding offshore wind farms and sea cables in a way that ensures both technical feasibility and the greatest possible consideration of nature and the environment.

Seabud is examined 100 meters into the ground
The North Sea is relatively shallow even 80-100 kilometers out to sea, where the artificial island and offshore wind farms are to be built. In the study area, the sea is between 25 meters and 50 meters deep.

In May, specialized ships from the two sea study companies therefore begin at the work of investigating and mapping the surface of the seabed and the geological layers down to 100 meters below the seabed.

Ice ages, sea battles and boulders
The geophysical conditions on and below the seabed are characterized by both the geological development history of the earth and by the human own activities throughout history.

Sandbanks, reef created by biological life and boulders are examples of geological elements that the ships from Fugro and MMT must map meticulously.

But the ships are expected to also sail across a few shipwrecks in the area from the largest sea battle of world history, the Jutland Battle of 1916, and they will have to identify so -called not exploded objects, ie typically grenades and mines from World War II.

The man -made conditions on the seabed, which are to be mapped, also belong to existing search cables and pipelines as well as more contemporary traces such as waste, equipment from fishing and rifts in the seabed from ship anchors, etc.

The geophysical studies, together with later drilling samples, must result in a detailed, digital mapping of the seabed and the geological layers under the seabed throughout the area during the upcoming artificial energy island in the North Sea and surrounding offshore wind farms.

Energiø in the North Sea:
An energy island is a gathering place for large quantities of energy from offshore wind. From the energy island, the energy is transformed and forwarded to several countries.
The energy island in the North Sea will supply 3 GW offshore winds increasing against 10 GW later.
The energy island in the North Sea becomes an artificial island construction consisting of one or more types of lower boxes 80 km. Out in the sea from the Danish coast - initially with an area equal to 18 football fields. 
About 200 wind turbines on the sea will produce the 3 GW in the first phase when the energy island in the North Sea is in operation. The wind turbines will probably be higher than before, perhaps up to 260 meters high. It is higher than, for example, the pylons on the Great Belt Bridge.
DKK 210 billion are the estimated total investment costs for the energy island in the North Sea including 10 GW of offshore wind farms, electrical plants on the island and transport cables to land.

Title: Industri og fjernvarme: Energiøer før 2030 er afgørende for vores elektrificering
Full text:
A broad electrification of the industry and the district heating occurs only when there is security about the adequacy of green power, says trade organizations. Therefore, players who have to convert to EL are dissatisfied that the energy islands are only fully developed after 2030.

That's how the message from partner in EA Energy Analysis Hans Henrik Lindboe sounded here at Gridtech a few weeks ago. The opinion originated from the fact that the settlement circle behind the Energy Islands with its latest agreement has postponed the full realization of the islands to the other side of 2030.

Therefore, the island's total offshore wind capacity of 5 GW will not contribute big to the fulfillment of the 70 percent target, and according to Hans Henrik Lindboe's calculations, this will mean that green electricity generation capacity will be lacking within the country's borders by 2030 due to rising electricity consumption from a broad Electrification.

At Dansk Industri, therefore, you now also hear dissatisfaction from the members, which finds it unacceptable that such a large amount of green power will not be available until 2030.

“Our members have expressed dissatisfaction with the current schedule for the islands. Therefore, we have now gathered a number of members in energy in a working group to provide good advice and input on how we can accelerate the realization of the islands. There is a need to tighten the chain and can be tightened, ”says Troels Ranis, industry director for DI Energi.

The energy islands are essential brick
He emphasizes that DI is pleased that a broad political agreement has been made to realize the islands.

“But that being said, we will be really happy to get some speed in that realization. After all, electricity production from the 5 GW offshore winds that are affiliated lies as the foundation of the ambition that the Climate Partnership for Energy and Supply has set about almost fully phasing out fossil fuels by 2030, ”says Troels Ranis and continues:

"And the transition of the energy and supply sector is again a crucial prerequisite for a large part of the CO2 reductions in the other business sectors."

Regardless of the deferral of the energy islands, the effort to electrify widely in society is already underway. An example is in the food industry, which is among the largest energy consumers at home.

Here, DI is currently running a project with 20 business cases, where it is trying to analyze to analyze how deep the food industry can be reduced to the process technical level. But it will be beautiful wasted forces compared to the 2030 goal, if not also the ambitions for the energy islands' schedule are raised, explains Troels Ranis.

"It's one thing is to find out how much we can electrify, but if that electrification cannot be attributed to a CO2-neutral electricity supply, then it has no value in relation to the climate goals."

District heating will not be tied to electricity
In the heating sector, a comprehensive electrification has already begun until 2030, where district heating has as an independent goal of being completely fossil -free. In the past year, the number of large heat pumps in the district heating has exploded.

The further transition by 2030 will mean that the district heating producers are going from being a net producer of electricity to becoming a net consumer - and even one of the country's largest.

This is because the cogeneration plants in the competition with VE are expected to find it more difficult to get economy in electricity generation and will therefore be dramatically down in the coming years. Of course, for the electrification of district heating, it increases the importance of how the VE development is emerging.

“If there is not enough green electricity, then prices are rising a lot, and then you get a situation where it is neither competitive nor particularly green, because it will mean, among other things, the import of coal -based electricity. It is in direct contradiction to our own climate target, ”says Jesper Koch, Head of Analysis at Danish District Heating and head of the Green Energy Think Tank.

Among other things, because of this uncertainty, it is crucial for the district heating companies that in the future they continue to have the freedom to organize their supply so that it must not only be based on electricity.

»In view of the prospect of a possible lack of green power from the Energy Islands by 2030, it is particularly worrying for us that signals are sent to the same time that district heating should just look to get over on electricity - and only electricity - for the future , 'Says Jesper Koch.

“In any case, we will very much need to be 100 percent dependent on one source of the district heating supply. The contribution of district heating to both sector integration and competitiveness is based on the effective use of a wide pallet of green energy sources, ”he says.

Uncertainty gives hesitation in electrification
However, Jesper Koch does not believe that the question of the energy islands' schedule is specifically something that fills the current electrification decisions of the district heating companies, as they are still a bit out in the time horizon.

But there are already examples of how fast uncertainty about the future can lead to hesitation with electrification.

"Just to give a very contemporary example of how sensitive this area is, we have experienced district heating companies that hesitate with investments in electric kettles because of Energinet's work in adjusting the model for counter -trade in the electricity market," explains Jesper Koch with reference For the pending debate in the electricity industry to make the trade for special regulation more competitive.

Something similar will be the consequence if the energy islands and the abundant green power continue to be out of reach, he believes.

“This is about district heating to become 100 percent green by 2030 and at the same time maintain its competitiveness and minimize investment risks. We are in the process of investing in large, electric heat pumps, but if the energy islands are waiting and electricity prices are rising, then the district heating companies will simply cut down on electricity investments and safely for alternative green investments, ”he says.

Title: Sådan kunne et europæisk brint-net se ud i 2040
Full text:
A vision of 40,000 km of hydrogen pipes across Europe is a bid for hydrogen in the green Europe of the future. But gas and hydrogen behave differently.

Hydrogen based on renewable energy is in high price, and several European countries, especially the Netherlands and Germany, are far ahead with plans for the expansion of pipelines for transporting the hydrogen. This is mainly due to the need to replace fossil hydrogen with green alternatives for example in the steel and refinery industry.

Now 23 owners of the infrastructure for the transport of gas (TSOs) have been put together to formulate a vision of how the hydrogen can be transported from the production sites, for example, an energy island in the North Sea, and out to the consumption sites, joined forces to show how to expand with pipelines in a coherent hydrogen network in Europe.

In total, there are 40,000 kilometers of pipelines from northern Sweden to southern Italy and from Spain in the west to Greece in the east:

"A large number of European TSOs are keen to promote the green transition, and the network is thus our suggestions on how we can utilize the existing natural gas network for hydrogen and where there will be a need for extensions," says Stine Grenaa Jensen, There are area manager in Energinet Gas TSO.

Since such a conversion of parts of the natural gas network and expansion with new pipelines is not equal in a hand turn, the time frame is set to 2040.

But some areas of Europe are already far ahead, explains Stine Grenaa Jensen:

»In Germany and the Netherlands, there is a strong focus on getting the fossil hydrogen out of the processes in the steel and refinery industry. Therefore, you can probably also expect that this is where we will first see the establishment of a larger network, ”she says.

Denmark is going to be in progress
The TSOs that have participated in the visions have contributed the need for green hydrogen they see in the future and with the infrastructure they believe to be able to contribute.

This also applies to Denmark, where strokes have been drawn on the map. Among other things from the natural gas stock in Jutland and from an upcoming energy island in the North Sea:

“But we have also drawn new pipelines for our neighboring countries who would like to have access to hydrogen. This applies to both Sweden and Poland, ”says Stine Grenaa Jensen.

Converted natural gas lines
Part of the Danish hydrogen tube may be to consist of natural gas compounds that need to be converted to handle hydrogen. This is something that the technicians have been investigating for a number of years, and the right solutions are continued.

Therefore, it is also noteworthy that the British TSO, National Grid, plans to convert large parts of the British natural gas network to hydrogen.

Elsewhere, you will be able to see how new pipelines should connect existing natural gas lines across borders. There has also been room for a vision of hydrogen transported from plants in North Africa to Europe.

The steel becomes crispy
But even though the vision is that part of the existing transmission system for natural gas should be used for transporting hydrogen, different barriers can occur.

This explains Asger Myken, senior project manager at the Danish Guest Technical Center. For example, it is known knowledge that hydrogen can present challenges with components such as valves, regulators and compressors. On top of that, there is a risk that hydrogen will affect the steel in the pipes, so that the material becomes "crispy" and thus more easily breaks down.

At the same time, the European natural gas network is built with a large variation of components and to different standards:

"This does not mean that one would not be able to use the natural gas network for the transmission of hydrogen, but it will require the individual parts to be assessed individually. For example, this may mean that some components need to be replaced or the pressure in the pipe must be lowered, ”he says.

PTX strategy will come until the fall
In Denmark, several hydrogen projects are underway, including in Fredericia and Copenhagen, where hydrogen is expected to be produced on the basis of electricity from renewable energy.

Therefore, hydrogen is also an important component, both in IDA's Energy 2050 from 2016 and in IDA's climate response from last year. The climate response shows, among other things, that 40 GWh storage capacity for hydrogen must be established in order to ensure a flexible interaction between the production of green electricity and hydrogen.

But since a political strategy is still missing, Energinet has difficulty establishing an upcoming development plan, both in terms of stocks and pipelines.

Stine Grenaa Jensen emphasizes that the primary strategy is to use so much of the green Danish current for direct electrification:

“But it is clear that there will be a surplus and some of it must be converted to hydrogen, which can either be value -adding here in Denmark or can be exported. In this process, it is important that the infrastructure does not become a bottleneck, ”she says.

Title: Nu vil også Ørsted og ATP bygge energi-ø
