Accepting a fixed island
Ørsted has previously beaten the drum that it would be cheaper to build a number of platforms instead of a fixed island in the North Sea for connecting the offshore wind farms, but with the announcement of the new consortium the company has accepted that it will be a lower box- Ø in the sea.

"We look forward to making our contribution to realize this epoch -making infrastructure project with the best technological solutions and with the lowest costs and risks for the benefit of Danish society," says Mads Nipper, CEO of Ørsted in one press release.

For ATP, Bo Foged, CEO, estimates that the energy island of the North Sea is a really interesting investment opportunity for ATP, because it can both ensure good stable pensions, develop Danish positions of strength and at the same time become a crucial lever for the green transition in Denmark:

'Of course, the investment is not without risk that members must be compensated for, but Ørsted and ATP are a strong partnership, which has the right complementary skills to solve such a task. And then I am also pleased that with the collaboration we can ensure that the return from the project through ATP benefits all Danes, ”he says.

Market Consultations are underway
In a political agreement from February, it was stated that the energy island of the North Sea is a social task that is best solved by activating relevant competence across the state and market via a shared ownership between state and one or more private actors, where the state must, however be majority owner.

Now there are a number of so -called 'market consultations' between the Danish Energy Agency and interested parties, where one must determine the detailed process of the supply of the island.

Among other things, it must be decided how big the island should be.

According to a discussion proposal for this market dialogue, published by the Danish Energy Agency, a full-scale-energy island in the North Sea (ie with the connection of 10 GW offshore wind) is expected to cost 10, 9 billion. DKK in construction costs.

Title: Strid om betaling for elnettet kan true den grønne omstilling
Full text:
Under the surface, a rebellion in the energy industry lurks due to a passus in the summer's climate agreement that requires the VE developers to pay large parts of the extension of the electricity grid.

Energy Connection of VE systems can become expensive

Apparently, the Danish climate effort is going well: According to the latest official climate writing from last week, we have come much closer to the climate target over the past year.

Specifically, the so -called climate shoe - ie the CO2 reductions we have to find - has shrunk with just over eight million. ton, from 20 million. to 11.8 million ton of CO2 in 2030.

The explanation is especially found in the effect of the two climate agreements for waste and for energy and industry, which was concluded last summer - and saw that the interest in building new biogas plants has exploded.

But in the same climate agreement for energy and industry, you also find a passus, which has to that extent got developers of sun and wind farms out of the chairs and which according to them hold a potential threat to the green transition.

The passage is about who should pay for the expansion of the electricity grid to the green transition. And in this summer's climate agreement, politicians changed the principle that has been in force since the 1990s: that expenses for the expansion of the electricity grid in connection with the connection of new WE plants are initially paid for by the local electricity distribution company, which can then send The bill on to all the country's electricity consumers via a so-called equalization scheme, which is paid for via the PSO tariff on the electricity bill.

Instead, the politicians decided to let the bill move on to the WE producers from 2023 via some brand new geographically differentiated connection contributions and incorporation starters, which have not yet been designed.

The purpose of the change is, according to the agreement, to save electricity consumers money and at the same time to encourage the WE developers to place the plants where the electricity grid is already strong enough to buy and transport the road stream.

The change was completely behind the Danish energy industry. According to CEO Knud Erik Andersen of the VE developer European Energy, it was listed in the negotiations a late night time, and since then the industry has been trying to understand the new tariffs' extensive consequences for the renewable energy projects of the future.

It has not made the frustration less among the RE developers. Partly because clarification of how the new tariffs should be designed have long prospects, which slows down all new WE projects. Partly because the wording of the climate agreement can be interpreted as the fact that the Ve developers have to pay not only the costs of connecting the specific plants, but also a large part of the relatively large investments in the transmission and distribution network that the green conversion's increased electrification will require.

Big Summer at Game
And there are large sums at stake: According to a report from Ramboll - which the trade organization Wind Denmark has ordered - DKK 80 billion will be invested in the period from 2020 to 2040. DKK in grid connections, foreign connections, transmission networks and connection of energy islands, of which the VE developers will have to pay about DKK 30 billion. Ramboll has calculated.

In addition to this, the WE enclosers can look forward to extra expenses in the form of a grid connection fee as well as incorporation rigs from 2023, giving them a total additional cost of DKK 300 million. DKK annually until 2030.

The calculation is based on the Danish Energy Agency's projections for use by Energinet from 2020, with electricity consumption in 2030 expected to increase by 83 per cent. Compared to today- pris-felt as a result of new electricity consumption for heat pumps, electric kettles, large data centers, transport and power-to-x plants.

According to Director of Wind Denmark Jan Serup Hylleberg, this means that a large part of the VE projects will not be able to be realized and that we may therefore risk being missing WE capacity in 2030:

»The equalization scheme costs in the order of DKK 300 million. DKK per year. If the price of saving them on the Finance Act is that we need to again provide subsidies for new renewable energy capacity to reach the climate target, then we have shot ourselves in the foot, ”he says.

Carrot rather than whip
VE developer Better Energy's CEO, Rasmus Lildholdt Kjær, finds it very reasonable that the developers themselves pay for the direct connection for the individual plant, but not that he has to pay for new transmission lines in relation to a necessary expansion of the transmission network :

"One should collective costs and make it attractive for people to join the electricity grid- not punish them," he says, pointing out that, for example, this is the case in the gas field today, where the regulation just promotes connection to the gas network by collectivizing connection and net costs.

Another purpose of the new legislation is to get the WE developers to establish new plants where the grid is already strong, so that you need to spend as little money for online expansion as possible.

That argument is greeted with a main shake of the RE developers, which calls it a basic condition of WE-Extension, that suitable seats for sun and wind are far from the cities where the large electricity consumption lies.

In advance, the lack of electricity grids in the outer areas is a very big challenge for the WE projects. It typically takes two years to get the project connected to the distribution network and between two and five years if a project is to be connected to the transmission network. Even though there is already available capacity in the transmission network.

Better Energy, for example, has had to restrict its solar cell projects on Lolland-Falster from 2,000 MW to 700 MW, because electricity consumption in the islands is low and because the transmission network is not strong enough to transport the green power to consumers in, for example, the Copenhagen area.

So far, politicians-despite several meetings-have refused to change anything in the agreement, and climate minister Dan Jørgensen (S) maintains in a committee response in connection with a representative from the WE companies that the measures in the climate agreement are considered to contribute to a more cost-effective green transition , because electricity producers will contribute to the costs they give rise to more.

It is also stated in the answer that how much the developers must pay will appear in a new tariff method that Dansk Energi must develop for the distribution network and which must be approved by the Supply Authority. For the transmission network, it is Energinet that will develop the new tariff models.

Dansk Energi won't seize
Thus, the minister thus plays the ball to the trade organization Dansk Energi, which, however, refuses to seize it before there is clarity and instead returns to the politicians.

The trade association has both VE developers and grid companies as members, and therefore the influential industry organization must find a solution to the tariff question that all parties can see themselves in:

"We think the agreement text is very unclear, so - together with Wind Denmark - we have written to the minister and asked him to clarify the text on a number of points, and we also await a specific legal text. Before it is in place, it is not credible to make a bid for a tariff model, ”says Deputy Director Anders Stouge of Dansk Energi.

He is upset at all over the whole course of the climate agreement:

"We had clearly preferred that the politicians retain the collective equalization scheme and just moved it over to the Finance Act-as they actually agreed to do it back in 2016 when abolished the PSO scheme," he says.

In the brand new climate writing from the Danish Energy Agency, it is estimated that the extension with solar parks - of which the private developers stand for the majority, and which is mainly done without grants - will continue at a fast pace until 2030, where there will be 8,500 MW solar capacity, which is 4.5 times more than today.

The capacity from the rural mills is expected to only rise by 1,000 MW - from 4,700 MW today to 5,700 MW in 2030.

The Bill on the new tariffs is expected to be made in the fall, and then the next act is waiting in the fight for payment for the expansion of the electricity grid.

Title: Mangel på arbejdskraft: Vindmølleeventyret skaber jobfest på danske havne
Full text:
The Danish commercial ports are expanding in large style as a result of new activities from a growing wind turbine adventure at sea. It will lead to a lasting job party at the ports - and the engineers will be needed, says the trade organization.

Well over half of Denmark's approximately 50 commercial ports are now in some form with the wind turbine sector.

From the large port in Esbjerg - which has shipped 80 percent of all installed offshore wind capacity throughout the North Sea - to the small Klintholm Harbor on Møn gives the wind turbine adventure these years to major extensions, more activity and thus more jobs on the Danish commercial ports.

“It is a clear trend that the wind turbine adventure is filling up more and more on the Danish ports. When you look at how the ports expect them to grow in the coming years, there is no doubt that it is the wind area that is the engine of that growth, ”says Tine Kirk Pedersen, director of Danish Ports, which represents the Danish commercial ports.

The optimism is mainly due to the European Commission strategy for offshore wind, which was announced last year. Here, the goal is that offshore wind turbines must be erected with a capacity of at least 60 GW in European waters by 2030 and as much as 300 GW by 2050. Today, the total European capacity is around 25 GW.

Tine Kirk Pedersen has high hopes that a large part of the many new orders will be won by Danish companies and thus expand the activities of the Danish quays. And there are good chances of having that wish fulfilled.

Last year, the organizations Danish shipping companies, Dansk Energi and Wind Denmark had a study of the employment effects of the sea wind. The study showed that each GW offshore wind set up in Danish waters gives rise to 14,900 full -time equivalents over the lifetime of the mills. 1,400 of the man -years are in the so -called 'Blue Denmark'.

And since Danish companies are so dominant in the offshore wind industry, a good bite of the workplaces also accrues Denmark, even though an offshore wind farm is set up in Europe. Thus, a European offshore wind farm of 1 GW contributes approx. 3,100 man -years for Danish wind companies, the study shows.

Ports embrace wind
Rønne Harbor is a good example of a commercial port that has seriously felt the wind turbines' entry and adopted the new business area.

Until a few years ago, the activity was relatively limited, but that has changed in connection with the installation of Denmark's largest offshore wind farm, Kriegers Flak, which has been shipped from Rønne.

With the prospect of also being the natural choice for the upcoming Energiø project at Bornholm of 2 GW (almost 3.5 times Kriegers Flak) and large offshore wind ambitions in the other Baltic Sea region, Rønne Harbor now has expectations to ship approx. 15 GW until 2040.

»With Rønne Harbor's ambition to become the central shipping harbor of wind turbines in the Baltic Sea, the harbor has had major expansions. Thanks to the big investment in wind energy in the Baltic Sea, it seems that the harbor will succeed in creating a unique position, ”says Tine Kirk Pedersen.

Also jobs to the engineers
The Kriegers Flak project has also thrown off jobs at the aforementioned Klintholm Harbor, which has been chosen by the park's operator as a service port. This means that 35 new jobs are now moving into one of the country's smallest commercial ports, which for the same reason is undergoing considerable physical expansion.

And although these jobs will preferably be skilled labor, Tine Kirk Pedersen also sees plenty of potential for new engineering positions at the ports.

“We often hear from the wind turbine companies that are active in the Danish ports, that the level of education is getting higher and higher, and you need to be able to be more and more. Of course, there are many skilled workers working on and around the ports, but the need is growing for highly educated labor, which comes from the vemor world, ”she says.

Finally, the Danish commercial ports are also in the process of positioning themselves as a focal point in the upcoming power-to-X industry in Denmark. Together with the trade organization Dansk Energi, Dansk Energi recently published a green port strategy, in which the two organizations see that the ports can serve more purposes in the power-X industry in areas ranging from storage and filling of ships and trucks to production itself. of the fuels.

“We are experiencing great interest from actors who would like to physically position themselves on the ports and would like to enter into strategic collaborations with the ports around Power-to-X. It will also include engineering workplaces at the ports, ”says Tine Kirk Pedersen.

Lasting job party
Although the expected growth depends on an extension that is by nature a temporary activity, Tine Kirk Pedersen has no doubt that the wind turbines have created a lasting job party on the port areas.

“The development plans are so extensive that the activity itself continues for many years to come. At the same time, we also see now that the oldest parks are getting too old and need to be peeled down - here the decommissioning that needs to happen will be the next business area the ports can look into, ”she says.

In addition, the trend with the ever -growing offshore wind turbines also draws on the fact that the components of the mills will increasingly be produced on the ports.

“The wind industry itself already states that more of the production will move completely to the ports in the future as the elements become too large to be transported along the road network. Road transport has already begun to be a limiting factor today, ”says Tine Kirk Pedersen, adding:

"We are, to say the least, not worried that this is a task that ebbes out - neither in the short nor the long term."

Title: Regeringen: Øget elektrificering giver mangel på knap 2 GW havvind i 2030
Full text:
The electrification of transport and industry is important contributions to the climate target. But we lack an expansion of VE that can match the increase in electricity consumption.

The target of 70 percent CO2 reduction by 2030 requires a rapid and deep electrification of the fossil sectors in society. But there is no prospect that the increased electricity consumption can be covered by production from Danish wind turbines or solar cells by 2030.

With months of delay, the government has finally presented its electrification strategy, which draws the framework for how to lift the task of getting more of the community's gears to run on electricity.

Central to the new strategy is eight benchmarks, which put the fence poles around the government's more concrete initiatives in the field in the coming months and years. One of the benchmarks is to ensure plenty of green power for the growing electricity consumption:

“When we need to electrify, we need more green power. The government will work to ensure that the expansion of renewable energy takes place as the national - and in the long term foreign - consumption increases, so that the electrification of society becomes 100 per cent. Green, 'it sounds in one of the government's new benchmarks.

But this particular benchmark is far from a course against Denmark, especially in the perspective of the Climate Act and its binding target of reducing 70 percent of greenhouse gas emissions in 2030 compared to the level in 1990.

The engineer has previously described how there is a prospect of a lack of green power for the upcoming power-to-X industry, which will supply the so-called indirect electrification of especially the heavy transport.

But now the government's own calculations show that direct electrification also risks getting green power if it is further brought up by upcoming political initiatives.

Increases electricity consumption significantly
In connection with the preparation of the strategy, the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Supply has made a number of scenario calculations, which are an attempt to illustrate full electrification potential-and thus CO2 reduction potential-by increased electrification by 2030.

The calculations are made for three selected sectors, which today have a considerable fossil energy consumption. These are the transport sector, households (primarily heating) as well as business and agriculture.

According to the calculations, these sectors can make a contribution to the climate target of an additional DKK 5 million. tonnes of CO2 reduction in 2030 if they are noticeable undergoing a strong accelerated electrification in the coming years.

In addition, electrification will indirectly give rise to an additional DKK 1 million. tonnes of CO2 reductions by 2030 by virtue of the sectors' conversion away from wiring gas (primarily as a result of household phasing out gas fires and the industry's transition to electric heat pumps, ed.). This increases the projected proportion of CO2-neutral biogas in the wiring gas, measured against final consumption.

In total, there is the potential for a further reduction of just over DKK 6 million. tons as a result of increased direct electrification. The government is currently missing reductions for DKK 11.8 million. tonnes by 2030, which is why an additional electrification effort in the strategy is emphasized as one of the most important tools for the redemption of 70 per cent target.

If the above potential is fully fulfilled, it will give rise to an overall increase in Danish electricity consumption in 2030 of 8.8 TWh, the calculations show. According to the government's own figures, this corresponds to the annual production from approx. 1.9 GW offshore wind turbines. In comparison, Denmark today has a total offshore wind capacity of 1.7 GW.

The extra production capacity of just under 2 GW must be laid on top of the expansion already planned by 2030. A large-scale offshore wind park typically takes 6-8 years to realize, so if the mills are to be ready by 2030, the politicians would immediately have to decide on new Concrete offshore wind offerings very soon.

Energian alytics: Thin strategy
However, the government states in the strategy that the increased electricity consumption from electrification measures will not necessarily mean a need for more wind turbines and solar cells.

"The extent to which electrification will in practice require continued expansion of renewable energy depends on whether consumption coincides with the times when the wind blows and the sun is shining," the strategy reads.

However, that interpretation understands energy sale and partner in EA Energy Analysis, Hans Henrik Lindboe, not at all. He interprets the requirements of the Climate Act so that Denmark on an annual basis itself must produce all the WE-EEL that contributes to CO2 reductions in the climate accounts.

What is done by exchange with abroad for balancing production and consumption during the year should be inferior, he believes.

“If the Climate Act is to be interpreted so tight that we cannot recognize abroad as a warehouse for Danish sun and wind on an annual basis, then it will be difficult. That, I hope, is a misunderstanding, 'he says.

Overall, he thinks the new strategy is drawing a reasonable vision for the development.

“But as a strategy considered it is thin, I think. Many options are set up, but no concrete direction is required. There is a lack of prioritization of where you want to put in first and here should secure adequate WE capacity and a concrete roadmap for electrification in the industry is very high on the list, ”says Hans Henrik Lindboe.

WE-Extension hit by challenges
Regardless of how much extra is electrified by 2030, there is currently no prospect of an additional expansion of neither offshore wind or renewable energy in a size order that can meet 70 per cent target.

According to the Danish Energy Agency's so -called climate status and projection (formerly known as the basic projection, ed.), Denmark will already, with the adopted electrification measures in the absence of green electricity by 2030, where the VE share of consumption will land at 97 percent.

Here, among other things, the two planned state tenders are recognized on offshore winds, Thor and Hesselø parks, as well as an expectation that the market-driven expansion of solar cells will more than quadruple the current capacity to 8,500 MW by 2030.

The deficit is mainly due to the fact that the government's schedule for the two energy islands of a total of 5 GW offshore winds back in February was shot to the other side of 2030. However, the new strategy now states that the energy islands must be realized in 2030 'or as soon as possible thereafter'.

In general, the WE expansion that the government has relying on until 2030, through the spring and summer, however, has been affected by one bad news after another.

On Friday last week, the supply of the country's largest offshore wind project has been drawn to up to 1,200 MW - the Hesselø offshore wind park - paused due to unforeseen difficulties with the seabed conditions in the designated area. It is still unknown what the seabed problems will have of importance to the project.

In addition, there is a result that the large coastal offshore wind farm Omø South of up to 320 MW must be dropped after the mills' sea area has been designated as a nature conservation area for the sake of bird life for 11 hours. It happens after nine years of planning.

Inside on land, things are not much better. The private WE resorts have been complaining for months that no new connection agreements are being made with the electricity grid companies. The reason is that the industry lacks clarity on how the bill should be settled when the government's announced restructuring of the payment for the development and operation of the electricity grid comes into force in 2023.

In addition, a number of large WE projects have recently been felled as a result of decisions in the House of the Board that have gone against the projects. In March, for example, the Plank Complaints Board found that the country's largest commissioned onshore wind farm, Thorup plain, has been set up illegally. The future of the 18 mills is still unclear.

All of this has got the trade organizations Dansk Energi and Wind Denmark on the barricades. The two organizations have long pointed out that the green effect balance in 2030 will not go up if the climate goals are to be met.

Back in April, Dansk Energi released its own analysis, which showed a mano of green power of 7 TWH in 2030, while Wind Denmark last week released a similar inventory in which the mano was a total of 27 TWH in 2030 - however, with a condition of a long Higher electricity consumption for, among other things, the export of PTX fuel, which the official projections do not recognize.

The government's electrification strategy must already be followed up in the autumn with new initiatives, while a separate PTX strategy is also expected towards the end of the year.

However, the organization of the wind industry demands that the government also prepare a definite WE strategy that ensures that the climate goals are supported by sufficient green power.

»An electrification strategy without electricity is like a water park without water. There is a need for the government and the Folketing to take responsibility for enough green power as well as by 2030. Otherwise, the rest of the climate effort loses its meaning. We therefore call for the government and the Folketing to develop and adopt an actual WE strategy in addition to the electrification and PTX strategies, ”Wind Denmark CEO Jan Hylleberg said in a press release last week.

Title: Vindmøllebranchen ryster på hovedet af Energinets markedsdesign for energiøerne
Full text:
Energinet will create separate buddies for the upcoming energy islands, but the upcoming market design will mean that the wind turbine current is most often settled at the lowest possible price. And that threatens the wind turbine developers' investment desire in the huge project.

When the hybrid connection Kriegers Flak Combined Grid Solution (CGS) went into operation last year it was a true world sensation. In collaboration with his German counterpart, 50Hertz, Energinet had committed a technical new break by connecting two countries' electric systems via a wind farm on sea for the first time in the world.

In terms of electricity, the solution also entered new trails. In fact, so emphatic that the market design behind the solution was not allowed at all when the connection went live in 2020.

The reason was the EU's Clean Energy Package, which had made it a few years before that all cross -border electricity connections should make 70 percent of its capacity available to the free electricity commerce, and that it was generally no longer allowed to give priority to priority The web for WE systems.

The market design at Kriegers Flak was based on just giving priority access to the wind energy in the cables. The philosophy was that the connection was primarily intended as a landing of wind turbine power, and that the excess capacity on the connections could be seen as a bonus that could be made available to the market, explains international chief engineer at international electricity markets in Energinet.

“After all, everyone thought it was a good idea at that time, as we thus utilized the infrastructure better. But since then, the interpretation of the rules of the internal market has become such that goods must have free access across borders, and that principle fought the market design fundamental courage, ”he says.

But the first thoughts behind the market design for Kriegers Flak connection were devised all the way back in 2007, long before Clean Energy Package got in the way well over ten years later. Therefore, Last year, Energinet was granted an exemption to move on with the trade-discriminatory market design.

Bud zones on the sea
But of course that model does not go when the upcoming energy islands-such as Kriegers Flak connection are the prototype-must have designed their electricity market framework.

»Kriegers Flak has given us some experience about these hybrid projects that we can draw on. Now, of course, we know that we should not build the market design around priority access, because we do not get many friends out of the regulatory side, ”says Morten Pindstrup, explaining that the considerations of identifying some basic principles, like the new one, began Market design had to live up to.

Energy's principles of the energy islands' upcoming market design reads:

It must be non-discriminatory
It must be transparent so that all actors can understand the mechanisms
It will have to follow applicable rules
It must be scalable
Based on this list of basic conditions, the Danish TSO reached to simply move the existing market model out to sea by creating separate offshore Bud zones for the Energy Islands-a model that also supports the European Commission in its offshore wind strategy.

“There was no logical reason to deviate from the zone model just because we replace the grass with water. So we decided to move on with a solution where we do the same offshore as we do onshore, ”says Morten Pindstrup.

Wind turbine owners are losing
Thus, although the market design is well known, there is one serious challenge in Energinet's proposed model: The actors who have to set up the wind turbines do not care at all.

"The design has the challenge that the wind turbines set up in connection with the island and thus will stand inside this separate Budzone, all else being equal, will be a little worse off than if, for example, they were connected directly to the domestic market," says Morten Pindstrup.

The reason for the distribution of the energy islands' offshore wind turbines must be found in the method of the EU's market algorithm finds prices in the individual bid zones.

The algorithm-also called the European market coupling mechanism-optimizes the flow of power between Europe's bud zones by moving electricity from a low-cost area to a high price area and putting prices in the individual areas thereafter.

Is an energy island located in its own bid zone with connections to, for example, two other price areas - e.g. Western Denmark and Germany, which are typically low and high price areas respectively- the electricity market logic will ensure that as much of the island's cheap wind turbine power is sent to Germany.

But because the islands' interconnectors to the respective countries will probably not be dimensioned to be able to transport all production from the associated wind turbines, the connection to the high price area will often be saturated and a bottleneck will occur.

Since there is no consumption in the island's own bid zone (at least to a start), the island's current can only be sold to the low cost area, which means that the market coupling mechanism allocates the energy island's bud zone - and all the wind turbines within the zone - the same spot price as the low cost area.

Tightening legs for support model
Even in situations where the price distribution between Western Denmark and Germany is the other way around, the mills associated with the energy island will end with a spot price that matches the cheapest of the areas where there is free trading capacity, and it does not in any way give a sustainable investment case, says the wind turbine industry. .

“Our comment on Energinet's Budzone model has been through the process that it reduces the incentive to invest in the Energiø project because everyone but Energinet is losing on the model. Without a greater consideration of investor security, a regular offshore wind turbine project with a radial network connection will be more attractive to an investor if you only look at the price formation in the spot market, ”says Wind Denmark's electricity market manager Søren Klinge.

He thus points out that the owner of the island's cables - which is likely to be Energinet - stands to serve on the market design via the so -called bottleneck income. And that this income is done at the expense of the wind turbine owners' inferior settlement.

We will return the bottleneck income.

For with systematically low spot prices for the Energy Islands, the associated wind turbines will in all likelihood need a safety net in the form of state aid, which is expected to be in the form of a so-called 'contract-for-difference' (CFD), the state guarantees the wind turbine owners a minimum price on the stream.

As the name of the model suggests, the state covers the difference between the realized electricity prices and up to the agreed minimum price found in the tender.

The model is also available in a double-sided version where the state receives money from the operator in cases where the electricity price is above the agreed minimum price. In this way, it opens up that the given support over time goes to zero.

But the market design also makes it significantly less attractive for the state to enter into such a support model, explains Søren Klinge.

»The Budzone model results in a very high electricity price risk. If it is coupled with a state -guaranteed minimum price via a CFD, then it is the state that takes you the very high risk, and I can have my doubts about whether any state will be interested in, ”says Søren Klinge.

A guard against a runaway tax bill could be to put an absolute support ceiling in crowns and ears in the tender conditions - such a ceiling is, for example, part of the conditions in the upcoming technology -neutral supply for wind turbines and solar cells on land. But such a ceiling would only bring the risk back on investors in the wind farms, he points out.

Share out of bottleneck income
The objections from the wind industry are also ashamed of something that is very much in mind, says Morten Pindstrup.

"Of course, we have to listen to the objections that the mill owners and developers have, because it is of no use that we make the world's best market design if no one dares to invest in it," he says.

And the most important ace the TSO has in the sleeve in this regard is precisely the aforementioned bottleneck revenue. Morten Pindstrup explains that you are by looking at ways in which the wind turbine owners can share in revenue as a kind of supplement to a support model.

One way could be by competing parts of the transmission right on the interconnectors as part of the offshore wind farms' offerings. The lowest bid for shares of the transmission rights will thus stand better than competitors.

Søren Klinge is familiar with the idea of ​​redistributing bottleneck revenues by exposing the transmission rights. But he still thinks the sketches for the compensation scheme are too vague that they can give investors sufficiently calm in the stomach.

“For example, there is a challenge in the current time limit of transmission rights, which can only be given for a few years at a time, as the rules are now. The rules, as I see it, must first change so that they match the investment horizon of an offshore wind farm, which is at least 20 years old. If the supply does not provide security for these rights throughout the life, investors cannot go into it, ”says Søren Klinge.

Time is scarce
In any case, it is urgent to find a market design and some tender conditions that work for the wind investors, for the development of new market models takes a very long time, he points out.

»Such a redistribution of bottleneck income is necessary to get through at European level, as the current market design is rooted in European law. And in such a change there is a temporal challenge - it's not something you just do, because you are down here and pill in the core of the internal market for energy. There is a very long way to go, ”says Søren Klinge, estimating that such a process can easily take several years.

According to the Danish Energy Agency's estimated roadmap for the project in the North Sea, the associated offshore wind will be able to take out tender in mid -2027. And the market model must be ready before then, says Morten Pindstrup, who also completely agrees that time is scarce.

"This design should preferably be completely chopped in stone before making the wind turbine supply on the energy islands, because it will be quite decisive for which business cases offer the wind farms to make," says Morten Pindstrup.

And he also assures that the development of the market design and rule changes at EU level will be involved with the involvement of the actors as far as possible.

“There are really, really many ducks that have to stand in a row in this project. Every time one of them is not in a row, it reflects a risk that the actors have to relate to and in the end it is the one they will pay for. Therefore, these risks are something we do a lot to uncover before we get to a tender, ”he says.

The next step in working with the market design is a so -called bid zone study, which Energinet must make in collaboration with the countries to which the islands must be connected. Title: Energiøens enorme havvindparker truet af ny fuglefredning
Full text:
It will be 'very difficult' to find space for 2 GW offshore wind turbines at Energiø Bornholm, whose Ministry of the Environment's proposal for new bird protection areas is not adjusted, Energinet writes in a consultation response. However, the Energiø project is best served by the area peace, says environmental expert.

After a long -long process, the Ministry of the Environment is now stumbling close to identifying six new bird protection areas in the Danish waters.

But now it turns out that one of the ministry proposed protection areas off Bornholm carambers with the preliminary study area for the state's own, huge offshore wind project of 2 GW, which will be connected to one of the country's two upcoming energy islands.

And if the designation occurs after the strokes that the Ministry of the Environment has currently drawn up in the new so -called Habitat Order, the Møllers' possible set -up area will be reduced to such an extent that it will be 'very difficult' to find space for 2 GW offshore winds.

This is what the cash message from Energinet sounds like in a consultation response to the executive order change, which Gridtech has gained access to.

»This [the designation, ed.] Most likely, will mean that the area for the installation of offshore wind turbines for the establishment of 2 GW offshore wind at Bornholm will be reduced so significantly that it is likely to be very difficult to establish 2 GW offshore winds in the area, "Writes Energinet in his consultation response.

The buffer zone restricts the mill area
In the new Habitat Order - which has just been consulted, but is not yet final - it is proposed to appoint a new bird protection area called Rønne Banke, which extends from the Bornholm south coast and all the way to the border of the exclusive economic zone to Germany. The designation is done for the sake of the duck bird Havlit, which is found in the area.

The new proposed area is adjacent to the already established preliminary study area for the two offshore wind farms for Energiø Bornholm. The parks will be placed 20 km from the coast south of Rønne and are divided into an eastern and western area, each of which will house 1 GW (see card further down).

Although the boundaries of the bird protection area just do not cross the moths' feasibility study area, Energinet in the consultation response points out that experience from previous environmental impact assessments from, among other things. Kriegers Flak shows that sea lit is lighter more easily if a minimum of a buffer zone of 2-3 km to the offshore wind turbines is established.

With an assumption of an extra buffer zone of 3 km along the borders of the new bird protection area, the designation will result in a reduction of 67.6 square kilometers of the eastern offshore wind turbine area and 4.7 square kilometers of the western offshore wind turbine area, Energinet writes.

"Especially for the eastern offshore wind turbine area, it is such a large area that it can mean that the project cannot be implemented as adopted in Climate Agreement 2020," says the consultation response.

This is because the gas lines Nord Stream I and Baltic Pipe run through the eastern area. And since the gas lines, according to other rules, must be kept free of wind turbines at a distance of 200 meters on each side of the pipe, the mill area will be reduced by an additional 18 square kilometers.

Thus, the eastern mill area is reduced to 212 square kilometers.

»Normally, an offshore wind farm of 1 GW will have to use an area of ​​approx. 220 square kilometers, taking into account that the offshore wind farm can achieve the required electricity generation and thus the expected reduction of the CO2 emission, ”Energinet writes.

As far as the western mill area is concerned, the bird protection area is intervening less here, but since it is already a limited area of ​​254 square kilometers, the reduction of 4.7 square kilometers can also prove to be problematic, Energinet points out.

Energinet is not very concerned
Although the problem raised in the consultation response may sound alarming for the large -scale project, there is not much concern to track with Energinet.

"I would not say that we are very concerned, but we are lagging here a risk that we also provide a solution to," says Energinet's top responsible for Energiø projects, Hanne Storm Edlefsen.

In its consultation response, Energinet suggests that the newly designated bird protection area be narrowed so that any buffer zone intervenes minimally into the mill area. On the other hand, extensions of the existing EC bird protection area could be implemented at Hyllekrog-Rødsand, it says.

»In order to meet the risk of us ending up having too little area available, we suggest limiting the current presentation slightly, and at the same time putting in a new area that is both larger and which actually has a larger occurrence of sea lit, 'she says.

Professor: The birds decide
But it is not the right way to go unless the wind turbine project will risk running into complaints and litigation, according to professor at the University of Copenhagen's Legal Faculty and an expert in the environment, Peter Pagh.

He explains that the European Court of Justice in a now 25-year-old judgment and with subsequent practice has made the legal position very clear in cases like this:

"In short, the court says that by designating and defining bird protection areas, it is only ornithological criteria that apply. One can popularly say that the 'birds decide'. According to firm practice, it must be understood that if a basis for designating an area for protection has been found, then the designation must also be done, ”says Peter Pagh.

If the authorities choose to comply with Energinet's desire to restrict the protected area of ​​Bornholm, the Energiø project is made in his assessment very vulnerable to complaints and litigation that risk stopping the project.

To understand why, it is important to know the nature of the Habitats Directive. 6, par. 4.

But the exception can of course only be brought into play if the area in which the mills stand in is also appointed protected area-according to Peter Pagh, it has been established in several EU judgments.

“The court has made it clear that if one fails to appoint despite the fact that there is a basis for appointment, the possibility also lapses to use the exception. Thus, the protection of the birds is absolutely applied, and then it is not at all possible to waive the rules, ”says Peter Pagh, elaborating:

“If you do not appoint the area now, an NGO can, for example, come on the back and claim that there was a basis that you chose not to follow in its appointment. And if that happens, it is completely certain that the court will judge in favor of the complaining party, ”he says.

The energy island has good chances of exception
Unless one can rule out that the mills will have a detrimental effect on the birds is a designation of the area as a bird protection area in Peter Pagh's assessment, therefore, the only way to go for Energinet and the authorities at this time.

For the Energiø project has good opportunities to live up to the requirements for exception, he believes.

“The most important thing is that the area is initially appointed, as it is now available, and then one must then do a habitat assessment and decide whether there is a basis for an exception. And it may very well be - it is even very obvious in this case, as the energy island is a project of a scale and importance, so the exemption provision would probably be able to apply here, ”says Peter Pagh.

However, Energinet does not agree with the professor that with the proposal in the consultation response, there may be a change in the design of the bird protection area, as it has not just been decided to appoint it.

"We are still in a consultation phase now, which is why we are trying with our solution to anticipate a potential conflict of interest from the start," says Hanne Storm Edlefsen, emphasizing that Energinet's consultation response is an expression of a professional input that tries to accommodate Both seabirds and offshore wind turbines. The final legal assessment is up to the Danish Environmental Protection Agency, she states.

The Ministry of the Environment informs GridTech that the present -hand response is currently being processed and therefore has no further comments.

Earlier this month, Energinet formally started the concrete preliminary studies on the sea around the Energy Islands. At Energiø Bornholm, the studies are carried out by Ramboll.

Title: Energiøer: De teknologisk udfordringer tårner sig op

It will require completely new technological solution when the energy islands are to be ready in 12 years. Researchers warn that we should start now if we are not to be left with animals and wrong technology.

If, in 10-12 years, we are to have a robust electricity system that can handle the large amounts of energy to be produced on the Baltic Sea and the North Sea and distributed via energy islands to both Denmark and other countries in the area, then we must find them to find them Technical solutions right now. Concerns are first and foremost that the whole system must be based on DC compounds (DC) and convert to ensuring and exchange the energy:

“We may have the individual hardware components available today. But there is no place in the world today where you have experience in dealing with such large quantities of renewable energy in a single insulated network without large stabilizing power plants. There is a need to do things in a whole new way, ”says Jacob Østergaard, a professor and center manager at DTU Elektro.

Also Frede Blaabjerg, a professor at AAU and one of the world's leading researchers in effect electronics, emphasizes that now we need to start if the solutions are to be ready on time:

“When we bet on an energy island that could potentially handle up to 10 GW electricity from wind turbines, we're out in something no one has ever tried before. It raises a lot of questions that we have to try to find answers to in good time, ”he says.

Risk of instability
In the report, which they have just released a number of other experts in the field, they point out, among other things, that with so much electricity generation based on high -tension DC (HVDC) we will go further and further away from an electricity system where stability and thus The frequency of 50 Hz is primarily based on the inertia from rotating generators at the country's power plants.

This means that we can no longer expect that larger and smaller outcomes of consumers or faults on high -voltage lines will be captured and automatically adapted by the power plants' safety systems:

When we have to base our electricity system to a much greater extent on a large number of converters, we need to develop new models to simulate how to regulate the energy flow and what happens in failure and outcome, ”says Jacob Østergaard.

This type of simulation must be further used to develop new control systems for the actual operation of the energy system. The risk is that even a minor error on the energy island, where 10 GW wind power must be distributed, could potentially spread and darken large parts of Northern Europe.

To reduce the risk, of course, there is the possibility of oversizing the systems, but it will inevitably lead to a higher price for the energy island, and thus other solutions may have been better.

The components are available
However, both researchers emphasize, so they do not think the islands are out of technical reach. Among other things, Frede Blaabjerg points out that the components needed to build a so-called multit terminal DC system already exists today. You can already look at the latest connection between Jutland and Norway, Skagerrak 4, which was put into operation in 2014. Capacity is here at 0.7 GW:

“The challenge is that no place in the world has built such a large system as the energy island in the North Sea requires. That doesn't mean we can't. 12 years to learn

Here, researchers agree that we can achieve it, but that there is no room to postpone the studies of the electrical technical aspects. There are also a number of options associated with starting something as pioneering as an energy island, they say:

»Today, for example, wind turbines must meet some very specific and expensive requirements in order to be connected to the electricity grid. But if we build them directly in connection with the energy island, then some of the requirements, among other things in relation to net stability, may be moved into the effect electronics of the HVDC connections that give birth to the energy ashore. In this way, the mills can be made cheaper, which could potentially reduce the price by a billion amount. These are such things we need to get clarified now, ”says Jacob Østergaard.

Also Frede Blaabjerg sees some technological possibilities in a system of DC connections on the energy island:

“If we choose to do so, then in Denmark we will be technological pioneers who will bring us internationally at the forefront. We have tried this before compared to large wind farms at sea. But if it is also to be a good and safe investment, then we need to start solving some of the technological challenges now. "

Title: En enkel fejl på energiøen kan sende Nordeuropa i sort
Full text:
The energy island in the North Sea must be connected to the rest of Europe via new and untested technology. Simulations show that new control concepts are needed if a major error is needed to propagate to the rest of the European electricity system.

New and untested technology reinforces the risk that an error on the energy island of the North Sea can propagate to the rest of the electricity grid on the continent and potentially put most of Northern Europe in the dark.

It shows simulations that researchers at DTU have done:

»A traditionally predominantly analogous electricity grid can be compared to a propeller aircraft that can easily hover a little further and land, even if one of the engines goes out. But a system based on several compounds of high -strained direct current to be linked is like a modern fighter jet: It requires advanced control, and if it fails, then the aircraft falls to the ground like a stone, ”says Jacob Østergaard, a professor and Center manager at DTU Elektro.

In a report that DTU has recently published in collaboration with AAU, the seriousness further emphasized:

"There is a lot at stake when driving an energy island of 10 GW: A mistake that causes 10 GW wind power in the North Sea to disappear from the electricity grid can potentially darken the entire European electricity grid."

The challenge for energy islands is about the technology called “Multiterminal HVDC”. This basically means that energy from the wind farms goes to an alternating current on the island itself. Here it is converted to HVDC (High-Voltage Direct Current) and distributed to the countries that are expected to be linked to the energy island, ie Denmark, Germany and the Netherlands. In the individual countries, converts will then again convert DC into AC stream by 50 Hz and send the energy out into the national high voltage networks.

The type of connection has been on the drawing board for a number of years, and in some places they have prepared to expand existing connections. This applies, for example, in Scotland, where a new HVDC connection, called Caithness-Moray, has been dimensioned so that in the longer term it can be linked to wind farms in the Shetland Islands.

In Denmark, the new wind farm on Kriegers Flak in the Baltic Sea is already connected to both Zealand and Germany, and can be utilized in days of winds to transport energy between the two countries. But since the electricity grid in Zealand and in Germany does not run synchronously, alternating current must be through a converter plant in Germany. The plant could in the future be connected to Poland.

Rotating machines in the electricity of the past
But the electricity grid on the energy island differs significantly from the type of electricity grid that we have known for about 100 years, where the frequency is held in place by large rotating generators at the power plants.

In the Danish network, the largest electricity-producing unit used to be 600-650 MW in the past, and so the net should be able to handle if it suddenly got a mistake and had to unplug (it could also be a high voltage connection that was linked).

The stability of the electricity grid and the ability to keep the frequency of 50 Hz depended on the inertia that was in the generators that continued to run. They could now be told to run up a bit in turns, so the frequency was again 50 Hz.

No inertia in the converter system
Out on the North Sea, there is no inertia that forms a stable frequency once the energy from wind turbines is converted to DC. If an error occurs on the energy island an error in the DC couplings or on the connections to land, the energy from the wind turbines must quickly be moved over to the other connections:

»If the direct current connections are loaded close to their maximum capacity, then the simulations we have run show that - if you do not design the control in a new way - a failure of one of the HVDC connections causes the system to collapse And ultimately can pull the electricity grid in Europe down. "

The challenge is that there is a need to develop new management concepts for the components that are part of the isolated AC grew on the energy island, ”says Jacob Østergaard.

One of the challenges is that the converters cannot use the frequency of a traditional generator to control if an error occurs - it must be artificially formed by the software that controls the converters on the energy island. So like the fighter jet that will fall to the ground because it can't hover itself if the engine sets out.

One of the solutions is new so-called "Droop Control Strategies" that Georgios S. Misyrisder, a PhD student at DTU Elektro, has worked with. In practice, it is about sending a signal to the other converters that tell how much and how fast they have to change their transfer of energy if one has fallen out:

“The collapses in the simulations we have seen have come when we have run with well-known droops strategies, where there is a fixed setting of how much to regulate up or down at a given frequency change. Therefore, we are likely to go into a new type called "adaptive droops", where we continuously adjust the individual converter's settings to the current situation, "explains Georgios S. Misyrisder.

In other words, this will mean that the changes in how much the individual converter should regulate the effect depends on how hard it is already, explains Jacob Østergaard:

"In this way, we can distribute the consequences of an outcome appropriately between the connections and an instability is avoided," he says, emphasizing that a simple solution to the problem would be to oversimage the entire system, both converter and direct power cables, but that it will increase costs Essentially and thus increase the electricity price from the energy island.

Title: Ramt af blød bund: Fagfolk spår dårlige chancer for vigtigt havvind-projekt
Full text:
The authorities must most likely look for another location for one of Denmark's largest offshore wind projects. It assesses a number of experts based on the preliminary preliminary studies that show that large parts of the seabed are very soft.

Our chance of reaching the climate targets in 2030 is under serious pressure while the supply of supply with electricity in Eastern Denmark can deteriorate. It is the scenario that is based on the assessment of technical professionals that it will be very difficult to realize Denmark's largest wind farm, Hesselø offshore wind farm of up to 1.2 GW. The seabed in the area is very soft.

A number of experts in geotechnics and offshore wind turbine foundations have, on the engineer's and engineer's sister media Gridtech's request, taken a look at the preliminary studies of the underground in the area north of Hesselø, which is currently publicly available. They estimate that the offshore wind farm is at risk of being canceled due to soft seabed.

The supply of Hesselø offshore wind farm was suddenly paused at the end of June, after finding "soft clay bottoms in particular the top 20-30 meters below the seabed", which the Danish Energy Agency then wrote in a press release.

Meanwhile, the board has published a preliminary geotechnical analysis that illustrates the extent of the challenge. The analysis is a so -called triaxial test of 80 sampled drilling samples that are picked up on the seabed where the soft clay type is identified.

The test measures the strength of the soil samples by compressing them in three directions, and the results confirm that the soft bottom extends at least 35 meters into the underground. Most of the measurements are around 20-40 Kilopascal (KPA), but according to several experts should at least be between 100-200 kPa in order to carry a mill foundation.

“These are very low values ​​that have been found. It appears that drilling samples have been taken down to 35 meters, without the values ​​in the plot having taken a significant jump in the measured strength. A normal wind turbine foundation will go down to about 20-30 meters, but based on these values ​​there will be very, very little support at this depth, ”explains associate professor at DTU Byg's section for geotechnics and geology, Thomas Guldborg Petersen.

“You would probably have to make these foundations significantly longer and have to use significantly more steel to make it stand. It will be expensive, and given the economy of offshore wind turbine projects, the probability is small that it would come up, ”he says.

Founding posts over 100 meters
Sea wind turbines are typically founded with monopiles, which are thick steel pipes that are embedded in the seabed and lift the mill itself at least 20 meters above sea level. The feasibility studies have mapped the sea depths in the area to between 24.7 and 33.5 meters.

If the minimum 35 meter soft bottom is added, which according to the experts will not contribute to carrying capacity, as well as the additional 20-30 meters, the foundations must be driven into a load-bearing soil type, the monopoly will at least be between 99 and 108 meters long.

However, it is unclear whether the underground will be firm enough to carry immediately below the 35 meters that have been taken drilling down to.

“There is far down to something called Fast Fjeld in this area. But that's not what you would be looking for either. For example, it would be a glacial deposit, such as moraine material. That would be quite ideal. Or some sand or some gravel that is naturally compacted and will be stable to build on, ”says Thomas Guldborg Petersen.

He has also taken a look in the publicly available geophysical study, which has just been published by the Danish Energy Agency.

“As far as I can immediately see, there are larger areas where they were clayed, and thus potentially problematic soil layers have thicknesses of up to 100 meters or more. However, there may also be some areas where fixed soil layers are found within an acceptable depth below the seabed, ”he says.

Smaller clicks possible
He emphasizes that, based on the information in the studies, there is a big difference in the firmness of the bottom in the area, which is backed by Lars Vabbersgaard Andersen who is a professor at the Department of Engineering, Aarhus University.

“There are definitely places on this seabed where you can't set up wind turbines, but there may well be smaller areas where it would be possible to set up smaller clusters of wind turbines. Whether it is aerodynamic and financially making sense to do is another matter, but I cannot assess that, ”says Lars Vabbersgaard Andersen.

Other experts that GridTech/Engineer has been in contact with, but who will not comment on quote, independently point out that the soft bottom conditions will also make it very difficult to establish temporary platforms while the park is being built-so-called jack-ups . It will make it difficult to make the construction work difficult, it sounds.

In addition, cables from the park will in practice be freely hovering in the soft bottom, which would also be problematic, just as the experts are also flagging a challenge by establishing so -called scouring protection of the foundations.

Sharpens lack of green power
It is still unclear what the temporary stopping of the tender is of significance for the schedule of the wind farm, which was set to operate in 2027. According to the Wind Denmark industry organization, it can mean as much as a year's delay at this time - if the park can be realized at all.

If the park is to be dropped, there is a prospect that the Danish lack of green power by 2030 will be even more pronounced than it already is.

There are various statements, but most recently a calculation from Wind Denmark has calculated the so-called VE-Manko for at least 45 TWH if the 2030 goal is to be achieved. Hesselø is expected to be able to deliver almost 4.5 TWh annually to the Danish electricity supply.

The large wind park is also an important role in the East Danish electricity supply security, which is already pressured and deeply dependent on getting electricity via foreign cables and under the Great Belt.

The tender paused
The Danish Energy Agency recognizes that the results can have an impact on whether the offshore wind farm at Hesselø becomes something at all. It writes Press Manager Ture Falbe-Hansen in an email to the Engineer:

»The Danish Energy Agency has just put the supply for Hesselø offshore wind farm on a break, because Energinet's preliminary seabed surveys have found soft clay bottoms in large parts of the area in the top 20-30 meters below the seabed. These bottom conditions can cause technical challenges for the establishment of the park, and therefore further analyzes are needed. "

Thus, the authorities have not yet officially dropped the hope of realizing the park and have called the actors for a technical dialogue about the soft seabed later this month:

"It is therefore too early to say whether Hesselø offshore wind farm can and will be realized and what the current break will mean for the schedule," writes Ture Falbe-Hansen

At the same time, however, the Danish Energy Agency has also initiated new screenings for alternative locations an offshore wind kick of Hesseløs size. In addition, Climate Minister Dan Jørgensen (S) has also required Energinet to expand the preliminary study area to Energiø Bornholm, where ships are currently in the process of initial work

With the expansion, this means that the mills' set -up area now has to be examined as far as 15 km from the coast. It should give room to expand the energy island's capacity from 2 GW to 3 GW, but it also requires a new political negotiation, as a distance requirement of at least 20 km to the coast has been enrolled in the agreement behind the island.

In addition, the existing mill area at Energiø Bornholm has already been challenged by an imminent designation of new marine bird protection areas, which the Engineer has previously revealed. One of the proposed bird protection areas is clutched by the energy islands of the energy islands, and if it is appointed, it is risked that even the politically decided 2 GW until the energy island can be realized.

Title: Regeringen tror på tonstung CO2-reduktion med PtX i 2030: »Det virker temmelig urealistisk«
Full text:
In the new report Climate program 2021, the Danish Energy Agency estimates that the potential for reducing CO2 emissions using PTX is DKK 9 million. tonnes annually. But experts and the energy industry consider it completely unrealistic

9 million ton of CO2. So big is the potential of Power-to-X (PTX) in Denmark compared to a reduced emission of the climate mass by 2030, according to the government in the report Climate Program 2021 from the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Supply. The play, which contains 30 different possible reduction efforts, is called "a total roadmap for the realization of the 70 per cent target in 2030".

The PTX is, on the whole, one of the technologies mentioned most times in the report and specifically it appears that PTX can lead to a reduction of about DKK 1 million. tonnes in business and industry and approximately DKK 8 million. tonnes in the transport sector in 2030, ie a total of DKK 9 million. ton.

Over the past year, the Engineer has continuously described that with the planned expansion with wind turbines, including the upcoming energy islands, there will be a lack of green power, both for increased electrification of society in general and for the production of green fuels via PTX.

And that is exactly why several experts completely disagree with the government's assessment of climate potential at PTX.

Quick head bill shows the need for 14 gw wind
Karsten Capion from the Green Think Tank Concito, with a quick main bill (see box), can determine that in Denmark there will not be enough green electricity to produce as much fuel via PTX as it takes to achieve a reduction of 9 DKK million ton of CO2:

»If we need to use the green power to replace gasoline and diesel in transport, then we have to install 14 GW of offshore wind turbines for this purpose alone. On top of that, we need a similar amount of carbon to transform it into liquid fuels and production plants ready by 2030 - it seems pretty unrealistic, ”he says.

14 GW corresponds to six times the current offshore wind turbine capacity in Denmark.

Alternatively, Denmark could import the green power from Germany or Norway, or perhaps even import finished PTX fuel:

"But shouldn't there be competition in 2030 for both the green power and the finished fuels?" He asks, emphasizing that if Danish-produced PTX is to fill so much, then the planning of both PTX and green power, in progress already this year or by next year.

Loudly put into the world of reality
In Dansk Energi, too, it is estimated that the technical potential shown in climate program 2021 has been set very high. That's what Martin Dam Wied, who is the industry manager at Dansk Energi, says with a special focus on new fuels:

»This is a theoretical potential of DKK 9 million. tonnes a year, but in the real world it is high. Realistically, we only think we can reach 1.5 to 2 million. tonnes and, if we really have to be ambitious, then you can recognize ships and aircraft and thus perhaps reach about 3.5 million. tonnes of CO2 in 2030, ”says Martin Dam Wied, emphasizing that it requires a political will to support the transformation of Denmark's share of international ship and air traffic, as it cannot be included in the national CO2 accounts today.

At EA Energy Analysis, where you specialize in models of the energy system, partner Hans-Henrik Lindboe is also unaware of the fact that the reduction potential for PTX must be DKK 9 million. Ton in 2030:

"We can quickly agree that it is completely unrealistic, as it would require all fuel for transport in Denmark to turn green as early as 2030. It is not at all a wise PTX strategy. Of course, you can imagine that you bought a large part of the green fuels abroad, but do not think that the green electricity is generally ripped off? ”He says, considering it more realistic that PTX will be able to contribute 1 to 1.5 million tonnes of reduction per year in 2030.

What is technically possible
In an email to the Engineer, the Danish Energy Agency, which is behind the calculations in climate program 2021 and a note on the technical reduction potentials for CO2 in 2030, writes that the 9 million. ton of CO2 “covers the technically possible realizable reduction by 2030 by the individual technologies, taking into account temporal and technical restrictions”

In the memo, the Danish Energy Agency also emphasizes that "it probably will not be possible in practice to implement measures that ensure a full fulfillment of the stated potentials."

Title: Forsinket udbygning: Energiøerne er det eneste rigtige – på det helt forkerte tidspunkt
Full text:
Denmark will erect the world's first energy islands in the North Sea and on Bornholm. Thus, the home country's homeland goes at the front of the next phase of the evolution of technology, but at the same time stretches legs for the offshore wind herself.

Energy delayed expansion

When the newly minted Social Democratic government, in late June 2019, together with its support parties, released the so -called understanding paper, the large impact number was that Denmark should commit to reducing its greenhouse gas emissions by 70 percent compared to the level in 1990.

However, the 19 -page document also included an underplayed, but at least as challenging ambition. In a single sentence, the then little known offshore wind concept was a 'Energiø' for the first time introduced in Danish politics:

"(The Climate Action Plan must) seek the possibility that Denmark by 2030 builds the first energy island with a minimum of 10 GW connected," the document stated.

The fact that both the objective and the mega infrastructure project had the same deadline-2030-was certainly no coincidence, and when the politicians adopted both the Climate Act and entered into the climate agreement for energy and industry, the fate of the two ambitions was sealed.

Meanwhile, the energy island has been halved in capacity and doubled in number, so that the state is now aiming to build an artificial island in the North Sea with 3 GW connected as well as offshore wind farms on a total of 2 GW at an energy island to be located on Bornholm.

More importantly, the time frame has shifted, so that most of the energy islands' green stream will only flow ashore in 2033 - three years late compared to the deadline of the statutory 70 percent target, which according to several scenario calculations requires much more green power to reach.

A plug in the extension of the sea
When the Energy Islands were finally agreed with the Climate Agreement for Energy and Industry, politicians decided to let the new island projects annex one of three previously decided offshore wind farms of at least 800 MW.

Since the same conciliation circuit just over six months later with a sub -agreement on the energy islands postponed most of the islands' capacity to the other side of 2030, the two agreements had de facto diminished the otherwise planned expansion of offshore wind this decade, which could be read in the state's latest climate change , measuring the effect of the policy led.

Thus, the state now has only two large offshore wind projects on the way before the time limit in 2030: Thor and Hesselø, each up to 1 GW. It is unclear if more will come before then.

Especially because the settlement circle behind the energy islands has put themselves in a bit of a clamp by conditioning the projects that they must be profitable. It requires a relatively high settlement price for the future offshore wind turbine, and it has the inappropriate effect that the state now has no interest in opening to offshore wind farms that can be erected and connected before the energy islands.

An example: When a citizen-driven offshore wind project of 100 MW back in October last year wanted an exemption to set up wind turbines in a small corner of the area the state had reserved for Energiø Bornholm, the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Supply Ministry of Supply, among other things, with this argument:

"An expansion with more offshore wind than what has already been planned by the state, everything else will lead to a reduction in electricity prices and thus impair the profitability of all other electricity producers, including the decided energy islands."

COWI calculations have also shown that the Energy Islands offshore wind turbines will be pressed in competition with conventional offshore wind parks that can produce green power six to nine cents cheaper per day. kWh.

The state is unanimous on the sea
When it comes to the extension of renewable energy at sea, the state remains quite unanimous. Thus, it still sits on a number of reservations of good areas that were made years ago for fear of hamstring among eager private offshore wind developers.

However, if a developer succeeds in finding a suitable area that has not been reserved, it is possible through the so-called open door scheme for offshore wind to apply for the authorities for establishment science outside state tenders.

But shortly before the summer holidays, the government, together with the Folketing, decided to reduce the scheme considerably by imposing a limit for possible projects of a maximum of 15 km from the coast.

Why so energy islands?
Among professionals, the Energy Islands have both advocates and fierce opponents. The criticism is typically based on a fundamental disagreement over whether the priority of large -scale offshore wind is the right one when renewable energy can be set up far cheaper on land.

But among those who buy the premise of offshore wind parks as the future power plants, consensus seems to be that the Energy Islands are the only right to launch the next stage in the evolution of technology: upscaling.

Someone who has at least bought the premise is the European Commission, which sees offshore wind as "a central component of Europe's energy system". Thus, by 2050, the supranational body aims that the expansion of the total European capacity reaches 300 GW by 2050, of which 180 GW in the North Sea.

It is about 25 times more than the existing capacity and prescribes a completely different approach to offshore wind, where, rather than thinking from project to project, the parks begin to think in context, also across countries.

With such a large buildup, it becomes necessary to search further away from the coast, which necessitates that the landing of the current is done via expensive direct current cables. This is where the concept of energy islands as collection points and distribution centers begins to make sense.

The islands bring the mains connection to the vicinity of the mills and provide better economy in the expensive DC cables from the island and to shore, because they act both landing and electricity trading cables between the countries.

In the longer term, it is planned that more islands in the North Sea come to, which are connected to each other and provide far greater outlets for the wind turbine stream.

Energinet has previously estimated that a large -scale development of several energy islands in the North Sea can be made 30 percent cheaper rather than 'Business as usual', where each wind park has its own network connection.

So it is when the gaze is lifted from Denmark and our climate goals that the Energiø concept really makes sense. With the EU's political big venture on offshore wind, advocates will even think that they are strictly necessary.

The problem is that politicians' stubborn insistence on economically sustainable energy islands seems to be a plug in the expansion of more offshore wind. Paradoxically, at a time when the political goals are screaming for just that.

Title: KRONIK: Energiøerne er vores fælles Mars-mission
