Title: Her er de største udfordringer for regeringens nye grønne plan
Full text:
The government's new plan for a green transformation of Denmark gets positive shooting targets from the business organization and researcher, but it risks quickly running into major challenges, it says. They point here to the biggest challenges for the plan to succeed

On Tuesday this week, the government, with Mette Frederiksen at the forefront, was able to present a new plan for how Denmark gets a more green energy system and at the same time phased out the Russian gas.

The main points can be seen in the box here on the page.

But in the plan, a number of points may have looked soluble for a political system, but which may not be solved so easily in the specific processes that need to be started to achieve the finish.

We have therefore asked two key players in the process to get the biggest hurdles to be overcome to succeed, both to make housing heating independent of natural gas and multiply the green electricity production.

First, it is Kamilla Thingvad, who is a director responsible for energy production and development and trade in the new business organization Green Power Denmark, which is a merger of Dansk Energi, Wind Denmark and Danish Solar Power. As the first challenge, she emphasizes that if the plan is to be implemented, then a very high pace must be kept in the rollout:

“We can see that the wind turbine development on land has been stagnant here in recent years. There can be many reasons for that; Local resistance and slow case management in the municipalities. Therefore, the treatment of the authority must be tackled significantly differently, and we propose that "Green Council" be created in the municipalities, where citizens help to define local plans for expansion with sun and wind and very specific project proposals. "

“As it is today, only the opponents are heard. On top of that, climate relationship is not a priority factor in municipal planning-ie not a so-called "national interest". That is, the municipalities are not obliged to make room for the installation of wind turbines and solar cells when they prepare local plans, ”she says.

When it comes to the requirement that in 2022 all households should have clear information about alternatives to oil and gas stoves, Green Power Denmark is positively stopped. But according to Kamilla Thingvad, you also experience some challenges in planning. Therefore, the municipal planning must be addressed:

“It is really nice that you want to expand the district heating to the Danish households. But in the calculation basis for local district heating projects, we often find that too pessimistic data is added to alternatives such as heat pumps. There are prices for the actual heat pumps, efficiency and cost of expanding electricity grids, which simply do not hold water. Therefore, we propose that the Danish Energy Agency set up a kind of "travel team" that can help the municipalities qualify the projects so that you get a more impartial assessment of the technical and financial basis for the expansion, "she says.

Slow complaint system delaying conversion
Long -term complaint process and a divided complaint system, is also one of the obstacles that Kamilla Thingvad points to as one of the most important challenges:

“As it is now, the complaint process is shared between the Plank Complaints Board and the Environment and Food Complaints Board. It makes the process slow and sometimes so long -lasting that a new EIA has to be performed. Therefore, it must be assembled in a board. On top of that, we must have looked through the planning basis well, so that we can better handle requirements for everything from the protection of creeks and streams, to coastal protection, protected areas and special rules for plants near churches. Many of the current rules have been created in another time, where there might be only the prospect of the construction of a few wind turbines. Today we are in a completely different situation with completely different needs, ”says Kamilla Thingvad.

Several experts and organizations have pointed out that the extension with electricity grid can become a stop block. And Kamilla Thingvad totally agrees. Again, it is the current rules of expansion that have largely been created in a regime where the web development took place on the back of the need to be addressed:

»The reinforcement of the electricity grid risks lagging behind the need at both distribution and transmission level, if the regulation does not support a significant timely expansion. Our concern is that it will end like that, even if a political position has been taken to change it. The network development is simply too slow, and we believe that the plans that are now presented and not only when there are specific projects must be expanded. "

Last but not least, Kamilla Thingvad is very concerned about access to qualified labor, which is absolutely necessary to make the government's plan succeed. Today, there is a deficit of employees who can implement the projects and it can give challenge number five:

“The skills needed to establish all the new projects are not present today. Everything is needed from strong current engineers, grid planners and control room staff to electricians and unskilled. If not get started in education and retraining, it can end up being a serious stop block, ”she says, and also just mentions something as concrete as the purchase of hardware, such as transformers, heat pumps and other equipment, as something that is right now on.

Then let's at the same time isolate the houses
Marie Münster is a professor at DTU with a specialty in energy systems and she also focuses on significant obstacles such as long delivery times on materials for expanding district heating, electricity grid and heat pumps:

“When looking at the government's desire to quadruple the way production of wind turbines and solar cells on land, it is also not possible to avoid the fact that the popular acceptance should be able to follow. Who does it become specifically to have a view of a wind turbine or a solar park? For example, can it also mean that the consultation phase should be shortened? ”She asks, calling the question of citizen acceptance" the elephant in the room ".

But she also wonders that the government in its eagerness to convert 400,000 gas stoves for housing heating completely forget to look at energy savings:

“We know that about 50-60,000 gas boilers can be converted to district heating a year, so why not spend the wait for the remaining to improve homes? It will be able to put a whole host of other craftsmen into work and such energy improvements never come back badly. In the end, it could mean that a smaller heat pump or a smaller district heating consumption is needed when the conversion has been completed, and no one can be unhappy with? So maybe there was here that the government should put in with help and advice to the homes where the need for energy renovation is greatest, ”she says.

Marie Münster has also stapled by the government's desire for far more biogas to replace natural gas. Specifically, the plan is to advance biogas production, so that the gas in Denmark by 2030 is 100 percent green:

“But in order to increase production, more biomass is needed and the question is what biomass is involved. For example, if it is corn used today, it may not be that good an idea. We can also choose to pull the biogenic CO2 out of biogas production or flue gases, but then we can stand with a dilemma of CO2 going back into the soil to achieve a negative emission or whether it should be used for green fuels. "

"On the whole, a discussion is missing about how we use the biomass resources we have available," says Marie Münster

She also emphasizes that many biogas plants can already increase capacity today, but this means that more trucks must be driven to the plants and more "valuable" biomass, such as maize, needs to be used to increase production.

Basically, Marie Münster believes that it is possible to convert the 400,000 gas stoves into an alternative, whether it is distance heating or heat pumps in 2028. However, she is more skeptical of whether it is possible to expand the electricity grid in line with the need, When expanding violently with renewable energy in the short term.

Title: Borgmester raser over manglende mobilsignal under strømsvigt: 'Det duer ikke i 2022'
Full text:
Bornholm's mayor wants to commit the telecommunications companies to have six hours of backup battery on the masts.

It is not sustainable that mobile coverage fails during a prolonged power outage such as the one that hit Bornholm in March.

After the engineer could tell how the six -hour power failure put down the island's telecommunications, several politicians call the situation as clearly unsustainable.

'Of course, it does not pigeonhole in a modern society. I think we should have progressed than that, ”says Mayor Jacob Trøst (C) in Bornholm Regional Municipality.

"Bornholm is in a somewhat special situation because of the submarine cable, and that should be taken into account when issuing frequency permits."

Nor does the parliamentary politician Peter Juel-Jensen (V), who is elected in Bornholm's Great Circle and born on the island, believe it is a sustainable situation.

»The basic infrastructure of a society must also be in place on Bornholm. After all, it has been the case that you couldn't call 112. Of course, it doesn't work, because all sorts of things can happen. It would be tragic to witness a death that is solely because of the need for the necessary help, ”he says.

Requirements for emergency power or new cable
The current on Bornholm disappeared, after the search cable between Sweden and Bornholm was torn over by the anchor from a ship.

Several of the island's telemaster was equipped with backup batteries, yet the connection was gone on the first 30 masts after only two hours. Only two of the island's masts were kept running during the six -hour power failure.

If the mayor of Bornholm is in the future, a claim will be written in the frequency of frequency, which obliges the telecommunications companies to secure mobile coverage all over the island for six hours.

“Mobile coverage is critical infrastructure, and it must be in the interest of society that it is prioritized. I hope this has been a wake-up call through the system that we have a problem here, ”he says.

Parliamentary politician Peter Juel-Jensen (V) believes that the most optimal solution to the problem is to ensure the power supply itself to Bornholm.

»Our challenge is the submarine cable to Bornholm. The solution I can see is that in connection with the planned energy island, another cable is established from the island. It will make good sense as the current submarine cable is fully covered. Therefore, I expect that another cable will still be needed to transport the power from the energy island away from Bornholm, ”he says.

Energy Island is a project that will make Bornholm a hub for 2 GW offshore wind farms.

Extra cable can be done
The idea of ​​connecting Bornholm's electricity network to the future energy island and wind farms is not entirely new.

Earlier this year, Energinet announced that the initial analyzes indicate that it can technically be done. According to Energinet, it would cost about DKK 230 million in construction costs.

Conversely, in the long run there will be money to save if you establish a cable in connection with the energy island. For the lack of mobile coverage is not the only consequence when the current cable is broken. As the engineer has previously described, Bornholm is primarily kept running by fossil energy sources when the cable is out of service. The renewable energy sources are often too fluctuating and uncertain to use when the island is not connected to the outside world.

Since the fossil energy sources are expensive, it costs extra to keep Bornholm running when there is error or damage to the cable. Six times within the last 20 years it has gone so wrong that the cable has been torn over.

According to Energinet's calculations, therefore, around DKK 676 million can be saved over 40 years if another submarine cable was established in connection with the Energy Islands.

Title: Sådan gik Kattegatforbindelsen fra klimaforbedring over klimaneutral til klimaskadelig
Full text:
The Road Directorate's calculations on CO2 emissions from a Kattegat connection have changed by millions of tonnes of CO2 in a few years.

In four years, the operation of the Kattegat connection has gone from being a climate benefit to society of between 600,000 tonnes to 5,600,000 tonnes less CO2 emissions to being climate-embraceable with a total of 626,000 tonnes of extra CO2 emissions over a longer period of time.

It shows an access to documents that the Engineer has obtained in the mail correspondence between the Road Directorate and the Ministry of Transport, where the calculations of the climate price on the bridge swing up and down.

Back in 2018, the Road Directorate's report 'A fixed link over the Kattegat- strategic analysis of a pure road connection as well as a combined road and rail connection' showed that the Kattegat connection overall would reduce CO2 emissions in Denmark by between 600,000 and 5,600,000 tonnes in the operational phase.

The calculation included the entire period between 2035 and 2080 and included CO2 savings, among other things, that fewer will take the aircraft and more would drive the shorter trip across the bridge over Funen.

Now an access to documents shows that the calculations regarding CO2 emissions have changed from a climate benefit to a climate loss.

The main reason is updates in the so -called land traffic model. The land traffic model is the Road Directorate's calculation model for traffic in Denmark, which in 2021 has been updated twice.

In the correspondence, the Ministry of Transport is right with the Road Directorate's CO2 calculations regarding the operation of the Kattegat connection.

The correction is due to the fact that the Ministry of Transport denies that an estimated savings on CO2 emissions from domestic aircraft can be included.

The correspondence shows that the Road Directorate no longer expects a plus, ie a CO2 gain. In January, the calculations from the Road Directorate instead show that the Kattegat connection results in a greater emission of 51,000 tonnes between 2035 and 2050 - solely on the operation of the project.

This calculation corrects the Ministry of Transport to a discharge of 626,000 tonnes-ie from a large possible million-sized CO2 reduction in emissions to an increased CO2 climate load of 626,000 tonnes.

In addition, the Road Directorate estimates that the establishment of the Kattegat connection will result in a emission of 2-3 million tonnes of CO2.

The access to documents shows how the Ministry of Transport fixes the Road Directorate's calculations.

When Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen announced in his New Year's speech that "by 2030 we must be able to fly completely green when we fly domestic in Denmark," then all the CO2 calculations overturned on the Kattegat connection.

When CO2 cannot be saved on the passengers choosing to take over a bridge over the Kattegat rather than flying and burning heavy emerging jet fuel into the atmosphere, yes it goes from the climate gain on the connection. Because with a future green air traffic, there are no benefits to the climate by sending people across the Kattegat.

Søren Garden, who is the program manager in the Green Think Tank Concito, believes that the winding course at the climate estimates does not an expression of incompetence or lack of good will. It is a consequence of the absence of a solid basis for the officials' analyzes.

Need for a mobility strategy
The situation with the Kattegat connection is an example of Denmark's need for a unified, national green mobility strategy that officials and politicians can use their priorities regarding the future infrastructure projects/climate targets. Then the officials can get the connected vessels together.

“We see some well -understood truths that will be different because the board is changing. Originally, it was believed that the Kattegat connection could save some CO2 on detour, but it is a little equal if the driving is more and more electric. You lack the overall plan for it. "

According to Søren Have, the absence of a unified strategy creates uncertainty in relation to climate imprints, the traffic needs - and not least the imprint of building plants at different times.

“It shows here how things are in motion. You have been sitting and counting on something, but the world outside has changed. Now you caught the mistake here, but you lack the overall plan for how we get the climate imprint from mobility in zero. "

Prerequisites in change
According to Søren Have, many of the prerequisites for climate and traffic calculations are rapidly changing. This means that projects that were previously climate -wise are not good anymore.

"We risk dropping our CO2 budget away on things we don't need."

Søren Have believes that there is a lack of overall mobility strategy that takes into account the climate goals and defines what is missing from infrastructure - and when it is appropriate to establish it. Without an overall plan, estimates like those on the Kattegat connection become very uncertain.

"We risk wasting money and labor in ministries on something where the resources were used better somewhere else because you have solved the problem in a different way - or because traffic does not grow, as much as you thought."

“Maybe we build some road infrastructure that we don't need. At worst, it can cause an energy island or some climate protection or a bus terminal or something else that was important for the green transition being delayed. "

Analysis: A joint declaration of 150 GW wind power in 2050 can quickly run into obstacles.

Today, four heads of state from Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium have signed a declaration that wind power in the North Sea and adjacent sea areas must be expanded, so that by 2050 there are 10,000 offshore wind turbines or the equivalent of 150 GW.

Together, they will be able to produce electricity for 160 million European households.

As early as 2030, according to the declaration, the countries will have erected 65 GW. However, these are plans that have already been announced in the individual countries. In Denmark, it is planned to build 10 GW, of which 2-3 GW will be built at Bornholm. The attentive reader will know that that goal has already been slipping by several years. The schedule for the energy island has moved from 2030 to 2033. At that time, 3 GW is expected in the North Sea. By 2040 the target is 10 GW.

Yet, the joint declaration is impressive from a political perspective. Such a plan will require a thorough coordination of the development both on sea and on land. That is why the EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is also present in Esbjerg together with Energy Commissioner Kadri Simson.

From a technological angle, 150 GW wind turbines including transport of electricity will pose a gigantic challenge, even if all political obstacles are cleared out of the way.

Let's take the five biggest challenges:

1. Where should the mills stand?
The first question, of course, is where the mills should be built. The North Sea is large, but the depth of the sea makes not all places suitable.

On top of that comes the consideration of fishing, Natura 2000 areas, protected areas, areas free of shipping and raw material extraction. In a report from 2019, the Danish Energy Agency has designated areas in all Danish waters, corresponding to 34,914 km2, which could potentially accommodate approx. 40 gw offshore wind turbines. This is the maximum potential with the then prerequisites. Thus, there is a need to vacuum the entire North Sea for potential seats for wind turbines and energy islands.

In the long term, the technology may give a helping hand. For example, the requirement for relatively shallow areas may become less relevant when floating wind turbine platforms are matured and economically viable.

2. Where should electricity be led ashore?
The next point is the question of where the energy should be carried ashore. This is very relevant, because with so much energy it is imperative that energy can be brought to the right consumption sites on land when the wind blows.

The classic example is Germany, where the renewable energy is predominantly north, while the densely populated areas and industry consumption are south in the country. But over the past decades, it has been almost impossible first and foremost because of environmental protests, to expand with high -voltage connections between the north and the south.

3. Should PTX be produced?
This is brought to us to the next question: Should some of the large quantities of electricity be converted into other energy carriers directly on the energy islands? This is not a new question, as it is already included in the considerations of the Danish Energiø.

Such PTX systems can help store part of the energy when it blows more than consumption can subside, and could further supply the ship transport with fuel. But it has never been tried before and the answer to how the weighting between the different fuels and technologies should be is completely unknown.

4. Is electric technology ready?
And while we are still out in the energy islands, we must also be able to handle a so-called 'multiterminal HVDC' system. These types of systems do not exist today in a larger style, and they are markedly different to operate than traditional partially analogous electricity grids.

In the Engineer we have described on several occasions the technological challenge and professor at DTU Elektro, Jacob Østergaard, has described it as a modern fighter jet: 

"It requires advanced control, and if it fails, then the plane falls to the ground like a stone."

The risk is that a serious error on an energy island where many offshore wind farms are connected can potentially darken parts of the European electricity grid.

5. Keeps the schedule?
Last but not least, there is the schedule. 2050 may well seem far out in the future, and once a hole is coming through, it may be that the expansion goes smeared. We have seen that with solar cells on land (was there anyone who said hockey stake?). But if we look at the approval of the last Danish offshore wind farm, Thor in the North Sea, then it happened in 2018, and the park is expected to go into operation in 2026.

We are nowhere near getting tender at the first park to be connected to the energy island, but it is still expected that we have 10 GW ready by 2040. So there is something in the whole planning that will already make many people perceive The statement as unrealistic. Several players have proposed new tendering models where private investors no longer have to wait for a tender from the state, but can just start on the designated areas.

It is ambitious that four countries now agree that wind power in the North Sea and adjacent marine areas is the way to a sustainable energy system in Europe. But if the declaration is not followed up as soon as possible by concrete actions, then it will quickly be seen as contentless. There is plenty to address when the political systems of the four countries have to explain the huge investment and at the same time have to avert local environmental protests. There are few who in 2022 look forward to getting a new high -voltage connection in the backyard.

But the fear is also that politicians have underestimated the technological challenges. Wind turbines of 15 MW are not yet a shelf product and the electronics that will connect the parks with the electricity system in Europe are far from fully developed. Therefore, the declaration must be followed up with more research and development, otherwise politicians risk putting back the green transition and not forward.

Title: Esbjerg-erklæring skriger på svar: 'Vi aner ikke, hvordan vi styrer energiøernes kraft i land'
Full text:
How we need to control energy systems with offshore wind power, energy islands and a stable electricity grid with the Esbjerg Declaration is currently again.

From the middle of this century we can look forward to the wind starting the wings of up to 10,000 wind turbines at sea. This is clear after European top executives with Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen as host on Wednesday signed a declaration of intent to build 150 GW offshore wind in the North Sea by 2050.

But before the European energy markets can benefit from the huge amounts of wind energy, there must be air under quite different wings.

With the Esbjerg Declaration, an offshore energy system consisting of energy islands and wind farms is added in the majority. And then we as a society face more challenges: We do not know today how such an energy system should work in practice.

Therefore, it must be cooked under the pot of research and development of energy systems, which will control the many gigawatts that the North Sea will produce, says the clear message from two of the country's leading energy scientists in connection with Wednesday's statement.

“The energy islands are presenting some major, new challenges for our electricity systems, which we do not today know how to solve. Therefore, it requires a lot of research and development at both universities and with manufacturers and developers of technology solutions, as well as for those who drive the electricity grid. It takes time, 'as Filipe Miguel Faria da Silva, associate professor at AAU Energy, puts it.

“It has taken over 100 years to develop the current electricity system. Now we have to develop a new electricity grid in a few decades, so this is a major development task, ”he says.

A system that requires control
The major task lies in developing a system that can accommodate the conversion between equal and alternating current, which will be necessary to transport the many GW wind power from the offshore wind farms via energy islands and ashore. Probably to more countries.

As a starting point, the wind turbines will feed power to local alternating current networks on the energy islands through a power electronic converter. On the energy island, the alternating stream is converted to DC and is carried ashore via high voltage cables (HVDC). In the case of more destinations, we get what is called 'multiterminal HVDC'.

Jacob Østergaard, professor and center manager at DTU Elektro, explains how the whole challenge lies in the fact that there is an energy system based on effect electronic converters. It requires a significantly larger portion of control than the synchronous generator-based system we know from today's energy system with large thermal power plants.

In the latter, you have a built -in inertia in the generators, which can be used to maintain the frequency in the event of outcome or other imbalances between consumption and production. In a pure converter-based energy system, it does not find inertia, so a wind farm puts out, it requires a momentary reaction in the control.

Alternatively, major power failure is risked across Europe.

The point was ready in connection with the release of a significant white paper on which both Jacob Østergaard and filipe Miguel Faria da Silva are co -authors. The release from September last year bears the title 'Energy Islands: A Mars Mission for the Energy System', and we have previously mentioned it thoroughly here at the Engineer. With Wednesday's declaration of intent, its pointer becomes relevant again.

Professor Jacob Østergaard uses a sharp analogy to describe the challenges we face with the multiterminal HVDC systems.

»Our current energy system can be compared to an old -fashioned propeller machine. If the engine puts out, we can still control and maneuver the aircraft and land safely. The energy islands of the future and offshore electricity network are based on converter technology that must be constantly controlled. It corresponds to a modern fighter jet. If the operating systems fail here, the aircraft immediately falls to the ground as a stone, ”the DTU professor implies.

We need to avoid recreating the horse -drawn carriage
Jacob Østergaard explains how many of the basic pieces are in place to create the necessary energy system. But the pieces must be put together in the right way if we do not have to tighten our legs for ourselves.

“It is not that we just take all the pieces that we know from our current electricity system, and put together for something that is not smart and well thought out from the start. We know that it is crucial to think in system solutions and overall considerations for the energy islands and a new offshore electricity grid to become robust and cost-effective, ”he says, highlighting how unknown lock-in effects can occur.

“It can be seen analogous to the development of the first cars. Here you started from what you knew from the horse -drawn carriage. Therefore, the first cars were built with big wheels, and the driver was sitting up front on a cushion seat before finding out that it was not smart, ”exemplifies Jacob Østergaard and continues:

"By starting our knowledge from the start in the Energy Islands and the upcoming North Sea extension, we can avoid" recreating the horse -drawn carriage "but building a" modern car "that is optimized for the purpose."

A question about right timeframe
As we at the Engineer have outlined prior to the signatures of the Esbjerg Declaration, the challenges of establishing the right multiterminal HVDC system are drawing as one of the central barriers to overcome on the road to 150 GW offshore wind in the North Sea.

According to Jacob Østergaard, for example, we still need to find the methods for managing the converter-based energy system, while we need to raise our knowledge from A-to-B connections with high voltage cables, as it is known from, for example, the Danish-Norwegian submarine cable to include also point c, d and e.

Therefore, it seems perfectly obvious to ask:

Is it realistic to reach the goal of a total system for 2050?

“It's something we're in the process of working on already. So even though there are major research challenges ahead of us, if we are to do it in a wise and cost -effective way, it is realistic, ”says Jacob Østergaard, who is backed by his colleague from AAU.

“Precisely the time frame is absolutely crucial here. I would think that if we start now, it will be possible to achieve the right solutions for 2050. But we cannot wait for research and development until 2040, ”says Filipe Miguel Faria da Silva.

Look to Bornholm
With the planned Energiø on Bornholm we have a unique opportunity to test, research and develop in a clear set-up, says Jacob Østergaard.

"The world's first energy island on Bornholm can obviously serve as a test center for future energy island solutions, as we can take important learning there under conditions that are significantly easier than far out in the North Sea," he says, elaborating:

"It is crucial to be able to test the solutions if the industry is to have the necessary confidence in that new solutions that can be simulated on computers at DTU and other universities will also work in reality."

Look further out into the world
Indonesia is another place where researchers will hopefully be able to draw on concrete experience with energy -shooting, reminiscent of what we want to see in the North Sea.

Or experience may rather be picked up at Aalborg University, where Filipe Miguel Faria da Silva is a research leader on a project to develop a concept for managing precisely multit terminal HVDC between the islands of the Indonesian island.

"We currently have no results ready for publication from the project in Indonesia, but we expect that there will be useful knowledge to draw on in relation to the upcoming work with energy islands."

As the engineer's sister media Gridtech has previously mentioned, several parallels can be drawn between Indonesia and the North Sea in 2050.

Today, Indonesia's main island of Java is mainly supplied with energy from coal power. If energy consumption is to be switched to VE, it requires flow from other islands. Power that is led ashore on the islands by means of underwater HVDC cables to the local AC networks and on to Java. And with a network of road -producing islands - "energy islands" - it is again talking about Multiterminal HVDC.

Thus, there may be relevant knowledge to harvest in Indonesia.

For with the Esbjerg Declaration's aim of thousands of offshore wind turbines coupled to several energy islands, it will be necessary to draw on all experience to reach the goal in 2050. For as filipe Miguel Faria da Silva says:

»One single energy island itself is a challenge. Now we want to multiply that challenge. "

Title: Projekt Energiøer' kræver ølkassetaler og high fives
Full text:
The vision of some islands that produce enough wind energy to supply both Denmark and other European and Nordic countries is coming to fruition. And as responsible for the electricity infrastructure, Deputy Director of Energinet Hanne Storm Edlefsen is in front of all the visible work with the Energy Islands.

It's never been done before. The whole world is coming along, and several of the technologies do not exist yet. But if the 210 billion project succeeds with the Energy Islands on Bornholm and in the North Sea respectively, it means partly a fierce acceleration of the green transition and partly a greater independence of geopolitical challenges for the energy supply.

"If we really need to have made the energy system green, then we need to use offshore wind, which has been redone via hydrogen for liquid fuels, for example heavy traffic such as aircraft and ships and heavy process industry," Hanne Storm Edlefsen states. Since the Energy Islands became a reality in the summer of 2020, she has served as Deputy Director of Energinet, who is responsible for the electric infrastructure of the huge project. 

The idea for the islands, which will be able to produce enough wind energy to cover five million households' annual electricity consumption, emerged back in 2017 as a brain Child between managers in Dutch Tennet, Gasuine and Danish Energinet. EU also welcomed the idea at a time when Denmark had not yet settled on a 70 percent reduction in its total CO2 emissions. 

In April 2017, Hanne Storm Edlefsen will be invited into the development of the 'Wish Islands' with the words of Energinet's director: "I have a project that will probably be a little difficult - so it's probably just for you!"

Hanne Storm Edlefsen would probably not let go of that challenge ...

“I'm probably optimistic of mind and have a great focus on where to go. We have to succeed in making a good model for this, because we have no other choice. And I have no doubt for a second that the Energy Islands are a really good idea, so we just have to make the setup right, ”she says of the background of why she has taken on such a big task. 

“It only becomes even more important when there is war in Ukraine. It's about being tied together in a good way so we look after each other. Having that focus also just makes you just go back and try again if something teases, ”says the program director. 

Pulling air in
Since then, she has become Deputy Director with responsibility for Energinet's work with the Energi Islands and so far 20 employees. 

"I can get a stomach suck and think" shut up, how crazy is it "and" How do we get from A to B this week? "Then I just pull in and remind me even though I have Skilled people and good partners - and then we take one thing at a time, ”she says.

“It's something I have from home. You don't give up if it teases. We give a hug and a high five, and then we're back on. "

When Hanne Storm Edlefsen was a child, her teacher parents had a conversation kitchen before it became a fashion word. They even took it so seriously that they had built a high chair for Lille Hanne - who were a nunnery - so she could participate in the conversation on par with her siblings. 

"I've always been involved and great demands have been made," she says.

For example, if there was something she would- as on a hike with the scouts- was asked to argue for her case and spent a long time sitting and writing pre- and against lists in her room to have counter-arguments ready The conversation with his parents. If they thought her arguments were too thin, it was back in the room to polish them off.

"So I've been trained in making decisions from when I was a kid, but I was taken seriously too."

Therefore, in Energinet, Hanne Storm Edlefsen is not pale to remind herself and the employees of what great work they are doing, even though they sometimes laugh a little at her eternal 'beer box trays'. 

“When something gets too sour or too difficult, I stand up and remind you that we are saving the climate. They should have no doubt that I have their backs. This is crazy and it is really difficult, but it is also really important, ”she says and continues shortly after:

"And if anyone can, then it's these heads, because they're just pissed out."

Speed ​​on the changeover
The snowball began to roll in May 2020, when a united parliament - only without the New Citizens' - decided that the energy islands should become a reality. 

It was a big news - which Hanne Storm Eldlefsen just just missed out in the first place because she was sitting at a Native American bonfire and 'peeling navel' on a management course without phone contact. 

“So it was quite special to wake up to reality and find out that what we had been going and developing for a few years suddenly had to be realized. And not just one island, but two, 'she remembers.

“It was great to find that what was a vision in 2017 had been grabbed and that others than we could see that it was a way of setting the size and speed of the green transition. Because that's what it's all about: scaling up and slowing down. "

The climate agreement that came a month later states precisely that the agreement must 'pave the way for global leadership in renewable energy and ensure an ambitious green transition of the industry. With the agreement, Denmark stands in front of an ambitious expansion of green energy and a significant investment in the green technologies of the future, such as CO2-catching and Power-to-X. ' 

Energinet's task is to take care of the preparatory environmental and seabed surveys, to develop and operate electricity cables between Denmark, the energy islands and other countries and to ensure that the Energy Energy from the Energy Islands is connected and integrated with the energy system on land. 

In other words, Energinet has responsible for what Hanne Storm Eldlefsen calls 'gear' - cables and transformer stations. 

In Energinet, the work is organized through the program 'Energy Islands', which she herself is director of. The program then contains a project that deals with Bornholm, and one that deals with the North Sea. A third project deals with the cross -cutting development activities where something new has to be developed that goes across the two projects.

In addition to the fact that there are naturally many unknowns in terms of technology, the program is also so great that it will go in and change the entire energy business because there is so much more wind coming into the system that needs to be controlled. 

"What we are doing will get rid of all our colleagues and are of great importance to the operation," explains Hanne Storm Eldlefsen.

"Therefore, it is an insanely important part of my team's job to anchor what we come up with."

The size is crucial
It is politically decided that Bornholm Island should produce 2 GW, but we are investigating the area for up to 3 GW. Capacity will mean how much space the wind turbines must have that customers in the market be secured, just as the electricity system must be balanced according to it. 

At the same time, Energinet prepares a business case on the electricity infrastructure, and then Hanne Storm Edlefsen is finally negotiating with the Germans how revenue and expenses should be distributed on the connection between Bornholm and Germany. 

The feasibility studies, which will be completed in 2024, are in full swing, as are the dialogue with the market and suppliers. 

"We are quite far in relation to being able to mature a construction project," says the Deputy Director. 

With the North Sea Island it is a little different because there is no island already. But it will be a public-private partnership where the state has to own at least 50.1 percent, and then the private party must be 'caretaker' on the island, while Energinet pays 'gear' and rent on the island. So far, Ørsted and Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners have each formed their own consortium with pension funds to offer the task as the private party. 

In one point of view in one of the Engineer's media, Hanne Storm Edlefsen used the analogy with a wedding to explain how far the cooperation with the other countries is in terms of diminishing electricity from the energy island of the North Sea. 

“We are engaged to Germany and Belgium and Kurtize Norway. We would like to marry Norway in the second half, so we need to analyze whether you can connect a Norwegian offshore wind area with a Danish energy island, ”she says.

Tranquility in the development box
Before reaching this far, there are some technical challenges that Energinet must have solved. 

It has never been done before to connect a large DC system at a very high voltage level to a small local alternating current that runs at a relatively low voltage level. The complicated lies in devising a control of the flow from the wind turbines so that it does not cause problems for the alternating stream net on Bornholm.

The 2 - maybe 3 - GW, the island must produce, are many times what normal power plants provide, and by comparison, Bornholm's current connection to Sweden is a small sewing thread. Therefore, it is crucial that Energinet connects the huge machine just right on the Bornholm net and causes the power to swing perfectly in tact.

"We would very much like to help develop a standardization and a modularly built system in connection with Bornholm, and then use it as a showcase and laboratory for what we have to build in the North Sea," says Hanne Storm Eldlefsen.

In the autumn, the engineer wrote that the risk of using new and unproven technology in the North Sea could be that you could darken all of Northern Europe if a mistake propagates to the rest of the electricity grid on the continent.

“There has been an extremely external focus on us, and it will continue to be. So it is extremely important that the engineers are calm to develop, ”she says, pointing out that her primary task is to give a direction on where the development is going, while the project managers have been given great mandate to find the solutions none For good reasons know in advance. 

“I give them room to be in a 'development box' without anything that binds them so that they can develop under free frames until it becomes serious. Right now we try some things, but when we then have to present something out in reality, we mix blood and look each other in the eyes and say, "This is what we go with."

In reality, there are ways to achieve the goal of existing technology, but according to the Deputy Director it is more 'hassle' and provides less stability in the energy system. So it would be smarter and cheaper to develop a standardization. 

"So we have a backup plan if we don't reach it," she smiles. 

All eyes on Hanne
Organizational it has been a bit of a challenge to gear the organization to seize the projects in the program without knowing how fast things are going to go, for 'what if you were politically decided not to make Bornholm or there was no interest From abroad ', as Hanne Storm Edlefsen says.

"It has been a condition, but it means that such common things like having control of staffing, project ingenering documents and ESDH systems, etc., we have taken a little one day at a time."

A condition is also the enormous interest she previously talked about - that everyone's eyes are aimed at her. How does she handle it?

“I - and Energinet - are not alone. The Danish Energy Agency also has a huge responsibility, so it is a strong partner. But what we do in Energinet is to be felt and felt because it is us who are doing the preliminary investigations and need to knock on the door of a farmer if we are to use his field. That is why we also have an important communication task, ”says the Deputy Director, who feels very committed to talking about what Energinet is doing. 

“We are going up on the scale and we need to get up to speed. So it is of no use that I think it is too difficult to negotiate with the Germans, or doubt whether we are now landing a technology, ”she says. 

"But we shake our hand, and I think that is healthy, because then we make every effort and go right back into Hannes box again if it doesn't feel 100 percent good in the stomach," she says, sending a greeting to her old Girl room on Funen and the argumentation exercise.

And then it also helps the Deputy Director to have a Helle on Funen, where she lives with her husband and son and lets up with mandatory sea baths and shelters with the scouts she is the leader of every Tuesday.

"When I am once in a while a little skiing and tired, and my husband says 'shouldn't we just sit on the couch', I remind myself that it's not wasted work. It's something where I can really say, That I've done it because it's important, 'she says, being touched by the thought.

"I remind myself regularly, and that's also why my colleagues laugh a little at me, because I can think of pulling it out of my pocket and putting myself on the beer box on such an ordinary foggy Wednesday," says Hanne Storm Edlefsen.

Title: Konsortium smider joker på bordet: Energiø skal være international data-hub
Full text:
According to DTU professor Lars Dittmann, it can be practically possible to establish a data center on the energy island, but it will probably be more expensive than doing it on land.

The energy island of the future in the North Sea must not only produce large quantities of green energy, but also be an international center for digitalisation.

This is the opinion of the energy company Ørsted and the pension fund ATP, which together are struggling to win the supply to establish the energy island.

The consortium has entered into an agreement to make it possible to connect the energy island with a 100,000 -kilometer fiber network owned by the company GlobalConnects. By offering green energy and fiber networks, the consortium hopes to be able to attract an international data center to the island, while the fiber connection can contribute to further digitization of offshore wind.

"The North Sea Energiø gives Denmark a unique opportunity to become the center of the future key technologies and thus attract significant investments in both renewable energy and digitalisation," says Rasmus Errboe, regional director of continental Europe at Ørsted, in a press release on collaboration.

Expensive but technically possible
It requires large amounts of energy to operate a data center. As the engineer has previously described, data centers within 20 years may end up standing for one -third of Denmark's energy consumption - and electricity consumption in the centers is already growing faster than expected.

Therefore, there may be nothing to say that Ørsted and ATP would like to utilize the energy from the energy island's wind turbines to a data center. And according to Lars Dittmann, professor at DTU, there is nothing practical in the way of connecting the energy island to the fiber infrastructure. He points out that the energy island no matter what would need to be connected to the fiber network.

»Modern wind turbines are so complex that it takes great data power to be able to control it. The question is whether to put some more if there is to be a data center, but it is not far out to it, so it can easily be done, ”he says, adding that the need for fiber capacity depends on what type of data center that ends up being placed on the energy island.

Nor should it cause any technical problems to establish the data center itself on the artificial island. However, Lars Dittmann cannot answer whether the idea is financially related.

“It will probably be more expensive to establish it on water, and it is expensive to get employees out there, so I don't know if it can pay off to get the energy in ashore. But it may be that they would like to utilize the seawater for cooling. You usually use as much power to cool as you do to get the computers to work, ”he says.

Esbjerg Declaration
The plans for the energy island as a center of digitization come only a month after the so-called Esbjerg Declaration.

Here, the Danish government signed an agreement with Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands to expand the plans for an energy island in the North Sea.

Originally, the energy island had to deliver 3 GW offshore winds, but after the Esbjerg Declaration, the target was upgraded to make the energy island an international center for green energy production. If all goes well, up to 10,000 offshore wind turbines will produce a total of 150 GW by 2050.

Title: DTU-forskere vil tæmme ustabilt elnet med fremtidens kvantecomputer
Full text:
PhD project at DTU demonstrates the first calculations of the role of quantum computer in the control of a future complex electricity grid with many fluctuating energy sources.

With the ever -increasing proportion of renewable energy sources in the energy pride, the complexity of our electricity grid increases. It requires control and monitoring to a different extent than we are used to today.

In parallel with the development of electricity generation and networks, there is also development in the available computer computing power. In particular, there are high expectations of what the future quantum computers will be able to solve.

The two parallel developments have got a PhD student at DTU Vind Brynjar Sævarsson to ask the question: What role can the quantum computer play in ensuring the stability of the future electricity grid?

“There is a lot of potential in quantum computers if they are built big enough. In that case, they seem to be used as a tool in the electricity system, ”says Brynjar Sævarsson.

First use of quantum computer on the electricity grid
The intersection of calculations on the electricity grid and the use of quantum computers to solve the calculations is a relatively untrained field.

As Brynjar Sævarsson and his colleagues describe in a scientific article accepted for presentation at a conference this fall, only a few researchers around the world have tried to make electricity network calculations on a quantum computer - and here immediately only on simulated quantum computers.

Thus, the researchers from DTU, as far as are known, are the first to actually complete calculations on current quantum computers. This was done in connection with five calculations on IBM's publicly available 5 and 7 QUBITS machines in collaboration with IBM.

Here Brynjar Sævarsson and his colleagues have solved the so-called Loadflow problem, which is a tool to analyze the flow of an electricity system to ensure that there is not too much power in individual lines and that all tensions are within the right area , explains the PhD student.

“We have found that we can use the quantum computer to make calculations on a small test system. These are some results we are really happy about, although the quantum computers are still very limited to what we can do with them, ”says Brynjar Sævarsson.

Solve more features at the same time
When Brynjar Sævarsson and his research colleagues from DTU have great confidence in the quantum computer's role in calculations on the future electricity grid, it is due to the possibility of having quubits in super posting and not only assuming the values ​​0 and 1 separately as with classic computers.

The quantum states make it possible to solve several functions with several variables at the same time, which in an electricity grid context can help to raise the security of supply.

»Quantum computers are suitable for making calculations on many different scenarios at the same time and parallel processes. It fits very well with an electricity grid with renewable energy, where fluctuations and uncertainties give rise to having to count on many parallel scenarios, ”says Brynjar Sævarsson.

Here he mentions forecasts for energy production from wind turbines as an example of a place where the quantum computer can be important.

Good options for necessary real -time calculations
Claus Leth Bak, professor at Aalborg University Energi, is not part of the DTU research project, but even works with computer calculations on the electricity grid in the form of complicated simulation models.

He explains how the green transition, including the giant energy island projects, means that more and more detailed and accurate simulation models of the entire mains are needed. Not only in Denmark, but also for the countries of the Energy Island projects are expected to be connected. Something we have also described several times here at the Engineer.

Claus Leth Bak believes that there is potential if you can supplement normal computer rainy power with quantum computers in the future for simulations of the electricity networks.

“As we get more renewable energy to the electricity grid, the control of the grid becomes far more complex. Therefore, online real -time management methods with adequate computing power is needed. To that end, quantum computers can play a role, ”says Claus Leth Bak.

Real -time solutions, according to Claus Leth Bak, call on great computing power, which it is hoped that the quantum computers of the future can deliver.

»Behind calculations on the electricity grid lies models that, in line with increasing complexity and uncertainties in the electricity grid, must also be increasingly complex. Today, the models often try to simplify to compensate for a lack of computer rainy power, ”says the AAU professor.

»The more computing power we have available, the more accurate global models we can make. And since the electricity grid will become more vulnerable to fluctuations in the future than we have been used to in the past 20-30 years, it is important with more accurate models for real-time calculations that can keep the electricity networks stable. Modern society is very dependent on the reliability of our electricity supply not impairing as a result of the green transition. "

Noise and small machines
But before we get that far, there are quite a few things that still need to be developed.

"There is still some noise in the current quantum computers, which also have some restrictions," says Brynjar Sævarsson.

He explains how at the same time it has been a challenge to build algorithms for the calculations with appropriate scalability. If the systems are greater than the test case, the algorithms have proved inadequate. And then there is the whole question of the size of the quantum computer, which today does not make it favorable compared to today's supercomputers.

»Theoretically, the methods of a quantum computer should be exponentially faster than on classic computers. Here is the result of our research that we can run the calculations on a current machine - we are still not faster than a classic computer, ”says Brynjar Sævarsson.

It gets the Engineer's journalist to ask if it is realistic at all that we have the desired quantum computing computing power available when the green transition seriously breaks through. For example, with a quadruple of the production of solar and wind energy alone on land with the current government's plans.

“It's hard to say how the development of quantum computers is going to happen. We see very positive results from IBM and others in building ever larger machines, ”says Brynjar Sævarsson. Han's hope is that research as his own can help the necessary algorithms to be developed, so there is a method ready when we Suddenly stands with an electricity grid based on up to 100 percent renewable energy.

And then the quantum computer hardly has to stand alone, the DTU researcher estimates. Rather, it should be seen as a supplement to the classic computers.

“The quantum computer can do something special, but it is not better at everything. Therefore, we will probably see that some tasks are solved on classic computers, while some are solved on quantum computers, ”says Brynjar Sævarsson.

Title: Elnettet i Tyskland forstærkes fra nord til syd, og det er godt for Danmark
Full text:
Three new high -voltage connections in Germany must ensure that electricity from the windblown north can be sent to the consumption sites in the south. Planning has been elongated and the commissioning has been delayed by several years.

On a drive down through Germany, it is difficult to avoid the sight of the huge high -voltage connections that cut through the landscape. Here sometimes four three -phase alternating current systems hang up to 380 kV on a single master's row, which in round numbers corresponds to a transfer capacity of 2,400 MW, or what could supply half of Denmark on an autumn day.

But despite the many high-voltage motorways, the electrical connection between North and Southern Germany is weak. This has been the case for decades, and as more and more wind turbines have been built north, including offshore wind turbines in the Danish part of the North Sea, the problem has been reinforced. On top of that, Germany has decided to stop electricity production at the country's nuclear power plants, part of which is in the southern part, where the largest electricity consumption is also located.

However, the challenge has been that old -fashioned high -voltage connections at Master are not something that neither environmental organizations nor resident groups love. Therefore, new connections must be laid as cables with direct current, and it provides both a gigantic additional expense and a complicated approval process.

But now there is a prospect that a large part of the problem will be solved, and when the German electricity grid is reinforced, it will also benefit Denmark. This is stated by Morten Pindstrup, an international chief engineer at Energinet.

“We could have wished that the expansion had happened somewhat faster. But now we get built the connections we have been asking for in Denmark for years. There is no doubt that it will help in our area when it becomes easier to move the energy south, ”says Morten Pindstrup.

warely ready in 2028
In particular, it is the cable connection called Suedlink, which consists of two 525 kV HVDC connections, which the Danish electricity grid will initially benefit from. The one connection that the Danish cable producer NKT is to deliver is at 702 km and goes from Brunsbüttel in Schleswig-Holstein in the north to Grossgartach in Baden-Württemberg in the south. The other is 558 km and goes from Wilster to Grafenrheinfeld close to Schweinfurt. The total transfer capacity is 4 GW, and it also gets connected to the cable Nordlink, which goes from Germany to Norway.

However, it has not been unproblematic to get the connections approved. The work started in 2012 and really it was planned that the construction itself could start in 2016 and with commissioning in 2022.

It is the two system -responsible German companies Tennet TSO and Transnetbw who are responsible for the connection. But numerous delays, partly due to resident protests along the route and from environmental organizations, have made the connection only come into operation in 2028. This despite the fact that the new German government, which took office in 2021, has declared it a project It must be "accelerated" and implemented with high political priority ".

Although Suedlink is initially the most important connection for Denmark, a slightly further east will also be built, which has been given the natural name of Suedostlink. The responsible network companies are here Tennet and 50Hertz.

With Suedostelink, the northern Mecklenburg-West Pomerania is connected, with a transformer station at the Isar atom power plant in Bavaria with two 550 km long 525 kV cables, which together can transfer 4 GW. Here, too, NKT is inside as they have to deliver cables for the last 275 km. The connection was adopted in 2015, but is only expected to go into operation in 2027:

“In the short run, Suedostelink will not mean so much to Denmark. But for Energiø Bornholm and his expected connection in Germany it may be interesting to move more wind energy further south in Germany, ”says Morten Pindstrup.

Carried out in spite of resistance
Despite the delays, Axel Happe, who is responsible for planning and authorization at 50Hertz, does not believe that it could have gone much faster:

"We have been in dialogue with public authorities, interest organizations and the general public since the start of the planning process in 2016. Over the years, a lot of questions have been raised and answered. In some cases where the route corridors passed villages, we had to explain our planning in more detail. And in many cases, together with residents, farmers or landowners along the route, we found solutions to sometimes very specific problems. Hard local resistance or general resistance to the cable project has been rare, ”he writes in a response to the Engineer.

Also further west in Germany, the web is reinforced with a cable connection called A-Nord from Emden in Northwest Germany to Osterath close to Düsseldorf and on to Phillipsburg just south of Frankfurt A.M. With another cable called Ultranet.

The question then is whether the new north-south connections in Germany are already too little when the development of the North Sea is gaining momentum.

“Every two years we make a prognosis for the electricity system in the network development plan. According to our latest prospects, where we look forward to the year 2035, the planned transmission capacity between Börde and Isar shows itself sufficiently, writes Alex Happe.

At the same time, he emphasizes that increased electricity consumption in Northern Germany is also considered. This applies to both the production of hydrogen and new highly electrified industries such as Tesla and Intel. On top of that comes increased consumption due to electric cars and heat pumps:

"With all these factors included, our projections still show that the planned connections have a sufficiently high capacity," writes Alex Happe, adding that the Russian invasion of Ukraine also emphasizes the need for a quick and reliable conversion of energy consumption in Germany and Europe.

At Energinet there is support for the German initiatives.

“Now, electricity is not the only way to move energy. Pipelines are also needed for hydrogen and production of methanol and ammonia for use in trucks and ships. But now we get the connections we have been asking for for years. It must go faster than it has done, and the question is whether it is enough when the expansion with wind in the North Sea is increasing, ”says Morten Pindstrup.

Title: Tysk forsker om PtX-udviklingsbehov: »svært at retfærdiggøre mange flere forskningspenge«
Full text:
PTX is one of the most hyped concepts of the time. But researchers and businesses are struggling to find the right technological solutions - both when it comes to making and using PTX.

Energy needed both push and pull

In energy technology, PTX (Power-to-X) is currently one of the very warmest topics. A good example is the Norwegian company HydrogenPro, which at a recently held symposium at Aarhus University could tell that it has conversations with potential customers about the sale of up to 12.6 GW electrolysis capacity.

It is assumed that globally today there is just under 0.5 GW capacity in operation. The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates that by 2030 there will be about 85 GW capacity in operation and that there must be around 3,000 GW of operation in 2050 if the CO2 targets are to be achieved.

HydrogenPro's pipeline should not be confused with fixed orders, but gives an indication of how much the hype is about the conversion of energy from wind and sun to hydrogen and from there to other energy carriers such as methanol, ammonia, aircraft fuel and gasoline. And HydrogenPro is just one of the companies that are struggling to get part of the development of advanced electrolysis units produced in 5.5 MW modules in China with electrodes from Aarhusian Advanced Surface Plating.

Last week, HydrogenPro told about a project in the US state of Utah, where 100 tonnes of hydrogen a day will be produced from a 220 MW electrolysis system, corresponding to 40 electrolysis units, each with a length of 8 meters, a diameter of approx. 2 meters and a weight of more than 75 tonnes.

These are the above figures that make most people today know what PTX means. Any politician, school teacher or company director can talk about us to utilize green electricity to produce new fuels that can replace the fossils.

Most people also know that the technology behind is far from new - nor industrial. Back at the beginning of the last century, Norwegian Hydro produced artificial fertilizers on the basis of electrolysis (and nitrogen) and during World War II, the Nazis allegedly held part of their war machine rolling with fuel made from the front coal.

Political support
This spring, the Danish government then signed a broad political agreement on a Danish strategy for PTX, aiming to expand the Danish electrolysis capacity to 4-6 GW in 2030.

The expectations of political support have already launched some actors, such as Ørsted and Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP), which have announced large projects in respectively. Avedøre and Esbjerg. Here, electricity from offshore wind turbines at energy islands in the Baltic Sea and the North Sea must be included in the manufacture of hydrogen, which can subsequently be converted into gasoline, methanol, ammonia or aircraft fuel.

So with the historical perspective and the political obstacles cleared of the way should it be straightforward? The arguments for embracing PTX have not diminished in the last few months with rising fuel prices topped up with political focus on security of supply.

But the symposium in Aarhus also revealed that although developments in PTX have taken huge steps over the last five years, there is not a single technology that has 'won'.

Should hydrogen production, for example, be done with traditional alkaline electrolysis, or should it be with the more advanced PEM or SOEC technology that has technological roots in fuel cells? Or should it be a completely different technology where electricity energy, biomass and residual products are used for direct production of liquid fuels using technologies such as Hydrothermal Liquefaction and Thermochemical Processes?

Companies such as German Electrochaea, Danish Circlia Nordic and Canadian Enerkem showed various technological solutions.

On top of that comes the question of the best end product. Should it be pure hydrogen for buses and trucks, ammonia and methanol for large ships and as a raw material in the industry or gasoline and diesel for the transport sector? On the whole: What does it take to find the right solutions?

We know the solution
A lot of balls are up in the air but one of the world's leading scientists, Dr. Ralph-Uwe Dietrich from Deutsches Zentrum Für Air- und Raumfahrt (DLR) couldn't help but be slightly annoyed when the engineer met him in Aarhus:

“I risk getting my research colleagues on the neck, but it's hard to justify many more research money for a problem where we know the solution well. Of course, we can make the processes more efficient and find better chemical solutions, but basically there are no technological barriers to PTX, ”he says, mentioning that in Germany there have been numerous demonstration projects, but because there is no commercial demand for the fuel the projects not extended.

But what is it missing? Professor Lars Ditlev Mørck Ottosen from Aarhus University has a response to this, because it is about scaling up, and it must go fast:

»Fossil fuels have been incredibly cheap and therefore the cost of PTX is the biggest barrier. But our calculations show that if we do not set ambitious demands to comply with the Paris Agreement, the PTX market will not come. Therefore, there must be a push from the politicians with demands for use and a pull from the industry. The latter has shown Maersk by ordering new methanol -powered container ships - this is something we need, ”he says.

And here Ralph-Uwe Dietrich agrees, because even though it is very much about technology, it is ultimately more money that is needed-and they need to be invested in production. ”We need investors to see a credible business model , and it requires political regulation. Let's start with a mixing requirement in the sectors where we need to have PTX - for example in aviation. Then we can continuously increase the pressure and make it more and more attractive to investors, ”he says.
The electrolysis units are 5.5 MW, weigh about 75 tonnes and are 8 meters high. The production capacity is about 100 kg per hour at 15 bar.
