Title: Klimavenlige materialer og bæredygtighedskrav til vindmøller kan blive del af offentlige udbud
Full text:
Climate Minister is responsive to proposals for sustainability requirements for energy projects.

When the state will in future have to supply wind farms on land and at sea, the tenders should contain climate targets, so that the manufacturers are encouraged to use more sustainable materials, thinks the think tank Concito and Tekniq employers.

Such a requirement will also be a helping hand for the Danish wind turbine manufacturers who are under pressure from Chinese competitors who, due to state grants and access to cheap steel, can manufacture the wind turbines cheaper.

To protect the European wind turbine industry, the European Commission introduced an anti-dumping duty in the import of wind turbine towers from China in December.

"In connection with an anti-dumping case raised by European wind tower manufacturers (including two Danish), it emerged that a single read Chinese towers sailed to Denmark from China emits as much as a Danish tower factory's total annual discharge," Troels Blicher Danielsen, CEO of Tekniq Employers, recently wrote in a debate post in the Altinget.

"So we risk derive more CO2 on a global scale if we do not focus sharply on climate and environmental requirements in both the construction and operational phase of energy islands and similar WE projects."

The war in Ukraine has only worsened the situation of the European wind turbine industry.

In June, the Wind Europe industry organization, based on a survey of its members, announced that the prices of raw materials for the wind turbines had increased by 30 percent. A figure that the Danish trade association has not wanted to comment on the Engineer. According to Wind Europe, steel is about 70 percent of a turbine.

CONCITO: Everyone is going to be in a green direction
"Basically, climate technology needs to enter all major tenders and construction projects, including wind farms, because there is great potential for the demand from demand to pull the market in a greener direction," Tobias Johan Sørensen, climate analyst in Concito, told the Engineer.

For him, it is obvious that the public shopping muscle of DKK 300 billion is used annually to demand climate -friendly materials, so that producers are encouraged to change faster.

However, when Concito suggests writing sustainability requirements into public tenders, however, it is not a deliberate attempt to give the Danish producers an advantage.

“It is really positive for the producers if they have a competitive advantage. But it can also be a Swedish producer of green steel, which can bid to the suppliers here of the upcoming steel, so it is not to distribute some producers over others. Everyone is going in a green direction, ”says Tobias Johan Sørensen.

Concito has not put forward a concrete model for how sustainability should be written into the tenders, but Tobias Johan Sørensen would like to come up with a proposal.

“My immediate bid would be that you have to work with a CO2 price of around DKK 1,500. It can also be higher. So when you provide a bid, you have an overview of your materials and their CO2 imprint and then this CO2 price comes on top. So if you can make a project with really low emissions, you also boast about that offer here, ”he says.

“How much it constitutes the total cost and how much it should weight can then be discussed. But I would initially look at how to get it into this offer, get it priced, so it favors those who choose the greenest materials and use them most effectively. "

Minister is open to the proposal
The proposal for sustainability requirements in public tenders meets responsiveness from Climate, Energy and Supply Minister Dan Jørgensen.

In a response to the Folketing's Climate, Energy and Supply Committee last week, he indicated that he is open to the proposal. It is intended that increased sustainability should be part of the consideration when, by the end of 2022, it should be discussed how the tender frames for offshore wind farms by 2030 should be arranged, he wrote.

"In agreement on green power and heating 2022, it must be stated that increased sustainability must be ensured in the supply of tenders in accordance with the principles of EU taxonomy for environmental sustainability and the Danish climate targets, as well as tools such as ESG and life cycle assessments," he writes.

Title: CO2 fra biogas kan give negative udledninger: Sådan gør vi
Full text:
It is uncertain whether CO2 from upgrading biogas does the most benefit in stocks or used for PTX. Surely it is that carbon from biomass becomes a scarce resource.

CO2-catching at sea, on land and in the air

Today we say goodbye annually to over half a million tonnes of CO2, which is led into the atmosphere of Danish biogas plants. But there are many good reasons for keeping the CO2 instead.

At the biogas plants it is relatively cheap to capture the CO2, and at the same time it is reasonably straightforward to transport in pipes. And then it contains carbon from biomass, which in the future can become a scarce resource.

No matter how paradoxical it may sound, it means in practice that while we are struggling to limit the amount of CO2 in the atmosphere, CO2 can be ripped on Earth for use in liquid green fuels made by so -called Power to X (PTX) and to Storage. This applies not least to the CO2, which is excreted every year and then emitted from Danish biogas plants in connection with the upgrade of biogas to pure biomethane.

In 'Status Report 2022', the Climate Council has dedicated an entire chapter to emphasize this scarcity.

»We can produce a limited amount of biomass because the size of the globe limits the cultivation area. Therefore, biogenous carbon can be in short supply in the long term, ”says Peter Møllgaard, Climate Council chairman. He thus introduces a concept we need to have in place to look at what will happen in the future with the Biogas CO2.

Negative emissions
There is a difference between CO2. When the climatic gas is discharged by the combustion of fossil fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas, carbon is released, which is not a natural part of the Earth's carbon circuit. We're talking about Fossil CO2.

When the climate gas is the conversation from decaying processes in the field, the flue gas from the straw -fired power plant or degassing in a biogas reactor, it is biogenic CO2. As long as new trees and plants are planted as a replacement for the utilized biomass, the CO2 will be absorbed again and thus does not contribute to the CO2 content of the atmosphere.

Climate analyst in the green think tank Concito Tobias Johan Sørensen explains that it is one of the primary reasons why the CO2 emissions from the biogas plants have not been tried before:

“Since the CO2 is biogenic, it does not appear in our climate accounts as discharge. It is on paper a Net-zero discharge, ”says Tobias Johan Sørensen.

"Now it has come into focus because we have to make all the reductions we can at all."

Both he and the climate council chairman, Peter Møllgaard, emphasize that we are currently in a situation where quick and cheap actions are needed to correct the balance of the CO2 accounts. And here biogen CO2 from biogas plants can play an important role if stored. Thus, carbon is drawn out of the circuit and negative emissions have been created.

Cheap stock on land
Now to the question of what will happen to the biogenic CO2 from biogas upgrade. If you ask Tobias Johan Sørensen and Peter Møllgaard, we must see to get started storing it - so it must be used for so -called CCS (Carbon Capture and Storage). Since the technologies for excretion of CO2 from Biogas are already installed on the biogas plants - because it is necessary to remove CO2 from biogas to be able to utilize it in the natural gas network - catch, shipping and subsequent storage of CO2 from biogas plants according to the Climate Council's calculations can be done for around DKK 500 .

"It is among the cheapest tons of our analyzes," says Peter Møllgaard, who points out that the Climate Council's assessment is that CO2 storage is cheaper than use in PTX processes.

In addition to the price of the catch, the location of the warehouse is important. Here, the CO2 from the biogas plants will initially have to be shipped to the more mature, underwater stocks, says Tobias Johan Sørensen. But if Gas Storage Denmark and GEUS 'ongoing studies of land -firm and coastal warehouses bear fruit, it is according to the climate analyst here that the CO2 should end.

"It will be cheaper for society and for companies to make the cheapest possible piping for stocks on land or coastal," he says, pointing to another expense item at CCS: Transport from point source to warehouse, which Tobias Johan Sørensen estimates, cheapest is done with tube.

It suggests preliminary calculations from the country's gas distribution network operator Evida as well. Peter Kristensen, Evida's Strategy and Development Director, says that a pre-screening has designated 35 major biogas plants with geographical locations, which add up to a common CO2 pipe rather than shipping with tanker cars. According to him, from here you can lead as much as 755,000 tonnes of CO2 into the net by 2030 "just by connecting things". And then the CO2 in parts of the grid can be carried in plastic pipes at normal pressure and temperature.

"There are no technical obstacles to getting started," says Peter Kristensen.

Electricity from two -thirds energy island
Evida's studies have looked at several scenarios for how the CO2 from the biogas plants is being utilized. Should it be shipped for CO2 collection from other point sources? Should it be sent in the direction of land -fixed stocks? Or rather port areas with shipping options and PTX production-which belongs to the common term CCU (Carbon Capture and Utilization)?

»After all, there is an alternative to transporting CO2 away from the biogas plants if you instead metanize the CO2 locally by adding hydrogen. We look at both as it has an impact on the design of the infrastructure, ”says Peter Kristensen.

The industry organization Biogas Denmark is among those who distinguish this alternative. This is partly due to the fact that the industry is actually experiencing a daunting interest from companies that will use the CO2 for PTX fuel. And many liters can be made of them.

While the Danish Energy Agency's forecasts are drawing for an annual biogas production ranging from 25 PJ in 2020 to 51 PJ in 2030, Biogas Denmark recommends that production rise up to 60 PJ at the entrance to the next decade. With such production, there will be over 2 million tonnes of biogenic CO2 available.

"With that amount of CO2, we will be able to absorb over 2 gigawatt electricity from wind and solar power by 2030. This corresponds to two-thirds of production from an energy island," says Frank Rosager, director of Biogas Denmark.

The figures come from calculations made in connection with 'Biogas Outlook 2021', which mainly adds to using the excess, biogenic CO2 for the production of electromethane using hydrogen. For the same reason, for example, Frank Rosager mentions biogas producer Nature Energy's ongoing project Efuel, which will present a new method for the production of electrometan locally at Biogas plants Midtfyn.

But if there are green PTX fuels, the hydrogen must also be green. And here we encounter another scarcity: Access to Green Power.

Both CCS and CCU
As you know, the energy islands are not built yet, so while we are waiting for the necessary capacity for large-scale electrolysis, Frank Rosager finds it likely that CO2 from biogas upgrade will initially find the CCS path for underwater stores in, for example, Norway.

»It is possible that we get a slightly strange course, where CO2 from biogas upgrade should first be used for CCS, since then CCU such as. PTX and then again CCS, ”says the director of Biogas Denmark. For the Climate Council there is also not an either or in terms of the use of the biogenic CO2 from, among other things, biogas plants. It must both be used to create negative emissions and be poured into the tank of internal combustion engines.

"Especially at this point, there are both and," says the Climate Council chairman, Peter Møllgaard.

However, with the limited amounts of biomass, the Climate Council proposes that as much transport as possible should be kept running on electricity or alternatively non-carbon-based PTX fuel such as hydrogen and ammonia, while only air traffic should be kept on the wings of biogenic carbon. And even then, the scarcity of biomass will set limits on how much we can restore the climate by storing biogenic CO2.

“In the long term, we need to do everything to reduce residual emissions from all sectors. Negative discharges cannot save us, ”says Peter Møllgaard.

Read more about biogas and CO2 on the next page
Facts storage of biogas-CO2 on the Finance Act

The first initiatives to store CO2 captured by upgrading biogas have been taken with the Finance Act for 2022. Here, DKK 2.5 billion has been allocated for projects that can create negative emissions over a support period of 8 years.

The funds can go to projects with plowing of bio -coal from pyrolysis or storage of CO2 from biogas upgrade or Direct Air Capture.

Awarded only one-third of the funds for storing biogas CO2, according to the Climate Council's 'Status Report 2022', the pool could lead to reductions of 0.25 million tonnes of CO2 equivalents as early as 2025 and 0.33 million tonnes five years later.

Title: Gaskrisen bremser ikke klimamål: Høj naturgaspris virker som en CO2-afgift
Full text:
Europe must set up approx. 400 GW VE a year from 2025 to 2035 to comply with the Paris Agreement. A higher gas price can have the same climate effect as a CO2 tax.

The Russian gas lines are slowing down slowly, the gas price explodes and the energy crisis rages in Europe.

Thus, the natural gas loses the role of 'the greener' alternative to coal and oil as we develop and roll out the green transition. Natural gas is a fossil fuel, but CO2 emissions are lower by burning than oil and coal.

But even though European countries are forced by Putin's hand on the gashans to lower their consumption, it is still possible for European countries to live up to their climate ambitions and comply with the Paris Agreement.

It shows a recently completed research project from Aarhus University.

The researchers have set up a model that shows how the energy consumption of European countries can be covered cheapest possible. The model uses existing technologies that can be produced and set up without the global warming exceeding the 2 degrees that are enrolled in the Paris Agreement.

And according to the researchers' model, it is still possible to comply with the Paris Agreement and at the same time meet European demand for energy, even if the gas supply is reduced.

At least that applies if the right political choice of renewable energy forms is taken.

"We must not waste time by making the wrong choices because of the challenges of the gas," says Gorm Bruun Andresen, an associate professor at Aarhus University and one of the researchers behind the model.

The gas crisis also causes a risk of more coal and falling climate ambitions in Europe.

"Of course, the current energy crisis is filling up very much right now, but in the long term, the green transition is a much bigger challenge."

Gas price has effect as CO2 tax
If the member states are to cut their natural gas consumption and at the same time live up to their climate ambitions, then a huge roll -out of renewable energy must be carried out throughout Europe, the researchers' model shows.

All in all, approx. 400 GW per years from 2025 to 2035. This is equivalent to building 200 plants the size of the offshore wind farm to be established in connection with the energy island of Bornholm in the Baltic Sea. Well to feel every single year.

It will result in a higher electricity bill for consumers. But the green transition will do so in any case.

Conversion to renewable energy on which the Paris Agreement is based will cause the electricity price to rise over the next 10-15 years. The difference is that without gas as a transitional technology, the price increase will take place already.

It may sound like a bit of a challenge for the democratically elected political leadership in the EU, but the researchers' model shows that the high gas price will help to drive the green transition in the areas - for example in private and in the companies - which do not would reschedule their energy consumption to meet the Paris Agreement, but because it can pay off.

A higher gas price will act as a form of CO2 tax that makes it more profitable to invest economically in renewable energy, carry out electrification in business and replace the household gas stove with heat pumps and district heating.

“Previously, you have invested in a transition phase with gas, and that plan you can not drive on for good reasons. Fortunately, there are some of the other things that we must also do to reach the finish that is accelerated by the crisis, ”says Gorm Bruun Andresen.

As an example, he points to the places in the industry where gas is used today for heating at high temperatures. Here, a higher gas price may act as motivation to replace modern elves, just as a CO2 tax would have done.

“Many of the green technologies are now the cheapest if you have to buy new ones. The problem is that you would prefer to avoid buying new as long as what you already have can still be used. The decision to change is now being accelerated by the fact that there is a high gas price, ”says Gorm Bruun Andresen.

Odd challenges
However, it varies greatly from country to country how easy it is to implement a green transition without gas. In Denmark, gas consumption is relatively low, and at the same time we are relatively far ahead with the electrification and setup of renewable energy.

Different it is in e.g. Germany. Here you are deeply dependent on the Russian gas, and the crisis has led, among other things, to reopening 10 coal -fired power plants.

“In our model, more coal is also used to cover the EU's energy consumption during the transition phase. But the higher CO2 emissions from coal compared to natural gas are then compensated by the large expansion of more green technology, ”says Gorm Bruun Andresen, adding that it is therefore necessary to accelerate the green transition further in the countries that open coal power plants .

“It is clear that more coal power is associated with a risk. There is a danger of ending up relaxing the climate ambitions, ”he warns.

High climate ambitions make it impossible to gas
As an extra detail, the researchers' model can be screwed to reflect a more ambitious climate policy. Thus, the model can also show a scenario where the temperature rise must be less than 1.5 degrees.

In this scenario, the gas crisis plays a much smaller role. To keep the temperature below 1.5 degrees, the gas had to be phased out by 2030, regardless of whether Russia had invaded Ukraine or not.

Title: Politikerne accepterer dundrende milliardunderskud på energiø
Full text:
Initially, the energy islands should only be built under the condition that the projects would be profitable. But now the ministry says the economy is probably not holding.

“We have agreed to run a risk in the preliminary investigations of DKK 10 billion. kroner. That's correct. "

This is how Carsten Kissmeyer corresponds to the Engineer, as he, as the Left's Climate and Energy Mayor, is asked why the Left for the energy summit between Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and a number of heads of state from other Northern European countries in Marienborg on Monday was co-signer on a new additional agreement on Energiø Bornholm , although new calculations from the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Supply suggests the project- Formerly a previous appointment - will cost a lot more money to establish and operate than previously assumed.

The calculations set out in a note that the Engineer has come into possession shows that only the project costs will run around DKK 10 billion. In addition, an extra socio -economic cost of two billion kroner.

The note concludes that the energy island is probably not profitable because the island will not be able to earn sufficient sums of sum home to the state through the sale of electricity.

“Our original approach that the green transition could carry itself, it is still our opinion that it will be able to do so. But that does not change that we are in a situation that is completely different than we did two years ago, ”says Kissmeyer.

Profitability was a condition
Positive economy - also called profitability - has been a political requirement from the beginning to establish the energy islands at all. It has so far been a red thread through all the political agreements.

The islands should only be built under the condition that the projects would be profitable. But now the ministry says the economy is probably not holding. This is what Marc Skov Jacobsen, senior economist at the think tank Kraka Advisory, tells the engineer's sister media Gridtech. .

Title: Biogas Danmark: Størst klimaeffekt når biogas-CO2 ender i et PtX-anlæg
Full text:
The biogas industry's industry organization has analyzed the climate effects by utilizing CO2 from biogas upgrade.

On an annual basis, more than half a million tonnes of CO2 is captured in Denmark while upgrading biogas to natural gas quality. And the figure could rise up to two million tonnes if biogas production is increased to 55 PJ in 2030.

The latter proposes the trade organization Biogas Denmark in the recently released report 'Biogas Outlook 2022'. Here, the climate effect is also examined by keeping this captured CO2.

As the Engineer has uncovered, the majority of the biogas CO2 today is derived to the atmosphere, but if the CO2 is instead sent to underground stocks at CCS or used as a carbon source for PTX production of fuels, there is a great potential to reduce the emissions of greenhouse gases.

Here, new calculations from Biogas Denmark show that at an annual biogas production of 55 PJ can be reduced annually by 1.8 million tonnes of CO2E by storage or between 2.5 and 1.3 million tonnes of CO2e when the production of electro-metan or electro respectively -Metanol.

At an annual production of 60 PJ Biogas, the reduction potential exceeds both storage and production of electro-metan respectively 2.1 million tonnes of CO2E and 2.8 million tonnes of CO2.

Electro-Metan has the greatest potential
According to Biogas Denmark, the greatest climate effect must thus be found by utilizing the captured upgrade CO2 to make electro-metan. Here, the CO2 is combined with hydrogen made under electrolysis using green power, with which the methane acts as a stock for storing electricity.

Such PTX production results in storing over 2 GW EL, or the equivalent of 'collecting 30 to 70 percent of the electricity capacity from an energy island in the hours when it blows maximum', as it sounds in the report .

Discussion of best use
In the report, however, Biogas Denmark has omitted to count on what they themselves identify as the most obvious use of the biogas CO2. Namely, to utilize it as a substitute for industrial CO2, which is today manufactured using natural gas.

At the same time, we are in a situation where neither energy islands have been built to fill the potential for PTX or matured underground stocks for CCS.

As the engineer has previously described, there is thus good reason to carefully consider where the CO2 from Biogas upgrade is best used.

Here, Biogas Denmark's director Frank Rosager has previously pointed in the same direction as the new report of the industry organization and named PTX as the best utilization of the CO2 in the long term.

Conversely, both the Climate Council chairman Peter Møllgaard and climate analyst in Concito Tobias Johan Sørensen sees really good opportunities for storing the biogas CO2, as this is a cheap alternative to the storage of CO2 captured from flue gases. However, the President of the Climate Council preferably sees the use of carbon in internal combustion engines limited to an absolute minimum.

Potential as well in Frozen Policy
Ultimately, the new report from Biogas Denmark emphasizes that there are climate benefits to be gained when utilizing the separated CO2, regardless of whether biogas production is being expanded to the industry's proposed 55 PJ in 2030 and 60 PJ in 2035 or holding the current line in a so -called frozen policy -top.

As a comparison to Biogas Denmark's own scenario, the trade organization is leaning on the Danish Energy Agency's climate status and projection 2022 (KF22), which projects a production of 51 PJ in 2030.

This results in reduction potentials of 1.5 million tonnes of CO2E for storage respectively, 2.0 million tonnes of CO2E for the production of electro-metan and 1.1 million tonnes of CO2E for the production of electro-metanol.

Title: Datacentre sænkes ned i havet: En undersøisk serverpark i spil ved energiøen i Nordsøen
Full text:
Later this year, the first commercial data center will be lowered underwater in the Pacific.

It will be more expensive to book space for your data in the cloud.

Tower-high electricity prices cause a number of data center owners to notify price increases, and most recently Microsoft and AWS have put the construction of new data centers in Europe on break. It is simply not profitable.

When Denmark is scheduled to open for the world's largest energy island in the North Sea, it may well be with one or more underwater data centers attached.

For while everyone is waiting for the delayed supply of the energy island, two consortia work to investigate possible data center solutions connected to the energy island. Nevertheless, a fiber and data infrastructure must be drawn so that both the energy island and the surrounding offshore wind farms are connected to the outside world.

"We can see that there is a growing need for server capacity for managing the wind farms, the electricity grid that will be balanced and the upcoming PTX systems," says Sofia Dinesen, Sustainability Director of GlobalConnect, which is part of the consortium with ATP and Ørsted in the tip, which wants to offer the establishment of the energy island in the North Sea.

Energy Island has room for commercial data center
When the infrastructure is in place anyway and there is access to cheap electricity from the offshore wind farms around the island, GlobalConnect suggests to establish a commercial data center in connection with the energy island.

»Such a solution will immediately be obvious for large hyper-scale operators who greatly demand green power. If the data center is placed on the energy island, it can be connected to the back of a meter, which gives a better price of the flow than is the case on land - for example in Jutland, which is just 80 kilometers from the energy island, ”says Sofia Dinesen.

Despite our modest geographical size, Denmark is a well-known face among the major hyper-scale companies such as Google, Facebook and Apple, all of which have placed large data centers on Danish soil.

»We are experiencing a great demand to be able to document co-imprint on the services and services we provide, both from public and private customers. We are working intensively to provide solutions to this - both here in the short run, but also in the longer term with new innovative solutions to, for example, the energy island of the North Sea, ”says Sofia Dinesen.

Right now, GlobalConnect is experiencing a great demand for green cloud solutions, and here a data center on the energy island can be the next generation.

»A lot of energy is wasted by cooling servers. Air is so far the best cooling method on land, but the circumstances of an energy island make it obvious to explore opportunities to use water for cooling, ”says Sofia Dinesen.

The second consortium, led by Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, has previously stated that Ramboll will explore the possibilities of establishing a commercial data center in connection with the energy island. However, neither CIP nor Ramboll have returned on the engineer's inquiry.

Although today there is no commercial data centers in operation underwater, the size of the project is an advantage, says GlobalConnect.

“It is quite natural that we also look at technical solutions for cooling with seawater, just as Microsoft has investigated. The island will only be ready in 2030, so there is time to develop and mature the technical solutions, ”says Sofia Dinesen.

Fiber cables should not be braided with power cables
Right now, all parties are awaiting the final offering from the state of the energy island, which is expected to come in 2023 after a series of delays.

Therefore, it is still unknown what specific requirements the state will make for fiber and data infrastructure for the island.

But it is not expected that they should be linked.

“We would rather not put fiber cables near energy cables because it requires a larger setup when crashing on energy cables, which is greater and requires more resources to maintain. If our fiber cable is torn over, we would need permission from the energy operators. So we expect to lie in the same area, but with 20 meters away, ”says Sofia Dinesen.

However, designing a data center requires some flexibility when you do not yet know about the dimensions and needs of the energy island.

“We have a slightly different modular design that can change over time. The design of the main island and small islands around is made as J-Tubes. It fits well with placing our network in an J-tube. Title: Ledelse kan forløse klimapotentialet
Full text:
It simply will not be possible to solve the climate crisis without the IT and technology sector. In digital solutions alone, according to the World Economic Forum, there is a CO2 reduction potential of 20 percent by 2050. Just as it has previously been the case in history, it is technological solutions that can lead us far along the way when we stand Facing big crises.

To release the huge climate potential will be the tech sector's big task in the coming years. But also great opportunity. For there are actors in both the public and private, who lack all sorts of types of climate solutions that can optimize, rethink, combine, streamline and accelerate and so on because they have to meet and reach their own climate goals very soon. 

How are you part of the solution?
It is my claim that almost all new technologies and digital solutions have a climate potential.

So any management in IT and tech must ask themselves: How can we help solve the climate challenge? Can our product help reduce CO2 for other sectors? Can it optimize processes? Can it rethink a problem? 

The development of video telephony was not originally intended as a climate solution, but today saves thousands of tons of CO2 (and time and money) annually through saved flights. GPS technology was also not intended as a climate solution, but can be used, among other things, for precision farming, which can significantly optimize food production.  

Management can redeem 
When, as a management in an IT or engineering company, you have strategically reconsidered your potential in a climate perspective, direction must be set. And here the management angle comes even more clearly into the picture. For things do not happen by themselves, and ineffective leadership should not be what delays results in a sector that is crucial for us to reach the goals. 

Climate potentials must be redeemed, coordinated, and humans must be kept to the fire. Whether these are large Energy Island projects where schedules must not be exceeded (simply for the sake of climate survival), or the conversions of small and large companies, where new technologies are being invested, new products are being developed and solutions are being tested through complex Innovation projects. Or it may be about value chains that need to be rethought radically. All this requires leadership that can redeem, smooth, and facilitate. So management is key. 

Management can create meetings
New climate solutions have to be found on the edges of the well -known industries (for example, where the digital sector meets agriculture or when residual products from a sector can be used in a completely different sector). Likewise, climate change often requires large and prolonged PPP (Public-Private-People) partnerships. 

Management must help ensure that different stakeholders can talk together. Each sector typically comes with different languages, worldview and interests. There will be dilemmas, misunderstandings, slides in schedules, etc. And here the arrow points again to the good management. 

Leadership can engage people
And not least, people are the component of the equation that is most often overlooked in major conversion projects. When management is fully inside a company's soul and redefines its DNA in a green direction, it must be ensured that the rest of the organization becomes part of the new understanding and direction. 

A new and increased focus on climate will create questions, confusion and perhaps even resistance among employees. They want to ask questions: What does it mean that my business has now set climate as overall goal? Does the changed tasks or new organization mean?

Here you start
The good climate leader in the IT and tech industry should ask itself: 

How can we help solve the climate crisis? Do we understand the full business potential? Make the climate analysis.
Do we have control of our own climate footprint? And how many reductions can we help make for other companies?
Are the employees on the new agenda? What about other stakeholders and outside world requirements (EU legislation etc.)? 
How do we best communicate our solution to the outside world? Do they know that we have a real solution? And are we sure we are not Greenwasher?
Climate management can be an exciting discipline that typically brings together a lot of management disciplines- change management, resource management, cultural and value management. And not least, it is perhaps the world's most important form of leadership as it helps to lift the most acute societal challenge we are facing.

Title: Tyskland truer dansk adgang til udenlandsk arbejdskraft: 'Helt oplagt at rykke på'

Title: Smeltevandsdal under havbunden: Nyt fund skaber tvivl om placering af energiø

The seabed in the North Sea can store problems for the artificial energy island in the North Sea, which will deliver 3 GW of offshore wind turbine power in 2033.

About 100 kilometers out in the North Sea, west of the West Jutland town of Thorsminde, the Danish Energy Agency has designated a favorable location for the artificial energy island, which will serve as a transmission stage for 3 GW offshore wind turbine power in 2033 and in the long term 10 GW.

But in the North Sea depth, one has encountered an obstacle. Studies of the underground show that there are about 100-170 meters below the seabed a sediment-filled valley, which is probably a remnant of the recent ice age. The valley crosses the entire area of ​​2.5 x 2.5 km that is done in preliminary studies.

Not all sediment layers in the valley have been clarified, and one of the two consortia that has shown interest in co -financing and building the energy island, the desired location discourages.

"The thick quaternary deposits in the Palee Channel pose a great risk to the construction work," writes the Vindø Consortium, which consists of the pension funds PFA and PensionDanmark and the energy company share, in a document to the Danish Energy Agency, which the Engineer has gained access to.

Vindø has hired a contractor and engineering team consisting of, among others, MT Højgaard and the Dutch construction company Boskalis, which makes excavations for the Fehmarn tunnel.

Ø becomes a minimum of 120,000 m2

There are also plans for there to be room for a power-to-x plant on the island. The island, the wind farms and the associated electricity infrastructure are estimated at DKK 210 billion. kroner.

“It can be compared to a fungus with water being squeezed out. At worst, stability fractures can happen, ”he explains.

“In geological times, there are a lot of rivers that have dug down, and in subsequent geological times they are filled with other material. What you are afraid of is that there are organic deposits that make the soil not very strong. You can only clarify that by doing studies. "

The canal under the seabed does not have to save on a headache.

It has not yet been decided whether the Danish Energy Agency will set aside money to examine the deeper unexplored sediment layers in the valley. And thus not whether the energy island should be placed in the field of 2.5 x 2.5 km.

The engineer has asked Mogens Hagelskær, Deputy Director of the Danish Energy Agency with the responsibility of the Energy Islands, whether it is the most likely location.

"It's the area we've been most aiming for, but I don't think you can say it's most likely," he replies.

Mogens Hagelskær points out that the final location will only be sealed when a contract is to be made with the private consortium that becomes co -owner and has to be responsible for the plant. Even after the contract, there may be small adjustments to the island location, he says.

Ultimately, the consortia in their final supply material can place the energy island, where they want, within a bounded area of ​​23 km2 in Danish waters, where low water depth has been identified.

More items are kept open

Title: Evida når frem til milliardgevinst på brintnet: 'Udokumenteret' og 'misvisende'
Full text:
A report on the socio-economic gain of building a pipe system for gastransport receives strong criticism from energy and economics experts.

These are harsh words that come from a number of Danish financial and energy experts in their assessment of a new report from the gas distribution company Evida on the socio-economic gains by building a pipe-based network for transporting hydrogen.

The report has been prepared by the consultancy Deloitte Economics, which states that the calculations are based on guidelines from the Danish authorities.

The report predicts that there will be a total net worth of DKK 16 billion if the network is built up as Evida has planned.

So why all the posture of hydrogen, pipes and social economy? After all, we have not even started to build the large PTX systems where the green hydrogen is to be produced?

The background is a broad agreement in the Folketing. It states that the necessary framework must be created for such a hydrogen network to be established. Because when the green electricity from wind turbines and solar cells begins to exceed electricity consumption and therefore hydrogen will be produced in large quantities, the hydrogen must be transported in pipes, in the same way that we today transport natural gas.

When there is a lot of hydrogen from the upcoming PTX plants, there must also be the opportunity to export hydrogen to Germany.

Politicians have to decide who should own the network. The election is between Evida owned by the Ministry of Finance and Energinet, which is owned by the Ministry of Energy and Supply.

Economic: Udocumented
Jan Bentzen, associate professor of economics at Aarhus University, believes that the calculations in the Deloitte report are largely based on assessments and quantifications of 'soft' values.

“If my students had handed it in as a task, then they were dumped. It is not just the results that are presented without any documentation or the possibility of calculating or evaluating reasonably. It is also the use of language that is in no way standard in such calculations, ”he says, pointing to mixes of words such as 'gain' and 'socio -economic net worth'.

Jan Bentzen says that socio -economic analyzes are very suitable for calculating the effects of major infrastructure projects in the long term - also 40 years in the future. But only if they include the specific effects in the calculations. For example, a bridge that replaces a ferry, or a natural gas network where the gas replaces another fuel.

"But the report is filled with 'assessments' of a wide range of soft effects that are far away from the hydrogen tube itself and which are impossible to quantify. For example, the value of 'expertise and know -how', which has a contemporary value of 4.7 billion, 'he says, calling the result' from the third reef in stormy weather '.

Professor: misleading
Brian Vad Mathiesen, a professor of energy planning at Aalborg University and, among other things, one of the researchers behind IDA's climate response 2045, calls it violently misleading to give such a bid for a net value when there is a lack of crucial knowledge.

This applies, for example, to experience with PTX plants that have not been erected yet, answer whether hydrogen should be produced on energy islands or on land, and the basic question of a national hydrogen network is needed at all.

"It's not because it can't be made a profit. But it cannot be proved with so many uncertainties, ”writes Brian Vad Mathiesen in an email to the Engineer.

Energian alytics: strange
Partner in EA Energy Analysis, Hans-Henrik Lindboe, calls it strange that Evida can find out to publish a report with such a decisive importance for an upcoming infrastructure project without publishing prerequisites and calculation methods.

"If you can't see how they actually arrived at their numbers, then the report doesn't matter," he says, and notes that Evida is a public -owned company that presents a positive number for an infrastructure project they like want money for.

"But they also have to give independent analysts the opportunity to go critically," he says, pointing out that a pipe network for hydrogen can easily prove to be a socio -economically good idea. The report just doesn't answer that question.

The engineer has asked Evida for background data for the report.

But Evida refers to Deloitte, who writes in an email that the economic and environmental data are covered by a declaration of confidentiality with Evida, but that Deloitte would like to ask for interviews and answer specific questions about assumptions and hypotheses leading to the results of cost -benefit analysis.

The Engineer has said no thanks to this, unless third parties - for example, the three experts who appear in this article - are given the opportunity to review the calculations.

Deloitte has subsequently, at the invitation of the Engineer, submitted some of the data that constitute the basis of calculation as well as detailed results. We have passed on to the experts.

But unfortunately, there is not much help to get in those figures, says Associate Professor of Economics Jan Bentzen:

“They just present some parameters and some results, without seeing how they are counted together. There is nothing that shows whether the model is correct and that we can thus rely on the results, ”says Jan Bentzen.

He claims that several parameters do not match the numbers usually used in socio -economic calculations. This applies, for example, to the discount rate and the net tax factor.

"It is embarrassing that Evida proposes investments for eight billion kroner without having the opportunity to review the calculations," he says.

Title: Kritik af EU-plan om at beskytte søkabler: 'Den tager ikke truslen fra Rusland alvorligt'
Full text:
The Commission's template plan for the protection of underwater cables is inadequate, according to a Danish expert in the field.

The EU Commission's new plan to monitor and protect underwater gas electricity and data cables is completely inadequate.

It does not diminish the threat against Europe's infrastructure, says the Danish professor of international relationships, Christian Bueger from the University of Copenhagen.

He specializes in threats to critical infrastructure on the seabed and wrote several reports on the subject, most recently to the European Parliament. 

In the wake of the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas tubes, the EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on October 5 presented a five-point plan whose only bid for increased surveillance is to make use of the existing ESA satellites.

But they don't make the big difference.

“Satellites are good if you know in advance what to look for. But you have to have ships, drones or other surveillance at sea to detect suspicious activity and to look down below sea level. As it is today, Europe is underwater blind, ”says Christian Bueger, who believes that we have overheard warnings for years.

In a report to the European Parliament in June, Christian Bueger and colleagues described how the EU has been aware of growing Russian submarine activity around underwater cables since 2015.

In 2017, EU received warnings from NATO that there was an unprecedented Russian activity around underwater cables.

It was also pointed out by Norway's intelligence service in a report at the start of last year.

NATO has also repeatedly warned that Russia has invested especially in ships and stealth-mini-submarines to destroy cables, as well as cut the cable to Crimea during the annexation in 2014.

We do not live up to our NATO responsibilities
The EU Commission's Fempunkt Plan contains - in addition to increased satellite monitoring - suggestions for a better cyber defense, as well as studies ('stress testing') of how vulnerable the infrastructure is in individual countries.

Another proposal is increased backup capacity as diesel generators and a strengthened collaboration with NATO and especially the United States.

However, the NATO articles show that precisely infrastructure is a national matter.

Member States themselves must be able to protect their infrastructure and be able to overcome attacks on it.

NATO calls it resilience and 'resilience is first and foremost a national responsibility', according to Article 3.

»Several countries do not live up to that principle, including Denmark. It only makes the challenge greater by base its green transition on an unprotected network of electricity cables for energy islands in the North Sea, ”says Christian Bueger.

Underwater cables can be sabotaged with an anchor
In the report to the European Commission, the researchers also point out that there is a big difference in how countries are trying to protect their cables.

Portugal and Spain, for example, have made it a military task to protect underwater data cables, while Denmark has outsourced that task to the industry.

"The EU has been very focused on the risk of cyber attacks, but closed his eyes to the physical cables on the seabed. We need to wake up and understand that we are currently seeing more signs that we are in a battle for physical infrastructure on land and at sea, ”says Christian Bueger.

In the report to the European Parliament, researchers have focused in particular on data cables on the seabed, which today contains 97 percent of all internet traffic and is the backbone of our data-driven society and economic transactions.

Still, the cables have "often been forgotten and have received minimal attention from the politicians," which has also left them repairing them to the industry, the report states. And that makes us extremely vulnerable.

In many places the cables are completely unprotected on the seabed and can be sabotaged with very simple means.

»You don't need advanced technology like mines or submarines at all. You can tear data cables by simply throwing the anchor and letting it pull the cable over. It is a simple task that can be performed with a civilian ship without arousing great attention, ”he says.

Need for more cable ships for repair
Today, repairs of data cables in large parts of Europe are covered by a joint agreement in the so-called Atlantic cable maintenance and repair agreement (ACMA) covering the Atlantic, including the North Sea.

ACMA has only two repair vessels in Europe, and that's not good enough, the criticism reads.

“In case we are exposed to sabotage in several places, we do not have ships at all to get the data cables going again. Therefore, we also recommend that the EU have its own repair vessels that are independent of the industry, as well as facilities with cables, ”says Christian Bueger.

Coordinated monitoring
At one point, however, there is a possibility that the EU can raise surveillance at sea relatively quickly.

Namely, the EU's new maritime security strategy proposes increased knowledge exchange across EU institutions and member states.

This is especially true of the three EU agencies the European Maritime Security Agency (EMSA), the EU Fishing Control Guard (EFCA) and the European Agency for Border and Coastal Guard (Frontex). They will be exchanging information for next year through the so-called CISE collaboration (Common Information Sharing Environment).

The work also includes military projects coordinated by the European Defense Agency, and here, according to Christian Bueger, it is obvious to impose on them monitoring infrastructure below sea level.

It does not happen today.

Title: Forsker angriber notat om a-kraft i Danmark: 7 løse påstande og faktuelle fejl
Full text:
"It seems that they have not understood the technology," says section manager at DTU Physics of note from 16 research colleagues who believe that nuclear power is a bad idea in Denmark.

A new note from 16 researchers, written to bring facts into the debate on nuclear power, is filled with misunderstandings, solve claims and factual errors.

This is the criticism of Bent Lauritzen, section manager at DTU Physics and one of the country's leading experts in the controversial energy technology, after reading 'Facts about nuclear power: input into a fact -based discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of nuclear power as part of the green transition In Denmark '.

“It seems that they have not understood the technology. I do not want to assess whether we should have nuclear power in Denmark, but at least one should examine it on a serious basis, and I do not think this is, ”he says.

He can point to strips of errors in the memo written by 16 researchers, including energy and economics professors from Aalborg University, University of Southern Denmark, DTU, University of Copenhagen and Aarhus University.

Here are a number of the most erroneous claims and assumptions that are far from an exhaustive list:

1. A-power involves a security risk
The note mentions that "wherever we place a nuclear power plant in Denmark, it will entail a security risk for the whole country".

However, Bent Lauritzen estimates that the last part of the statement is directly wrong.

"They draw a scare. Accidents happen, but at modern nuclear power plants it will not lead to a major disaster because they are being built with 'Core Catcher', double containment and passive safety systems that prevent the spread of radioactive material, 'he says.

Following the Fukushima accident in 2011, as referred to in the note, all reactors in Europe were exposed to a so-called stress test, which simulated total power outage and complete lack of the cooling to prevent a nucleus melting by constantly driving heat away from the core .

Not a single work was closed on the basis of the stress test, says Bent Lauritzen.

2. Atomic reactor not suitable for quick 'ramping'
Another misunderstanding is, according to Bent Lauritzen, that it is mentioned that a nuclear reactor with its steam turbine is not as suitable for quick 'ramping' as a 'purely technically much better' gasturbine that can run on green biogas in the future.

'Ramping' means that production is turned up or down depending on the fluctuating electricity production from wind turbines and solar cells.

“I don't know much about gas turbines, but the conclusion is wrong. Of course, you can make loading with nuclear power. These are all modern power plants designed to be able to. How can they make a report without being aware of it? '

3. Is based on uranium from Russia
Bent Lauritzen criticizes the claim in the note that "we hardly want to choose nuclear power technologies based on uranium from Russia".

First, fuel is produced to a reactor through several steps (extraction, conversion, enrichment and manufacture of final product).

Russia is included with all steps for part of the fuel we use in Europe, he explains.

“But European energy companies are aware that one has to get away from the dependence on Russian fuel technology. Therefore, we are working to increase conversion and enrichment capacity. It is already going on, and the time horizon to get away from Russian fuel is 2-3 years. "

4. A construction time of 15 years
Another criticism is the estimated time it takes to erect a nuclear power plant.

The memo is mentioned - based on the many years of delays on the three specific nuclear power projects; Olkiluoto 3 in Finland, Hinkley Point C in the UK and Flamanville 3 in France - that it takes 5-8 years to plan a new nuclear power plant, and that it takes about 15 years from the first shovel until it sends power out on the electricity grid.

»These are all EPR reactors (European Pressurized Reactor, ed.), And it's like using the IC4 trains as an example of future trains. These are works that were not completed, and when the construction of the EPR units began, you did not have the skills and experiences that you have today, ”says Bent Lauritzen.

If you look at the construction time for nuclear reactors built throughout the world in the period 1981-2020, construction time is an average of seven years.

For the six reactors that started up in 2021, it took an average of 7.1 years from the first spade to the production of electricity to the electricity grid, a new inventory from the World Nuclear Industry Status Report shows.

Three of the reactors that started electricity production last year are in China, which the researchers behind the new note will not include in their estimate of construction time because works erected in China (and India) place "other requirements for construction and security requirements than those, It applies in Western Europe '.

However, according to Bent Lauritzen, this is a wrong assumption.

“I am not aware that nuclear power plants in China and India are being built differently than elsewhere. In China, EPRs are also being built that are quite the same with them in France, so I am not convinced that the security requirements will be slackened. "

In addition, he refers to figures from the International Atomic Energy Agency, IAEA, which estimates that it will take 5-10 years from the political decision to the construction of a nuclear power plant.

"In high -end industrialized as Denmark we speak rather 5 years than 10 if the will is there," says Bent Lauritzen.

Bent Lauritzen also does not feel convinced that it is generally faster to build wind and solar energy when taking into account the capacity.

“If you look at the same production capacity, it may take even longer. The energy islands are first ready in the mid-2030s, so here we are talking about 10-15 years from the decision is made. "

5. The Prize estimates of the note
He also criticizes the price estimates on nuclear power that are included in the new note. Here, estimates from the International Energy Agency, IEA, are used, which is a reliable source.

But the problem is, according to Bent Lauritzen, that the researchers behind the memo put an 'extra cost' from the three Western European EPR reactors on, although this, according to him, must already be assumed to be included in the IEA's award estimates.

6. Capacity factor of 75 percent
In addition, he believes that it should have been taken into account that nuclear power plants can also be used for heat production, which significantly improves the economy of nuclear power.

In addition, IEA typically expects a capacity factor of 85 percent, but for EPRs and other new reactors, over 90 percent are expected.

»But the authors turn down to 75 percent. Here I miss a reason why they have done it, ”says Bent Lauritzen.

7. SMR works are not relevant
The note mentions small modular reactors briefly, but they are quickly depreciated as an option.

»Small modular reactors (SMR), which are under the development of, among other things, the Danish company Seaborg Technologies are not at present commercially available. International studies indicate that they will not be significantly cheaper than the current nuclear power technology. Against this background, there is nothing to suggest that the SMR works will be able to change the image we have described above. "

Bent Lauritzen is unaware of this.

"I don't understand why SEEABORG FOUND ADDRERATION reactor to write off SMRs when developing SMRs based on known technology," he says.

Although the first SMRs in the world probably cost the same as - or become more expensive - than conventional nuclear power, the whole driving force is just developing them just reducing the construction costs of factory making them with modules and simplified design, he explains.

Although Bent Lauritzen could continue to point out errors, he is pleased, after all, that nuclear power is now being debated in Denmark - both in the public and among researchers.

The engineer is working to get a comment on Bent Lauritzen's criticism from the 16 researchers behind the note.

Title: Risiko for en brintboble: En sulten branche investerer og tænker stort for tidligt
Full text:
It comes out with hydrogen projects in Denmark before we know how many we need and where to build.

In Denmark, there is a plan to produce hydrogen via Power-to-X, and you could almost hear a sigh of relief from the total Danish hydrogen industry, as the Danish Energy Agency's new analysis assumptions for 2022 were sent in consultation this fall.

The analysis assumptions are the official figures used by the Danish Energy Agency to plan the development of the energy system in Denmark until 2050.

In the previous data set from 2021, PTX was set to just 1 GW electrolysis capacity by 2030, but now you can read that 4.9 GW has been added in 2030 and up to 25 GW in 2050.

The planning figures from the board mean that many of the PTX projects that have already been announced can take the next step, because with the new figures there is also a signal of what we can expect from political initiatives in the coming years when This applies to legislation and possible support crowns

With 48 large and small projects lined up, there is plenty to address, and as the organization of the hydrogen industry director, Tejs Laustsen Jensen, says, the new figures have created a "huge appetite to get started".

This applies to both the specific PTX systems and the pipes that will connect them to consumers and may also be used for export.

Cheaper to use electricity directly
According to the hydrogen industry, today there is a total production capacity for hydrogen of 4.4 MW, and if we look at the overall capacity of all the 48 projects and coils the time until 2030, we are already far past the 4.9 GW, as the analysis assumptions Foreses: Probably closer to double.

However, critics - including the International NGO Bellona, ​​headquartered in Oslo - point out that the huge focus on hydrogen can end up with a regular bubble.

For the production of hydrogen will require huge amounts of electricity from renewable energy resulting in large energy losses.

Instead, it will be far cheaper, environmentally better and less complicated to use electricity directly in batteries to everything from cars, buses, aircraft and in heat pumps to heating.

For investors may find a construction site for a PTX plant and argue for a market as we have seen with projects in Esbjerg and Avedøre.

But state and authorities must be involved at a completely different level when a plan is to be laid out where and when new electricity grids need to be established in order to supply hydrogen production with energy and put pipes in the soil when the hydrogen is to be transported away.

In other words, it is a 'hen-egg-hen' situation about what should come first: the infrastructure that supports production, or production that gives rise to infrastructure, or the market to subside the product.

Future scenarios
Therefore, let's turn the time until 2030 and the port of Esbjerg.

Here, the international energy giant H2 Energy has built a PTX system of 1 GW electrolysis and an annual production capacity of 100,000 tonnes of green hydrogen.

The hydrogen can both be used by industries at the port and sent via a pipeline to Fredericia, where it supplies gas stations for heavy truck transport and the production of jetfuel at the local refinery.

We jump on to Skive, where GreenLab has been home to a small local network for hydrogen for a number of years.

But now you have started to lay pipes in the landscape, first to the natural gas warehouse in Lille Thorup and from there on to Aalborg. The plan is then that a connection will be built to the Esbjerg-Fredericia tube and from there to Germany.

The above could be the dream of the many, especially investors and developers of hydrogen solutions, who believe that a focus on hydrogen as an energy carrier is the future of a green Danish energy system.

They believe that many conditions are already suggesting that we are heading for a modern version of the 'hydrogen community'.

The idea is backed by the widely politically founded PTX strategy from the spring, the climate agreement from 2021, where 1.25 billion support crowns were allocated as well as several other major political agreements, which will, among other things, secure a quadrupling of the production of sun and wind energy on land as well as the possibility of five -folding of the production of wind power at sea.

On top of that comes the reinforcement and extension of the electricity grid.

Germany is in full swing
The development is in line with Germany in particular, where the planning of an infrastructure is fully planning that can handle hydrogen that must be used widely in the industry (steel and chemistry) and for transport.

For example, Germany today has 91 gas stations where cars, buses and trucks can refuel hydrogen. By 2030, it is expected that electrolysis capacity of 20-30 GW will be built in Germany alone.

The inspiration from the massive efforts of the abroad has been so well stuck that the international energy group H2Energy has threatened that if a hydrogen tube is not laid between Esbjerg and Fredericia when their 1 GW electrolysis egg in Esbjerg is ready in 2026, the plant will be dropped.

Conversely, it may turn out that there will be far more plants than planned if all advertised projects turn into something, maybe up to 13 GW by 2030, and it raises a crucial question about where and when the specific PTX systems should be in Operation in large scale, and at what rate to expand with a net of hydrogen tube. And not least what the hydrogen is to be used for.

In short, you risk investing too quickly and building some parts of the energy system that it later turns out that no need is needed.

Where to build?
Let's just specifically take the energy island in the North Sea: It has long been an open question whether all electricity from the offshore wind turbines is sent to land directly or whether PTX production is to be established on the island where it can supply ship traffic, alternatively, landed in land tube.

The disadvantage of PTX is that, unlike direct use of electricity in, for example, vehicles, for example, the technology results in a relatively large energy loss (about 30 percent for pure hydrogen production), and if they are far to sea, the Danish cities will lose a green source to district heating.

If, on the other hand, large PTX plants are built on land before the energy island has been established, there may be a need for the energy system to look completely different.

Then it can instead make sense to establish a network of hydrogen pipe on land, initially in Jutland, with connection to the warehouse in Lille Thorup. Precisely the route past a warehouse emphasizes how important that feature is in a well -functioning hydrogen network.

Far into the state, there are strong forces that will short -circuit considerations and look to get started.

One of the most eager players in the hydrogen ambition is the state -owned gas distribution company Evida.

Recently, it presented a report that described how a network of pipes dedicated to transporting hydrogen could be rolled out over Denmark over the next 40 years.

In the report, it was calculated that the socio -economic value of such a network would be about double up for every penny invested.

However, the report met strong criticism here in the Engineer and received dumping character by several economic and energy experts.

It was simply too early to put economy on large technical facilities, where there is not yet sufficient experience with the production technology and the market for hydrogen.

The other state -owned company, Energinet, is also on the field and has sparked several studies on hydrogen tubes. Among other things, a collaboration has begun with Energinet's German counterparty about a hydrogen connection between Denmark and Germany, which could possibly be ready by 2030.

The fact that hydrogen is to be transported in pipes, they have decided in Germany and the Netherlands.

Already, there are plans to convert natural gas pipes to hydrogen and build new pipes around the ruhr area and with connections to the Netherlands and Belgium.

German Environment Minister Robert Habeck has said that hydrogen will become one of the keys to the transformation of the German energy system. This applies, for example, to the large German steel industry, which has so far been 100 percent dependent on hydrogen produced from fossil fuels.

But if the German steel works are to use green hydrogen, a network of pipes will be needed, Robert Habeck stated after a visit to the German steel giant Thyssenkrupp.

In European cooperation between gast transmission companies, called EH2B, where Energinet also participates, it is proposed that most European countries be tied together by new hydrogen tubes as early as 2030. According to EH2B, by 2040 it should be possible to transport hydrogen around most of Europe by 2040 - In principle from Northern Sweden to Southern Spain and Greece.

And it might be needed. Under EU auspices, it is expected that by 2030 there will be 40 GW electrolysis capacity and the Commission has subsequently increased it to 100 GW, which corresponds to an annual production of 20 million tonnes of hydrogen.

What should the hydrogen be used for?
In Denmark we have no steelworks, but a large number of industries will also be able to utilize hydrogen, either directly, as it is today with fossil hydrogen on refineries, or converted to methane, ammonia or methanol.

It is, for example, the plan in Holstebro, where Everfuel, which is one of the Danish pioneers in the hydrogen industry, will establish a hydrogen hub. Here, hydrogen must be produced on a 100 MW electrolysis unit and then used in 'industrial processes and for transport'. The surplus heat must be used to heat Holstebro and thus phase out natural gas.

In the Danish Energy Agency's analysis prerequisites, there is also an indication of what we need to use the hydrogen for 2030. Just over half must be used directly as pure hydrogen. Here is a good bet that some part of the heavy transport will use hydrogen as a propellant. For example, it could be international truck transport through Denmark. But also a certain proportion of the country's buses, trains and passenger cars will potentially be able to run on hydrogen.

Production of Jetfuel will make up 20 percent, while the rest will be methanol, ammonia and methane. Title: Chefen for Vindø-projekt: »Jeg er jack of all trades, master of none«

Two jobs on hand

Toward a common target

"The result I am most proud of are the many hot calls and messages I got when I left the job as manager of the Tyra Generet-calls from employees who expressed genuine pride and joy of having been with," says he:

And there are good and very personal reasons why I needed to challenge myself in new ways, work in a new environment and be squeezed out of my comfort zone at all, which is an important driving force in my life. "

And the possibility of becoming head of establishing Denmark's largest construction project, which even spoke directly into the green agenda, was too tempting. He struck.

»The Vindø project is not only geared to deliver a significant part of the huge amount of green electricity that Denmark will need in the coming years.
