In a note sent by the ministry to the Folketing's Finance Committee on March 1 - and which was also mentioned in the Engineer in the spring - it appears that the government has previously had dialogues in the process of, among other things. Germany. But it is only dialogues, not real negotiations. 

Will formalize loose discussions
Nicolai Bech Kofoed does not know how far the parties have come in the negotiations. But they have hardly come further than to try to formalize the loose discussions the parties have so far had about everything from how the energy island's electricity can specifically help accelerate the green transition in Germany or be channeled into Power-to-X.

But if Denmark thinks it is more likely to land an agreement with Germany, why are they not doing it just here and now - why should it take so long?

“I think it's about uncertainty about whether one can get EU funds. It's about getting the gap up to profitability so that taxpayers don't have to pay unnecessarily, ”says Nicolai Bech Kofoed.

But that uncertainty also helped the negotiations stranded with Belgium, says Frederik Læsøe Nielsen, senior economist at Kraka Economics. Seen from his chair, Denmark is hardly going to win anything by changing its negotiating partner. It's more of a game for the gallery, the assessment says.

He has a hard time seeing what Germany should get out of covering a big hole in the business case for yet fictitious energy island when they have proven that they can earn great from landing areas for radial wind farms along the country's own coasts. In connection with a German offshore wind supply of a total of 7 GW, TotalenEnergies has offered the German state a total of DKK 15.4 billion. DKK for the right to set up 1 GW of offshore wind just west of Energiø Bornholm.

"You can wonder if the politicians are just trying to buy time and that they do not have political capital to put that project finally in the grave," says Frederik Læsøe Nielsen. 

He does not believe that the two countries will agree on an agreement that does not minus the bottom line for the Danes. It will continue to be a deficit business, he says.

"So the question is why they don't put the project in the grave instead of making an action that has the same effect as kicking an empty can down the road," he says. 

Tender despite billion deficits
Frederik Læsøe Nielsen and his colleagues have just released a report showing that the situation is not much better for Energiø Bornholm, which is scheduled to collect electricity from offshore wind parks near the sunshine lake from about 2033.


Here, the Danish Energy Agency estimates that the project requires DKK 31.5 billion. DKK in state aid, of which politicians will only cover the DKK 17.6 billion. kroner. They will not cover the $ 14 billion kroner, as the Board expects it will require in state aid to build the wind turbines. 

"In the report, we sharply criticize the previous process and the one we look into. It is not least the case that the civil service has already started a tender of the project for Energiø Bornholm, despite their own officials not believing that The project can be realized with the funds allocated, ”says Frederik Læsøe Nielsen.

The problem with that model is that politicians will only get a clear picture of whether the project is realizable after the last partial supply is completed. It is only here that one finds out whether the project exceeds the deposited state aid ceiling.

“It is forcing politicians to continuously enter into contracts with some private companies to perform the tasks, even if it is still uncertain whether it will happen. And those contracts are obviously not free to tear over again, ”he says.

"So our criticism of the forward -looking process is, in fact, also that the politicians have set us up to fail with very likely, and they have released the reins and let this play out in such a disaster in slow motion."

Title: Havne udvides uden fakta om miljøpåvirkning: »Det er meget ærgerligt«
Full text:
The Danish ports are getting bigger and bigger, but the real environmental impact of the many port extensions is uncertain. The solution is already available, researcher points out.

All the way around the Danish coasts, the Danish ports are in a rapid development. PTX adventure, CO2 capture and import increase requires larger ports. But when ports are built in Denmark, it is often with lack of illumination of the consequences.

Lack of illumination of environmental damage as a result of clapping and influencing mussel farming were some of the points in the environmental assessment of the port extension in Aarhus, which caused the project to encounter land when the Plank Complaints Board in May put a thick line under the need for a more thorough environmental assessment as the board rejected Aarhus Municipality's local plan and thus slowed down the large expansion of the Port of Aarhus.

The municipality ended up becoming its own runway man, as it was precisely an inadequate environmental assessment, which ultimately caused the Board of Appeal to pull the plug on the project. 

The project was subsequently dropped. But the crumpled architectural drawings and the local plan in the Recycle Bin at the City Hall in Aarhus are not alone as testimony to extensive environmental impacts in a port expansion.

According to a number of researchers with whom Ecotech has spoken, the fallible environmental assessment of the Port of Aarhus is only one in the series of careless environmental assessments of port projects.

It is not only the city of smiles that has dreamed of getting a new, larger waterfront. Just take the expansion of the harbor in the North Zealand coastal town of Hornbæk, which has previously been described in Ecotech. Here the consequences for local wildlife become clear. Because even though the environmental assessment says that construction work and the increased boat traffic as well as the noise from this will not have any significance for the Annex IV protected guinea pig, the critics tell another story.

And they are backed by scientists who believe it will have a great negative impact on the local stock of guinea pigs. Already, life is beaten below the surface of the Danish waters with oxygen depletion, birth shortages and to end up as a by -catch of fishing. In this way, port extensions become another violent press factor.

To that list you can also add Odense Harbor, where nature is like in the other two examples can become a stone in the shoe. In Kerteminde Municipality close to Odense, the planning process has just resumed, despite the many unanswered environmental issues.

If you extend the list of active port expansion projects at all, it suddenly becomes long. In 2017, Dansk Industri estimated that in the period between 2015 and 2020, Denmark would get about five million m2 of new port area. 

The big power-to-x adventure in the North Sea must be anchored in Esbjerg, which must be equipped for it. Right up north on the same coast, Hirtshals Harbor must be expanded significantly to be able to fill the role of hotspot for shipping CO2 for storage below sea level. 

And several of the other traditional port cities, such as Fredericia, Vordingborg and Frederikshavn, have also had projects approved by the Danish Transport Agency. 

One of the critics is Jesper Andersen, head of research at the Norwegian Institute of Water Research in Oslo, Niva. He sees the Port of Aarhus as an example of a trend in the consulting engineers' calculations, which do not take into account how several different environmental factors affect each other - also called the cumulative effects.

"If you made data and tool -based EIAs on total effects, looking at clapping and raw material recovery, or whatever else, you would get some completely different conclusions and effects would be much, much greater," he says.

Despite the many, very large, planned port extensions, you really know very little about the environmental impact of the projects, points out Jon C. Svendsen, a senior researcher at DTU Aqua.

“When doing a study of what a port may be going to get from biological effects, it is relatively simple studies. In Denmark, very rarely long -term effects of port expansions are documented. The biological effects that presumably occur in the years after a port expansion or construction are overlooked, for example in relation to the fish in the sea, ”he says.

The sea plays the starring role in Roman tragedy
Despite the lack of knowledge base, it is clear that the Danish waters are pressed. Port extensions are not the largest press factor - but one of many. 

If you take nutrients, environmentally hazardous substances, fishing, plants, sailing, raw material recovery plus new press factors such as microplastics, non-resident species and noise and put it together with climate change, a really bad picture is emerging for the state of the sea.

In English, it is called Death by a Thousand Cuts (translated: Death of a thousand stabbing) and, among other things, refers to Julius Caesar's death, where the senators changed to stick Caesar in the back. 

Just as a single senator could not be held responsible for the emperor's murder, so does port extensions. But they still have blood on their hands:

“The same is done with the Danish waters. There are so many who give it blow and punch. The Danish waters get worse and worse. Then even a small wind farm and a small port expansion can pull the condition in a negative direction, ”notes Jesper Andersen, who has helped to investigate the press factors in the Danish waters. And it does not appear that the bleeding will stop tentatively:

All the indicators show that nature and environmental conditions in 2030 and 2050 will have it worse than in 2020.

According to Jesper Andersen, this is partly due to insufficient use of data and tool -based methods in the environmental assessment reports of port extensions. It hides the overall environmental effects of the plants.

You also do not know exactly which - and how many - knives the many port extensions press into the back of the emperor. Jon C. Svendsen points out that there is a lack of scientific studies of biodiversity in and around ports before and after port extensions or newly constructed ports in Denmark.

"It's a possible effect we have a pretty bad understanding of," he says.

Instead, he suggests that more thorough and long -lasting post -port extensions should be done and the results of the environmental impact scientifically.

"You should not do it half a year later, because there is the colonization of port walls and other things not finished. You can guess with the existing knowledge, but until it is documented in the real world, it is only guesswork, ”he says.

'Danish style'
When preparing an environmental assessment report for, for example, port extensions, the cumulative effects are all too often written in 'Danish style', as you know from school time, explains Jesper Andersen. The consulting engineers use too many words and descriptions, but too few numbers and calculations.

When environmental assessments are prepared, data and tools are not sufficiently used to elucidate how, for example, noise, raw material extraction and increased traffic are affecting each other now and for several years in the future - also called the cumulative effects - he points out. 

“You have not really assessed the cumulative or total effects in any of these projects. It's very unfortunate, because we have super good data and the right tools to make the calculations, ”he says.

“The fact that you make a single port expansion or artificial island somewhere goes in the big picture. But if you take the sum of port extensions, bridge connections, energy islands and wind parks and the like, it is a huge impact that comes on top of the shit, primarily from a large area -intensive profession we already have, ”says Jesper Andersen with reference to the agricultural press factor.

Many of the tools and data on which the consulting engineers could use are already publicly available in, for example, the research project Økomar, which Jesper Andersen himself co -authored.

By using tool -based calculations to the cumulative effects, according to Jesper Andersen, it would also be possible to calculate the required size of nature restoration or compensation nature for the damaged nature during the plant. Such calculations could be made from half to all years, he believes.

The monkey lives with the authorities
The Association of Consulting Engineers (Free) has not wanted to interview. 

“In FREE, we have nothing to do with what specific data or methods our member companies use in the work with EIAs. It's up to the companies themselves, ”the association writes in a response.

At the same time, the association refers to a debate post in Zealand news from last year, where the director of the association defends the quality of environmental assessments in, for example, the construction of Lynetteholmen. 

The director Henrik Garver refers to the post that there will of course be consequences that cannot be excluded and that one can always set up 'worst-case scenarios'. 

But in the end, it is the authorities who need to assess and approve whether the environmental assessment is in order.

The consulting engineering company DHI, which makes environmental assessments, sees opportunities for environmental surveys in the future to be strengthened by haven's infrastructure projects if the tender criteria are changed, they write to the Engineer/Ecotech.

»We have conducted several studies on cumulative environmental effects in Germany and the USA and are also beginning to see a growing demand among our Danish customers. There is no doubt that in some cases environmental studies in Danish haven infrastructure projects could also be further strengthened with data -supported illumination of the cumulative effects. However, it requires the tender criteria not only to the price, ”says Nicholas Grunnet, vice president of the Marine & Coastal business - Nordic & Central Europe in DHI in a written response.

How does life come in the harbor?
Jon C. Svendsen, together with other researchers in an EU-funded project to bring biodiversity back into the port water. It must be done by simple optimization of the spun walls, but to understand the importance of the spun walls, it is important to understand the life cycle of different fish species.

In many fish species, the tiny fish need places to hide. Ideal hiding places for some fish species are mussel reefs, stone reefs and eelgrass in shallow areas out to 3-4 meters. 

But both eelgrass and mussel reef are in decline in many places. 

Similarly, stone fishermen have removed millions of boulders-and thus stone reefs-from Danish sea areas for at least 100-200 years. When you connect it with a port area, there is not much low tide left, as the fish at one point hits a port wall at a water depth about 3-4 meters.

"This means that there is usually everything else just loss of habitats when you build a port," explains Jon C. Svendsen.

The idea of ​​the project is to find a design and material on the spun walls that are more beneficial to biodiversity than the current concrete blocks. The hope is that it will be easier for organisms to settle on the special spun walls and thus benefit fish and crabs.

The preliminary results indicate that there is a tendency for the type 'Mangrove Seawall' compared to traditional spun wall. 

“It is a relatively good result because it indicates that there are opportunities to do something. This indicates that the actual design of the port wall plays a role, ”says Jon Svendsen, pointing out that there are, however, preliminary results.

Title: Synspunkt: Tidligere gasdirektør i Energinet: Brintkrise og udskudt grøn energi – er vi modige nok?
Outlet: Ingeniøren, Torben Brabo, President, Gas Infrastructure Europe
Full text:
The climate crisis has been pushing us for more than ten years. Before then, the political focus was on security of supply and markets. The situation today - with three contemporary crises - requires that the political dimensions be more than more. But are we brave enough?

We are on the way with the energy system of the future - less overall energy consumption - more ve - more electricity; But also complete conversion of the heat and transport sectors; and the overall industry.

What should we do? We don't have all the answers? But how have we really built the energy system we have today? What do other countries do?

In recent weeks' critical announcements of delayed hydrogen tubes in Denmark, Blue Hydrogen Canceled from Norway, Big Majors (Oil Companies) have renewed the desire for fossil fuels and shoots investments in VE, in general there is a lack of investment in VE and Efuels - we fall behind, and The Commission clearly raises a desire for more focus on payability for the competitive industry, etc. etc. All this made me think back ... 

Since the oil crises in the 1970s-80s we have in Denmark in) had "frameworks" and "tools" and "actors" (originating from legislation), II) that together created the necessary technology/infrastructure security and stability; III) so that financing could be found; IV) So the production of energy happened/changed, and v) consumers (probably) chose the new solutions that provided low -paid unit prices. This has given us a stable development framework for the past 40 years. 

Of course there were bumps on the road, but let's just look at what we really did:

From 1975-1985, Denmark:

We created the Danish Energy Agency (legislation on energy plans, action plans)
We created private DUC with AP Møller to produce (together with global American co -owners)
We created state DONG (now Ørsted) that built the infrastructure from the platforms in the North Sea up to municipal and borders (Sørør, transmission and stock)
We created five municipal distribution network companies (and gave them a financial framework that secured them)
We made municipal heating plans, with community analysis for which consumers should have district heating and gas; and who shouldn't
We secured the obligation to connect so that municipalities could force industry/citizens to new heat sources within 7 years
We made more subsidies and support systems
We succeeded!

There was probably no one who had the overall overview, but there were many sensible actions; There everyone worked in the same good direction and who supported each other. State's earnings have been 400-575 billion. DKK in 1980-2020 for "The Adventure in Nordøsen". We can do that again. But are we brave enough?

Personally, I mean we do enough or what we do do not have the desired effect. My secondary point is that we cannot conclude that we are not doing enough. At least not conclude at present, as it seems to me that there are tools, initiatives, collaborations, political superstructures, etc., which we have not yet looked at. 

So it's too early to say "stop".

This week, Germany has just approved their hydrogen nucleus (hydrogen backbone or wasserstof kern Netz). For most countries and companies in the EU, this means that you can now lean on German development. 

If one should consider actions that, like the "old" political frameworks, but devised in the present, then it could be:

Intergovernmental agreements between Denmark and neighbors, ensuring an overview of (large parts of) value chain (and risk sharing) across borders. Ensures that Danish (green) molecules have a paying customer;
that Denmark seeks/ensures concurrency in these decisions across borders; It has not been tried in this scale before, but should there be a time, then it is now; 
The state participates more actively with either infrastructure (such as DONG in 1980) or co -ownership (such as the North Sea Fund 2005) or expected co -ownership in Energiø (2021); 
Parallel to clarification about where and how hydrogen/Efuels can/should be used? a) Would it make sense to define geographical areas where natural gas should give way to electrification, and perhaps opposite in other areas where biogas goes to the industry provides a logical starting point to continue with gas for households, b) Include where gas or hydrogen can be used for peak load of electricity generation, or production of aircraft or ship fuel; 
The infrastructure can be recycled so that there is a greater logistical exercise in changing the energy system while the North Sea Natural Gas (from DK or N) is produced and sold, and the biogas volumes are increased on the web and hydrogen takes over part of the infrastructure and CO2 is considered if sensibly and man Converts and ensures storage capacity. These are the same considerations that the other northwestern European countries are sitting. 
Maybe we should work specifically with them, the Esbjerg / Ostende countries (the countries with the large North Sea wind potential), since we are in the same boat as them. Similarly, there are "relevant regions" elsewhere in the EU.
One could also expand the regional energy infrastructure plans from electricity and gas (and hydrogen) to be total energy plans for all the energy berries (in a plan); Or you could take North Sea Wind Power Hub (Holland and Denmark with Energinet today) and expand with other countries. 
There is not a "silver bulged" solution or only one way forward. On all our options and decisions there are several choices. Let me give a few additional examples where I focus on the role of the state: 

A) The state as the central dominant actor (reminiscent of what we did in the 1970-80s) but is also the role that many Eastern European countries have given the state in recent years in relation to energy supply (purchase of energy) or securing new/expanded infrastructure (building of LNG/FSRU) or regulation (where maximum prices are introduced). Also in Germany. This model is not durable in the long run - for a whole sector - there are also too many commercial players, which he has the money and competencies - they need to be activated - perhaps through private -public partnerships. 

E) At the other end of the scale, one can imagine that the state is not taking any role (in a country) but only does EU legislation and markets follow with neighbors, with their many commercial players. Crises will arise and problems will come that cause benefits of benefits to rise, consumption will decrease, providing incentive to invest, which collectively ensures a larger supply and vups over time disappear the crisis/problems. This model is assessed by most to take too long; And with the climate crisis, we don't have that much time to give. We also have a political apparatus in the EU that, after Covid, energy crises and war in Ukraine, has developed a discipline where you respond much faster than before to problems. It is also seen in the United States (first with the support of fossil oil/gas (2021) and afterwards the Green IRA (2022)). 

The two models A and E are extremes, so the truth is probably between these. How can we create a design and regulation that together gives us (in the region) the best value creation?

Like in the 1990s, when we went ahead with the Nordic electricity market, and as we did in the 2000s and were among the leading (northwestern European) markets for gas (Model C), maybe by 2025-2035 we can take the driver's jersey again with the northwestern European neighbors and create the framework for an internal regional energy system. 

Where more fuels and energy carriers are perceived in parallel, technology neutral, where they relieve and compliment each other, ensure scale growth and low unit costs for both energy and infrastructure and storage. But that the state involvement is rethought (both academically but also) across borders. 

The role of the state must be dosed just enough for risks to fall so that private actors invest. Justified by the transformative challenges of the day is greater than the individual country can handle. However, with minor exceptions, of course Germany can take national steps that have since has a regional or European effect. 

Personally, I mean that you have to assess and analyze a lot, broadly, so that you have an overall impression of the change you want - the effects of the measures you are looking for - expected risks and benefits. 

Part of the debate today in Denmark is far more concrete, arguing for/against 'wind' or 'energy island' or 'hydrogen tube'. Or "What new consumers should subside the hydrogen?". You lose overview and contexts. 

The point is that all the parts are connected; And the solutions create the most value the more integrated they are. It's complex. 

We could ask wise people to help. Maybe CSEI (at CBS/Denmark) or FSR (in Italy) has just been formed for the purpose of analyzing and guidance of the 'big' questions that our societies must have solved. Other ideas?

Title: Økonomien vakler under milliardprojekt: Kappet forbindelse til Sjælland skal redde Energiø Bornholm

The government is considering new solutions for Energiø Bornholm in the light of rising costs and questionable economy. Scenarios without cable to Zealand or with extra connections to Germany and Poland are on the table, and the future of the project balances on a knife egg.

The hour of the decision is fast approaching Energiø Bornholm, which will harvest electricity from offshore wind turbines in the Baltic Sea and distribute it to Denmark and Germany. The economy is seriously faltering under the billion -dollar project, and by December 5, the government will have to decide whether the entire enterprise should live or die. 

Otherwise, the state energy company Energinet cannot give the bidders of the island's electricity infrastructure answers whether the project will turn into something before the end of January. 

The Ministry of Climate, Energy and Supply and the Danish Energy Agency are currently busy counting on whether the project can pay off.

The new calculations are behind closed doors, but sources close to the course tell the Engineer that the civil service still has difficulty getting society's gains and costs to go up. Other scenarios in games
One of the scenarios is about building Energiø Bornholm without the fiercely expensive cable to Zealand. Zealand lacks electricity
Making the calculations is far from a routine task, as a lot has happened since the ministry and board last looked at the matter. E.g. But where the assessments of the winnings are based on assumptions, it is certain that both Energinet and the private bidders in a little while need a lot of billions of dollars to realize the project.

The anger is smashing in Berlin

“The government has not really been explained to the Germans how many Danes are actually skeptical of Energiø Bornholm. Therefore, the Germans have in good faith started preparing cables and everything else, ”says Finn Lauritzen, and continues:

“Since cables and equipment are already in the mold, the Germans' anger may well be felt and felt if the Danes end up shutting down the project. Here, the relationship with the Danish government already bears the impression that Denmark did not hold what it promised in relation to establishing a hydrogen tube for Germany. "

Radial offshore wind costs a fraction

“Our point of view is that taxpayers don't have to pour so much money into it. It makes no sense no matter what Energinet has come to promise the Germans. For the same money you could get much further by building radial offshore winds elsewhere, such as at Hesselø and Kriegers Flak, ”says Finn Lauritzen, who estimates that the two wind farms will be able to be built for just 2-3 billion kroner.

"That being said, the government may well try to soak its head to see if it is possible to find an alternative concept that does not cost the box - for the sake of European solidarity in terms of succeeding with it green transition. "
